<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:ntk_parameterization}
For input dimension $d_0$, output dimension $d_2$, and width $d_1$, let
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbf u(\mathbf x;\theta)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}
 \sigma(\mathbf w_m^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b_m)\mathbf a_m,\\
 \boldsymbol\xi_m&=(\mathbf w_m,b_m),\qquad
 \theta_m=(\boldsymbol\xi_m,\mathbf a_m),\\
 \theta&=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{d_1})\in\mathbb R^{d_1d_\theta},
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eqn:network_main}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is the scalar activation,
$\mathbf w_m\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, $b_m\in\mathbb R$,
$\mathbf a_m\in\mathbb R^{d_2}$, $d_\theta=d_0+d_2+1$, and $\gamma\geq0$.
With the ridge functions
$\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}=\mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)$
of a neuron $\boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b)$ in output $q\in[d_2]$,
$\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)=d_1^{-1/2}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}
a_{m,q}\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi_m,q}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:pde}
\label{def:linear_pde}
\label{def:scalar_collocation_constraints}
After decomposing every vector-valued PDE, initial condition, and boundary
condition into scalar rows, each constraint $i\in[N]$ is a linear observation
of $\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)$ with a loss scale $s_i>0$, of one of three types.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \emph{Strong-form pointwise.} For $\mathbf x_i\in\overline\Omega$,
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 P_i(\theta)&=s_i(\mathcal A_i\mathbf u)(\mathbf x_i;\theta),\qquad
 (\mathcal A_i\mathbf u)(\mathbf x)
 =\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}(\mathcal A_{iq}u_q)(\mathbf x),\\
 (\mathcal A_{iq}v)(\mathbf x)
 &=\sum_{\alpha\in I_{iq}}
 a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x)\,\partial^\alpha v(\mathbf x),
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eqn:scalar_constraint_main}
\end{equation}
where every \(I_{iq}\subset\mathbb N_0^{d_0}\) is finite and the
coefficients are finite at $\mathbf x_i$; Dirichlet, Neumann, Robin, mixed,
and variable-coefficient conditions all have this form.
\item \emph{Weak-form functional.}
$P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))$ with
$\lambda_i(f)=s_i a_i(f,v_i)$, where $\mathcal X$ is a trial space
containing the candidate solutions, $\mathcal V_i$ is normed,
$a_i:\mathcal X\times\mathcal V_i\to\mathbb R$ is a continuous bilinear map,
and $v_i\in\mathcal V_i$ is a fixed test function.
\item \emph{Finite-measure nonlocal.}
$P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))$ with
$\lambda_i(f)=s_i\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int_D f_q\,d\nu_{iq}$ for a compact
$D\subseteq\overline\Omega$ and finite signed regular Borel measures
$\nu_{iq}$ on $D$.
\end{enumerate}
The scale $s_i$ carries the loss normalization, for example
$s_i=N_r^{-1/2}$ for a group of $N_r$ residual rows, and all three types
enter the same loss and tangent Gram matrix.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:pinn_loss}
\label{def:ntk}
Let $\mathbf v_P(\theta)=(P_i(\theta))_{i=1}^N$. If $y_i$ denotes the unscaled
target for row $i$, set $[\mathbf v_T]_i=s_i y_i$, so predictions and targets
use the same row scaling. Define
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbf r(\theta)&=\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta),
 &\mathcal L(\theta)&=\|\mathbf r(\theta)\|_2^2,\\
 [\mathbf J(\theta)]_{i,:}&=\nabla_\theta P_i(\theta)^\top,
 &i&\in[N],\\
 \mathbf K(\theta)&=\mathbf J(\theta)\mathbf J(\theta)^\top.
\end{aligned}
 \label{eqn:loss_kernel_main}
\end{equation}
Here $\mathbf J(\theta)\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_1d_\theta}$. We write
$\mathbf K_{(k)}=\mathbf K(\theta_{(k)})$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:gradient_descent}
For a step size $\eta>0$,
\begin{equation*}
 \theta_{(k+1)}=\theta_{(k)}-\eta\nabla_\theta\mathcal L(\theta_{(k)}).
\end{equation*}
We abbreviate $\mathbf r_{(k)}=\mathbf r(\theta_{(k)})$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{assump:main}
The vectors $\theta_{m,(0)}$ are i.i.d.\ from a width-independent,
compactly supported law $\mu$. The constraint design and target are fixed
before initialization or sampled independently of it; in the latter case all
probability statements are conditional on their realization. Let $\mu_h$
denote the $\boldsymbol\xi$-marginal of $\mu$.
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- assumption-2: body_md -->
\label{assump:pde_classes}
The fixed finite family of linear rows satisfies the clauses for one of the
following classes. A subscript ``reg'' marks sufficient regularity for
population-NTK existence and GD; ``pd'' marks the additional feature richness
used for the exact positive-definiteness criterion.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item[\textup{(\(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}\))}]
The rows are of type (i) in~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, with largest order
$r_{\max}<\infty$, and $\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{r_{\max}+1,1}(\mathbb R)$.
\item[\textup{(\(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}\))}]
In addition, $\sigma$ is real analytic and nonpolynomial, $\gamma>0$, and
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$.
\item[\textup{(\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}\))}]
The rows are of type (ii) in~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, the trial space
$\mathcal X$ is a real Banach space of $\mathbb R^{d_2}$-valued functions
embedded continuously in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})$,
so that $\mathcal X$-valued derivatives and limits may be computed pointwise,
and every loss-scaled row $\lambda_i$ belongs to $\mathcal X^*$.
The one-neuron map
$\mathcal G(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}a_q\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$
is twice continuously Fr\'echet differentiable into $\mathcal X$ on an open
neighborhood of every fixed parameter tube generated by $\operatorname{supp}\mu$.
\item[\textup{(\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}\))}]
In addition, $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$, every
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$ is real analytic into
$\mathcal X$, and
\begin{equation*}
 \overline{\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}:
 \boldsymbol\xi\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1},\ q\in[d_2]\}}^{\mathcal X}
 =\mathcal X.
\end{equation*}
\item[\textup{(\(\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}\))}]
The rows are of type (iii) in~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, and
$\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^2(\mathbb R)$.
\item[\textup{(\(\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}\))}]
In addition, $\sigma$ is real analytic and nonpolynomial, $\gamma>0$, and
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$.
\end{enumerate}
Each ``pd'' label denotes its displayed condition together with the
corresponding ``reg'' clause; the bias-free case $\gamma=0$ admitted by
\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} is used only in the appendix, chiefly for the
counterexamples of \Cref{sec:hypothesis_sharpness}. Row independence is not
assumed here: it is the design-side certificate below. Conditional
output-weight centering is imposed only for GD.
<!-- end assumption-2 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:positive_definiteness_certificate}
For a fixed loss-scaled row design, a \emph{positive-definiteness certificate}
is an exact proof that $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$. By
\cref{eqn:block_pd_certificate_bound}, it suffices to prove either
$\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\succ0$ or
$\mathbf K_{\mathrm{hid}}^\infty\succ0$; the other block need not be checked.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:limiting_ntk_rank}
Under~\Cref{assump:main} and clause
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes},
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ exists and
$\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$. If clause
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ also holds, then
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 &=\left\{\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N:
 \sum_{i\in I_{\mathbf x}}c_i\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)=\mathbf0
 \ \forall\mathbf x\in\mathcal S\right\},\\
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 &=\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}
 \dim\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x):i\in I_{\mathbf x}\}.
\end{aligned}
 \label{eqn:exact_dntk_rank}
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ if and only if every
local family $\{\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x):i\in I_{\mathbf x}\}$ is linearly
independent.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:functional_ntk_rank}
Under~\Cref{assump:main} and clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes},
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ exists and
$\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$. If clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ also holds, then
\begin{equation*}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\ker\mathcal R_\lambda,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\operatorname{rank}\mathcal R_\lambda
 =\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\}.
\end{equation*}
Thus $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ if and only if
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N$ are linearly independent in $\mathcal X^*$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank}
Under~\Cref{assump:main} and clause $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes},
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ exists and
$\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$. If clause
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$ also holds, then
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\ker\mathcal R_\nu,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\operatorname{rank}\mathcal R_\nu
 =\dim\operatorname{span}\left\{
 \bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_1,\ldots,\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_N\right\}.
 \label{eqn:nonlocal_rank_main}
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ if and only if
$\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_1,\ldots,\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_N$ are linearly independent.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} under $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$,
respectively \Cref{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity} under
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$, verifies the abstract row bounds, so
\Cref{thm:linearNTK} gives existence and convergence. The nullspace follows
from \Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity}, respectively from
\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity} applied to the combined residual and
boundary tuples.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:local_row_regularity}
Fix $R>0$. The rows satisfy $(\mathsf G_R)$ if there are width-independent
constants $A_{0,i},B_i,L_i<\infty$ such that, for every $z_0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$
and all $z,z'\in\overline{\mathbb B}_R(z_0)$,
\begin{equation}
 |h_i(z_0)|\leq A_{0,i},\qquad
 \|\nabla h_i(z)\|_2\leq B_i,\qquad
 \|\nabla h_i(z)-\nabla h_i(z')\|_2\leq L_i\|z-z'\|_2.
 \label{eqn:gd_row_condition}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}
Under~\Cref{assump:main}, suppose $(\mathsf G_R)$ of
\Cref{def:local_row_regularity} holds and
$\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0$. Let a
positive-definiteness certificate give
\begin{equation*}
 0<\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty),
 \qquad \Lambda:=B_*^2,
 \qquad c_{\mathrm{Ch}}:=\frac14+\frac34\log\frac34.
\end{equation*}
A lower bound on either NTK block in \cref{eqn:block_pd_certificate_bound}
may serve as $\lambda_0$. For $0<\delta<1$, suppose
\begin{equation}
 d_1\geq\max\!\left\{
 \frac{R_K}{c_{\mathrm{Ch}}\lambda_0}\log\frac{2N}{\delta},
 (320+128\sqrt6)\frac{L_*^2\Lambda\overline r_\delta^2}{\lambda_0^3},
 \frac{16B_*^2\overline r_\delta^2}{R^2\lambda_0^2}
 \right\},
 \qquad 0<\eta\Lambda\leq\frac12.
 \label{eqn:linear_pde_convergence_conditions}
\end{equation}
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every
$k\in\mathbb N_0$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \max_{m\in[d_1]}
 \|\theta_{m,(k)}-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2&\leq R,\\
 \mathbf K_{(k)}&\succeq\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N,\\
 \mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})
 &\leq(1-\eta\lambda_0)^k\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)}).
\end{aligned}
 \label{eqn:linear_convergence_main}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:classwise_gd_convergence}
\label{cor:pointwise_full_rank_gd_convergence}
\label{cor:functional_gd_convergence}
\label{cor:nonlocal_gd_convergence}
Under~\Cref{assump:main}, suppose
$\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0$ and one of the following
certificate conditions from~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ holds and every co-located coefficient family
is linearly independent;
\item $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ holds and the combined functional family is
linearly independent in $\mathcal X^*$; or
\item $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$ holds and the combined measure tuples are
linearly independent.
\end{enumerate}
Then $(\mathsf G_R)$ holds and
$\lambda_0:=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)>0$. Consequently, for
every $0<\delta<1$,~\cref{eqn:linear_pde_convergence_conditions} implies
\cref{eqn:linear_convergence_main} with probability at least $1-\delta$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
In each branch the cited rank condition proves
$\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\succ0$, hence
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ by \cref{eqn:block_pd_certificate_bound};
$(\mathsf G_R)$ follows from \Cref{prop:linearNTK},
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity}, or
\Cref{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity}, and
\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} applies.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Matrix Chernoff gives
$\mathbf K_{(0)}\succeq3\lambda_0\mathbf I_N/4$ with high probability. Inside
the radius-$R$ tube, singular-value perturbation controls the gap through
$(L_*/\sqrt{d_1})\|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2$, the loss induction gives
$\max_m\|\theta_{m,(k)}-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2
\leq4B_*\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2/(\sqrt{d_1}\lambda_0)$ and closes localization,
and an integral Taylor remainder gives one-step contraction; the three width
terms in~\cref{eqn:linear_pde_convergence_conditions} enforce exactly these
three steps. Full proofs are in~\cref{sec:ntk_proof,sec:convergenceproof}.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:relu3_fourth_order_obstruction}
Let $\rho_3(z)=(z_+)^3$ and consider the one-dimensional equation
$u^{(4)}(x)=1$. For the two-layer trial function
\begin{equation*}
 u_\theta(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}
 a_m\rho_3(w_mx+b_m),
\end{equation*}
every fixed finite collocation set $\{x_i\}$ avoids the kinks
$w_mx_i+b_m=0$ of $\rho_3$ almost surely whenever each $(w_m,b_m)$ has a
Lebesgue density, as for the Gaussian hidden-layer initialization
of~\citet{Gao2023}. On that event,
each summand either vanishes locally or agrees there with a cubic polynomial, and hence
\begin{equation*}
 \partial_x^4u_\theta(x_i)=0,
 \qquad
 \nabla_\theta\partial_x^4u_\theta(x_i)=\mathbf0.
\end{equation*}
Every such residual row and column of the finite-width and expected
infinite-width tangent kernels is therefore zero, whereas the target $1$ leaves
a strictly positive minimum achievable loss. Moreover, $\rho_3$ is $C^2$ but not
$C^3$, since $\rho_3'''$ jumps from $0$ to $6$ at $z=0$, so even third-derivative
constraints require additional care. Thus the fixed
cubic-ReLU second-order result of~\citet{Gao2023} does not extend to arbitrary
higher-order strong PDEs without changing the activation or formulation.
This example does not contradict~\citet{Jin2026}: their assumptions exclude
$\rho_3$ for fourth derivatives, and their Remark~1 prescribes a matching
rectified-power unit instead.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:shared_point_rank_obstruction}
Consider the closed interval $[0,1]$ and collocate at the boundary point
$x_\star=0$ both the PDE operator
$\mathcal A_\star=\partial_x+x\mathcal I$, where $\mathcal I$ is the
identity operator, and the Neumann boundary operator $\mathcal B=\partial_x$.
For positive scales $s_\Omega,s_\partial$, define
$P_\Omega=s_\Omega(\mathcal A_\star u_\theta)(x_\star)$ and
$P_\partial=s_\partial(\mathcal B u_\theta)(x_\star)$. Although
$\mathcal A_\star\neq\mathcal B$ as written operators and both evaluated rows
are nonzero,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal A_\star u_\theta(0)=\mathcal Bu_\theta(0)=u_\theta'(0),
 \qquad
 s_\partial\nabla_\theta P_\Omega
 -s_\Omega\nabla_\theta P_\partial=\mathbf0.
\end{equation*}
The joint $2\times2$ Gram block has determinant zero at every width. This
singularity shows why pairwise-distinct-point positivity does not automatically
apply at a repeated physical location under only a nontriviality check on each constraint.
Coincidence is not itself an obstruction: replacing
$\mathcal A_\star$ by $\partial_x+\mathcal I$ gives the
independent local coefficient rows $(1,1)$ and $(0,1)$ in coordinates
$(u,u')$. Under the hypotheses of~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank}, this pair
yields a PD limiting NTK although the sites coincide.
Linear independence of the local coefficient vectors, rather than coincident
sampling alone, distinguishes the two cases.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:vector_coupling_rank_obstruction}
For $\mathbf u_\theta=(u_{1,\theta},u_{2,\theta})^\top$, fix one physical
point $\mathbf x_\star\in\overline\Omega$ and impose there
\begin{equation*}
 P_1=u_{1,\theta}(\mathbf x_\star),\qquad
 P_2=u_{2,\theta}(\mathbf x_\star),\qquad
 P_3=u_{1,\theta}(\mathbf x_\star)+u_{2,\theta}(\mathbf x_\star).
\end{equation*}
Then $\nabla_\theta P_3=\nabla_\theta P_1+\nabla_\theta P_2$, so the joint
NTK is singular at every width with null direction $(-1,-1,1)^\top$. Thus scalar
positivity for each output coordinate does not by itself imply positivity of
an arbitrary coupled, scalarized multi-output constraint family. Multiple
components alone are not the problem: for example, $u_1+u_2$ and $u_1-u_2$ have
independent coefficient rows. \citet{Jin2026} allow vector outputs with operators
acting componentwise; the additional issue here is coupled constraints at a
repeated site. The local vectors $\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)$ record both the
component and derivative indices, and their joint linear independence is the
exact criterion under $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$; see also~\Cref{ex:vectorvalued}.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:duplicate_active_subspace}
Let $\ell$ be any nonzero pointwise, weak, or nonlocal constraint covered by
\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank,prop:functional_ntk_rank,prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank},
and duplicate its scaled prediction:
\begin{equation*}
 P_1(\theta)=P_2(\theta)=\ell(u_\theta).
\end{equation*}
If $g(\theta)=\|\nabla_\theta P_1(\theta)\|_2^2$, then the full tangent
kernel is
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf K(\theta)=g(\theta)
 \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 \ker\mathbf K(\theta)=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)^\top\}
 \ \text{ whenever }g(\theta)>0.
\end{equation*}
Thus every theorem that assumes a strictly positive full Gram matrix excludes
this system. Equal targets $(c,c)^\top$ are nevertheless compatible: the
error remains in $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{dup}}=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)^\top\}$, and the
compressed kernel on $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{dup}}$ is positive whenever
$g(\theta)>0$. The certificate required
by~\Cref{cor:active_subspace_convergence} concerns instead the population
value $\mathbf U^\top\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\mathbf U
=2[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{11}$ with $\mathbf U=(1,1)^\top/\sqrt2$, which is
positive under the applicable ``pd'' clause because the single nonzero row
$\ell$ is linearly independent; under the ``reg'' clause alone it can vanish
(\Cref{ex:weak_analyticity_necessity}). Given this certificate, conditional
centering $\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0$, and the
compressed width and step-size conditions,
\Cref{cor:active_subspace_convergence} gives geometric finite-width GD
convergence. For unequal targets $(c_1,c_2)^\top$, the objective satisfies
\begin{equation*}
 \|\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_T\|_2^2
 =2\Bigl(\ell(u_\theta)-\frac{c_1+c_2}{2}\Bigr)^2+\frac{(c_1-c_2)^2}{2}
 \geq\frac{(c_1-c_2)^2}{2}
 =\|\Pi_{\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}}\mathbf v_T\|_2^2,
\end{equation*}
where $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)^\top\}
=\mathcal U_{\mathrm{dup}}^\perp$ is the structural nullspace
of~\Cref{def:structural_spaces_compatibility}. This is the irreducible term
in~\cref{eqn:structural_loss_compression}; it is attained whenever some
$\theta$ gives $\ell(u_\theta)=(c_1+c_2)/2$, which holds at every width as
soon as $\ell(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q})\neq0$ for some $\boldsymbol\xi$ and
$q$, since $\ell(u_\theta)$ is linear in the output weights. This single
construction applies, for example, to duplicate collocation rows and to
duplicate weak test functions.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{ex:sharp_interface_weak}
On $(-1,1)$, let
\begin{equation*}
 \kappa(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x<0,\\2,&x\geq0.\end{cases}
\end{equation*}
The divergence-form operator $-(\kappa u')'$ cannot be expanded at $x=0$
as a strong-form finite sum of classical derivatives with pointwise coefficients unless
an interface interpretation is added. Take the network trial space to be
$\mathcal X=H^1(-1,1)$ and the test space to be $H_0^1(-1,1)$. For
$u\in\mathcal X$ and $v\in H_0^1(-1,1)$, the continuum weak row
\begin{equation*}
 \ell_v(u)=\int_{-1}^{1}\kappa(x)u'(x)v'(x)\,dx
\end{equation*}
is bounded on $\mathcal X$. Dirichlet values are imposed by the two separate,
bounded trace rows $u\mapsto u(-1)$ and $u\mapsto u(1)$. The distinction
between trial and test spaces is essential: an unconstrained tanh ridge
$x\mapsto\tanh(wx+\gamma b)$ generally does not belong to $H_0^1(-1,1)$.
\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson} verifies, rather than assumes, the
Banach-valued analyticity, density, and joint independence required for this
precise formulation. This example lies outside the strong-form
differential-operator theorem
of~\citet{Moser2026}, which explicitly sends sharp interfaces to a weak
formulation.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:gaussian_moment_obstruction}
Consider the analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma(z)=\exp(z^4)$ and a
nondegenerate Gaussian preactivation $Z$. Then
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]=\mathbb E[\exp(2Z^4)]=\infty.
\end{equation*}
Consequently, the ordinary infinite-width covariance and NTK expectations are
not finite for this activation under Gaussian initialization. This illustrates
why population-kernel statements require moment existence in addition to
activation regularity and nonpolynomiality. Our compact per-neuron
initialization ensures the relevant moments are finite on compact input and
parameter sets; in particular, one nonzero value row has a finite positive
limiting Gram entry under our assumptions.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:linearNTK}
Use the network and loss in
\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization,def:pinn_loss}, and suppose the
row-regularity condition in~\Cref{assump:general} holds. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item At initialization, the deterministic infinite-width NTK exists and has
the Gram representation
\begin{equation*}
[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{ij}
=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}
\left[\left\langle\nabla h_i(z),\nabla h_j(z)\right\rangle\right]
=\sum_{p=1}^{d_\theta}
\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}
\left[\partial_{z_p}h_i(z)\,\partial_{z_p}h_j(z)\right].
\end{equation*}
Thus it is the sum of \(d_\theta=d_0+d_2+1\) positive-semidefinite
contributions, and bounded continuous parameter-derivative functions in an
\(L^2(\mu)\) space define each contribution. If every width-\(d_1\) network uses the first \(d_1\)
vectors of one infinite i.i.d.\ sequence, then
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) almost surely; for separately
resampled widths, convergence is in probability. For finite-order pointwise
differential constraints, these parameter-derivative functions are analytic
when \(\sigma\) is real analytic.

\item Suppose the fixed design has a positive-definiteness certificate in the sense
of~\Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate}, so
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0\), and let
\(0<\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\) be a certified
lower bound. Define
\begin{equation*}
c_{\mathrm{Ch}}=\frac14+\frac34\log\frac34.
\end{equation*}
For \(0<\delta<1\), if
\begin{equation*}
d_1\geq \frac{R_K}{c_{\mathrm{Ch}}\lambda_0}
\log\!\left(\frac{N}{\delta}\right),
\end{equation*}
then
\(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\geq3\lambda_0/4\) with probability at
 least \(1-\delta\). For the pointwise class under clause
 \(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}\) of \Cref{assump:pde_classes}, sitewise
 coefficient-vector independence gives
 the required positive-definiteness certificate through
 \Cref{lem:jinwu_sigma_independence,prop:limiting_ntk_rank, 
 sec:pointwise_positivity_certificate}.

\item If \(\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}\), which holds almost surely
under~\Cref{assump:main}, then for every
\(\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\), direct perturbation
of the prediction Jacobian gives
\begin{equation*}
\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K(\theta))
\geq\left(
\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})}
-\frac{L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}\|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
\right)_+^2,
\end{equation*}
and \(\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K(\theta))\leq B_*^2\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{assump:general}
Under~\Cref{assump:main}, fix a target \(\mathbf v_T\) and a
finite collection of prediction components. Assemble them in
\(\mathbf v_P(\theta)\in\mathbb R^N\), and consider the loss
\(\mathcal L(\theta)=\|\mathbf v_P(\theta)-\mathbf v_T\|_2^2\). Write
\(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_{d_1})\), choose \(R>0\), and define the
product neighborhood
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})
 :=\left\{\theta:
       \max_{1\leq m\leq d_1}
       \|\theta_m-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2\leq R\right\}.
 \label{eqn:abstract_product_tube}
\end{equation}
For each scalar prediction component \(i\), one loss-scaled linear row
of~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, require
\begin{equation}
 P_i(\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}h_i(\theta_m),
 \qquad
 h_i(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)
 =\mathbf a^\top\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi).
 \label{eqn:predictionmap}
\end{equation}
The fixed data encoded by \(\mathbf f_i\) may define any fixed scalar linear
observation satisfying the representation in~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} and the
bounds in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} below. For a strong-form
local differential row, they include its sampled evaluation point (its
collocation point), its evaluated operator coefficients, and its loss scale
\(s_i\). Require deterministic constants
\(A_{0,i},B_i,L_i<\infty\), uniform in $d_1$, such
    that, for every \(z_0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\) and all
\(z,z'\in\overline{\mathbb B}_R(z_0)\),
\begin{align}
 |h_i(z_0)|&\leq A_{0,i},&
 \|\nabla h_i(z)\|_2&\leq B_i,\nonumber\\
 \|\nabla h_i(z)-\nabla h_i(z')\|_2
   &\leq L_i\|z-z'\|_2.
 \label{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}
\end{align}
If \(\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\) and every
\(\theta_{m,(0)}\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\), which holds almost surely
under~\Cref{assump:main}, then
\(\theta_m\in\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\theta_{m,(0)})\) for every \(m\), so
the bounds in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} apply to every neuron of
\(\theta\) with center \(z_0=\theta_{m,(0)}\). Every statement in the
appendices that applies these bounds on \(\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\) is
made on this probability-one event \(\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}\); where
a statement does not repeat the qualifier, it is understood. Define
\begin{equation}
 A_{0,*}^2=\sum_iA_{0,i}^2,\qquad
 B_*^2=\sum_iB_i^2,\qquad
 L_*^2=\sum_iL_i^2.
 \label{eqn:abstract_aggregate_constants}
\end{equation}
For later use, recall $d_\theta=d_0+d_2+1$ and set
\(\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_\theta}\) by
\([\boldsymbol\Psi(z)]_{ip}=\partial h_i(z)/\partial z_p\), $p\in[d_\theta]$.
Differentiating~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} in \(\theta_m\) gives
\(\nabla_{\theta_m}P_i=d_1^{-1/2}\nabla h_i(\theta_m)\), so
\(\mathbf J(\theta)=d_1^{-1/2}[\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_1)\ \cdots\
\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{d_1})]\). The
gradient-Lipschitz bound yields the quadratic Taylor remainder used in the
optimization argument through the integral of the gradient difference; this
derivation does not require an everywhere-defined Hessian. The condition
imposes neither analyticity nor nonpolynomiality.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Finite-order strong-form differential constraints satisfy the condition under
\Cref{assump:main} and order-matched activation smoothness. For a tested weak,
integro-differential, or fractional row, one must first
verify~\cref{eqn:predictionmap,eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} for
that row; linearity and bounded coefficients alone do not imply the
required bounds.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity}
Under~\Cref{assump:main}, so that \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) is compact, let
\(\mathcal X\) be a real Banach space of \(\mathbb R^{d_2}\)-valued functions
embedded continuously in \(L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) of its domain, so that an
\(\mathcal X\)-limit that also converges almost everywhere coincides almost
everywhere with its pointwise limit (this identifies Fr\'echet derivatives
with classical parameter derivatives in the corollaries below; the lemma
itself does not use it), let
\(\lambda_i\in\mathcal X^*\), \(i\in[N]\), be fixed bounded linear
functionals, and set
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal G(z)
 =\mathbf a\,\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)\in\mathcal X,
 \qquad z=(\mathbf w,b,\mathbf a)\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}.
\end{equation*}
Fix \(0<R<\infty\) and define the compact
parameter tube
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal Z_R=\operatorname{supp}\mu+\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\mathbf0)
 =\{z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\operatorname{supp}\mu)\leq R\}.
\end{equation*}
Suppose that \(\mathcal G\) is twice continuously Fr\'echet differentiable
as an \(\mathcal X\)-valued map on an open neighborhood of \(\mathcal Z_R\). Define
\begin{align*}
 M_0&=\sup_{z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu}\|\mathcal G(z)\|_{\mathcal X},\\
 M_1&=\sup_{z\in \mathcal Z_R}
       \|D\mathcal G(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}},\\
 M_2&=\sup_{z\in \mathcal Z_R}
       \|D^2\mathcal G(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\end{align*}
Here \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) is taken with respect to the Euclidean norm
on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\); for \(D^2\mathcal G(z)\) it is the bilinear norm
\(\sup_{\|\dot z\|_2=\|\widehat z\|_2=1}
\|D^2\mathcal G(z)[\dot z,\widehat z]\|_{\mathcal X}\).
These constants are finite. For the rows
\(P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))\) of types (ii) and (iii)
in~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, since
\(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)=d_1^{-1/2}\sum_{m}\mathcal G(\theta_m)\) and
\(\lambda_i\) is linear, the scalar maps
\(h_i=\lambda_i\circ\mathcal G\) give the representation
in~\cref{eqn:predictionmap}, with
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi)]_q
 =\lambda_i\!\left(
   \mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)\right),
 \qquad \boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b),
\end{equation*}
and satisfy~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} with the explicit valid
choices
\begin{equation}
 A_{0,i}=\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_0,
 \qquad
 B_i=\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_1,
 \qquad
 L_i=\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_2.
 \label{eqn:bounded_functional_regularity_constants}
\end{equation}
The same conclusion holds if \(\mathcal G\) is continuously Fr\'echet
differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(\mathcal Z_R\) and there is a finite
constant \(M_{1,1}\) such that
\begin{equation*}
 \|D\mathcal G(z)-D\mathcal G(z')\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq M_{1,1}\|z-z'\|_2
 \qquad (z,z'\in \mathcal Z_R).
\end{equation*}
In this \(C^{1,1}\) case, take \(L_i=\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_{1,1}\)
in place of the third choice
in~\cref{eqn:bounded_functional_regularity_constants}.
In particular, Banach-valued real analyticity on an open neighborhood of the
tube implies the displayed \(C^2\) hypothesis and hence all three bounds.

As a specialization, let \(\mathcal V_i\) be normed, let
\(a_i:\mathcal X\times\mathcal V_i\to\mathbb R\) be a continuous
bilinear form, fix \(v_i\in\mathcal V_i\), and define the loss-scaled weak
row
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_i(f)=s_i a_i(f,v_i),\qquad s_i>0.
\end{equation*}
If \(\|a_i\|_{\mathrm{bil}}\) denotes its bilinear operator norm, then
\begin{equation}
 \|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}
 \leq s_i\|a_i\|_{\mathrm{bil}}\|v_i\|_{\mathcal V_i}.
 \label{eqn:weak_functional_dual_norm_bound}
\end{equation}
Consequently, substituting the right-hand side
of~\cref{eqn:weak_functional_dual_norm_bound} for
\(\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}\)
in~\cref{eqn:bounded_functional_regularity_constants} gives valid
\(A_{0,i},B_i,L_i\) for every such weak row. Any bounded boundary
functional on the same trial space is covered by the first part of the lemma.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Compactness of \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) and finite dimensionality of the per-neuron parameter
space make \(\mathcal Z_R\) compact. Continuity of
\(\mathcal G,D\mathcal G,D^2\mathcal G\) therefore makes
\(M_0,M_1,M_2\) finite. Linearity of \(\lambda_i\) and the coordinate
decomposition
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal G(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)
 =\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}(\mathbf a)_q
   \mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)
\end{equation*}
give the claimed per-neuron representation. The Banach-space chain rule gives
\begin{equation*}
 Dh_i(z)=\lambda_i\circ D\mathcal G(z).
\end{equation*}
Boundedness of \(\lambda_i\) gives
\(|h_i(z_0)|\leq\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_0\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\), and since
\(\nabla h_i(z)\) is the Riesz representative of \(Dh_i(z)\),
\(\|\nabla h_i(z)\|_2=\|Dh_i(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_1\) on \(\mathcal Z_R\).

Fix \(z_0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\) and
\(z,z'\in\overline{\mathbb B}_R(z_0)\). Their line segment remains in
that ball and hence in \(\mathcal Z_R\). The Banach-space fundamental theorem of
calculus, applied to \(D\mathcal G\), yields
\begin{equation*}
 \|D\mathcal G(z)-D\mathcal G(z')\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq M_2\|z-z'\|_2.
\end{equation*}
Composition with \(\lambda_i\) proves the Lipschitz-gradient estimate and
therefore~\cref{eqn:bounded_functional_regularity_constants}. The
\(C^{1,1}\) variant is the same argument with its defining Lipschitz bound.
Finally, continuity and bilinearity give
\begin{equation*}
 |\lambda_i(f)|
 \leq s_i\|a_i\|_{\mathrm{bil}}
       \|f\|_{\mathcal X}\|v_i\|_{\mathcal V_i},
\end{equation*}
which proves~\cref{eqn:weak_functional_dual_norm_bound} and the weak-row
specialization.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:weak_H1_row_regularity}
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{d_0}\) be a bounded open set and take
\(\mathcal X=H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\). Suppose the per-neuron
initialization law is width independent and compactly supported, fix
\(0<R<\infty\), and assume
\(\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^3(\mathbb R)\). Then
\begin{equation*}
 z=(\mathbf w,b,\mathbf a)
 \longmapsto
 \mathbf a\,\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)
 \end{equation*}
is a \(C^2\) map into \(\mathcal X\) on an open neighborhood of the compact
tube \(\mathcal Z_R\) of~\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity}.
Consequently, every fixed finite family of weak
rows \(\lambda_i(f)=s_i a_i(f,v_i)\), where \(\mathcal V_i\) is normed,
\(a_i:\mathcal X\times\mathcal V_i\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and
bilinear, and \(v_i\in\mathcal V_i\) is fixed, together with any bounded boundary
functionals on \(H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\), satisfies
\cref{eqn:predictionmap,eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}, with the constants
in~\cref{eqn:bounded_functional_regularity_constants}.

Here a boundary functional is covered only if it is already a bounded element
of \(H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})^*\), for example because an appropriate
tested trace theorem applies. Pointwise Dirichlet evaluation is not
automatically bounded on \(H^1\) when \(d_0\geq2\), and pointwise Neumann
evaluation is not generally bounded on \(H^1\); those rows require a smoother
trial space or a bounded tested trace. This corollary verifies
$(\mathsf G_R)$, equivalently the row bounds in~\Cref{assump:general}. It does
not establish~\Cref{assump:main}, centering,
Banach-valued analyticity or ridge density, joint functional independence, or
a positive-definiteness certificate.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Write
\begin{equation*}
 t_z(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b,
 \qquad
 \ell_{\dot z}(\mathbf x)=\dot{\mathbf w}^{\top}\mathbf x+
                       \gamma\dot b
\end{equation*}
for a parameter direction
\(\dot z=(\dot{\mathbf w},\dot b,\dot{\mathbf a})\), and use
\(\ell_{\widehat z}\) analogously for
\(\widehat z=(\widehat{\mathbf w},\widehat b,\widehat{\mathbf a})\).
The candidate first and second Fr\'echet derivatives of
\(\mathcal G(z)=\mathbf a\sigma(t_z)\) are
\begin{align}
 D\mathcal G(z)[\dot z]
 &=\dot{\mathbf a}\,\sigma(t_z)
   +\mathbf a\,\sigma'(t_z)\ell_{\dot z},
 \label{eqn:H1_ridge_first_parameter_derivative}\\
 D^2\mathcal G(z)[\dot z,\widehat z]
 &=\dot{\mathbf a}\,\sigma'(t_z)\ell_{\widehat z}
   +\widehat{\mathbf a}\,\sigma'(t_z)\ell_{\dot z}
   +\mathbf a\,\sigma''(t_z)\ell_{\dot z}\ell_{\widehat z}.
 \label{eqn:H1_ridge_second_parameter_derivative}
\end{align}
Their spatial weak derivatives are represented by their classical
derivatives. In particular,
\begin{align*}
 \nabla_{\mathbf x}D\mathcal G(z)[\dot z]
 &=\dot{\mathbf a}\mathbf w^\top\sigma'(t_z)
   +\mathbf a\dot{\mathbf w}^{\top}\sigma'(t_z)
   +\mathbf a\mathbf w^\top\sigma''(t_z)\ell_{\dot z},\\
 \nabla_{\mathbf x}D^2\mathcal G(z)[\dot z,\widehat z]
 &=\dot{\mathbf a}\!\left[
      \mathbf w^\top\sigma''(t_z)\ell_{\widehat z}
      +\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\sigma'(t_z)\right]\\
 &\quad+\widehat{\mathbf a}\!\left[
      \mathbf w^\top\sigma''(t_z)\ell_{\dot z}
      +\dot{\mathbf w}^{\top}\sigma'(t_z)\right]\\
 &\quad+\mathbf a\!\left[
      \mathbf w^\top\sigma'''(t_z)\ell_{\dot z}\ell_{\widehat z}
      +\dot{\mathbf w}^{\top}\sigma''(t_z)\ell_{\widehat z}
      +\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\sigma''(t_z)\ell_{\dot z}
      \right].
\end{align*}

Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) and work on the enlarged compact tube
\(\mathcal Z_{R+\varepsilon}=\operatorname{supp}\mu+\overline{\mathbb B}_{R+\varepsilon}(\mathbf0)\),
whose interior is an open neighborhood of \(\mathcal Z_R\), as
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} requires. Boundedness of \(\Omega\) and
compactness of this tube uniformly bound \(\mathbf x\), all parameters,
\(t_z(\mathbf x)\), and the affine functions
\(\ell_{\dot z}(\mathbf x)\) for unit parameter directions. Hence
\(\sigma^{(j)}\), \(0\leq j\leq3\), is bounded and uniformly continuous on
one compact interval containing every relevant affine argument. The displayed
formulas and their spatial derivatives are consequently uniformly bounded in
\(L^\infty(\Omega)\), in operator norm over unit directions.

Taylor's theorem in the scalar affine argument, with its remainder uniform on
that compact interval, shows from the same formulas that the difference
quotients defining~\cref{eqn:H1_ridge_first_parameter_derivative, 
eqn:H1_ridge_second_parameter_derivative} converge in
\(W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\). Uniform continuity of
\(\sigma^{(j)}\), \(j\leq3\), also makes the two displayed derivative maps
continuous in their corresponding operator norms. Thus
\(z\mapsto\mathcal G(z)\) is \(C^2\) into \(W^{1,\infty}\) on an open
neighborhood of \(\mathcal Z_R\). Since \(|\Omega|<\infty\), the embedding
\begin{equation*}
 W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})
 \hookrightarrow H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})
\end{equation*}
is continuous, so the same formulas are its first and second Fr\'echet
derivatives as an \(H^1\)-valued map. Apply
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} and
\cref{eqn:weak_functional_dual_norm_bound}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:weak_Hk_row_regularity}
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{d_0}\) be a bounded open set,
\(k\in\mathbb N_0\), and \(\mathcal X=H^k(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\). Suppose
the per-neuron initialization law is width independent and compactly
supported, fix \(0<R<\infty\), and assume
\(\sigma\in C^{k+2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)\). Then
\(z=(\mathbf w,b,\mathbf a)\mapsto\mathbf a\,\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)\)
is a \(C^2\) map into \(\mathcal X\) on an open neighborhood of the compact
tube \(\mathcal Z_R\), and every fixed finite family of bounded linear
functionals on \(\mathcal X\) satisfies
\cref{eqn:predictionmap,eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}, hence
\((\mathsf G_R)\), with the constants of
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity}. If moreover \(\Omega\) is a
Lipschitz domain and \(k>d_0/2+r\) for
an integer \(r\geq0\), every pointwise evaluation
\(f\mapsto\partial^\alpha f_q(\mathbf x)\) with \(|\alpha|\leq r\) and
\(\mathbf x\in\overline\Omega\) is bounded on \(\mathcal X\), so pointwise
Dirichlet rows (\(r=0\)) and pointwise Neumann or higher-order boundary rows
(\(r\geq1\)) are admissible weak rows in every dimension.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Write \(t_z(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b\). For a multi-index
\(\beta\) with \(|\beta|\leq k\),
\(\partial^\beta_{\mathbf x}[a_q\sigma(t_z(\mathbf x))]
=a_q\,\mathbf w^\beta\,\sigma^{(|\beta|)}(t_z(\mathbf x))\), which as a
function of \(z\) is a polynomial in \((\mathbf w,\mathbf a)\) times
\(\sigma^{(|\beta|)}(t_z(\mathbf x))\). On the enlarged compact tube
\(\mathcal Z_{R+\varepsilon}\), whose interior is an open neighborhood of
\(\mathcal Z_R\), the arguments
\(t_z(\mathbf x)\), \(\mathbf x\in\overline\Omega\), range over a compact
interval on which \(\sigma^{(|\beta|)}\), \(\sigma^{(|\beta|+1)}\), and
\(\sigma^{(|\beta|+2)}\) are bounded and uniformly continuous, because
\(\sigma\in C^{k+2}_{\mathrm{loc}}\). Hence each
\(z\mapsto\partial^\beta_{\mathbf x}[\mathbf a\,\sigma(t_z(\cdot))]\) is
\(C^2\) into \(C(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\), with the pointwise
formulas as its derivatives, and since
\(C(\overline\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^2(\Omega)\) continuously on a bounded
domain, the map is \(C^2\) into \(H^k(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\); this is the
proof of \Cref{cor:weak_H1_row_regularity} with \(k\) spatial derivatives in
place of one. \Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} then gives
\((\mathsf G_R)\) for any finite family of bounded functionals. For the last
claim, the Sobolev embedding
\(H^k(\Omega)\hookrightarrow C^r(\overline\Omega)\) holds on bounded Lipschitz
domains whenever \(k>d_0/2+r\)~\citep[Theorem~4.12]{Adams2003}, so pointwise
derivative evaluations of order at most \(r\) are bounded functionals on
\(\mathcal X\).
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity}
Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^{d_0}\) be compact. For \(i\in[N]\) and
\(q\in[d_2]\), let \(\bar\nu_{iq}=s_i\nu_{iq}\) be the loss-scaled finite
signed regular Borel measures of a type (iii) row in~\Cref{def:linear_pde},
so that \(\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_i=(\bar\nu_{iq})_{q\in[d_2]}\), and
define
\begin{equation*}
 P_i(\theta)=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int_D
 u_q(\mathbf y;\theta)\,d\bar\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y).
\end{equation*}
Suppose the per-neuron initialization law \(\mu\) is width independent and
compactly supported (\Cref{assump:main}), fix \(0<R<\infty\), and assume
\(\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^2(\mathbb R)\). Then the induced per-neuron
maps satisfy~\cref{eqn:predictionmap,eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}; in
particular, clause \(\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}\) of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}
implies \((\mathsf G_R)\) of~\Cref{def:local_row_regularity}.

More precisely, write
\begin{equation*}
 \widetilde{\mathbf y}=(\mathbf y,\gamma),\qquad
 \tau_i=\left(\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}
 \|\bar\nu_{iq}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad
 \mathcal Z_R=\operatorname{supp}\mu+\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\mathbf0),
\end{equation*}
and set
\begin{align*}
 C_D&=\max_{\mathbf y\in D}\|\widetilde{\mathbf y}\|_2,
 &A_R&=\max_{(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)\in\mathcal Z_R}
       \|\mathbf a\|_2,\\
 T_{D,R}&=\max_{\substack{(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)\in\mathcal Z_R\\
                       \mathbf y\in D}}
       |\boldsymbol\xi^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y}|,
 &S_{j,R}&=\max_{|t|\leq T_{D,R}}|\sigma^{(j)}(t)|,
 \quad j=0,1,2.
\end{align*}
The following are valid choices:
\begin{align}
 A_{0,i}&=A_RS_{0,R}\tau_i,\nonumber\\
 B_i&=\tau_i\left(S_{0,R}+A_RS_{1,R}C_D\right),\nonumber\\
 L_i&=\tau_i\left(A_RS_{2,R}C_D^2+S_{1,R}C_D\right).
 \label{eqn:finite_measure_regularity_constants}
\end{align}
If \(\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0\), then also
\(\mathbb E[h_i(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)]=0\) for every row.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Define \(\mathbf f_i:\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\to\mathbb R^{d_2}\) by
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi)]_q
 =\int_D\sigma(\boldsymbol\xi^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y})
 \,d\bar\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y).
\end{equation*}
Then
\begin{equation*}
 P_i(\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}h_i(\theta_m),
 \qquad
 h_i(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)=\mathbf a^\top\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi).
\end{equation*}
Compactness of \(D\), local smoothness of \(\sigma\), and finite total
variation justify differentiation under each integral. For
\(\mathbf v,\mathbf v'\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\),
\begin{align*}
 D[\mathbf f_i]_q(\boldsymbol\xi)[\mathbf v]
 &=\int_D\sigma'(\boldsymbol\xi^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y})
   \mathbf v^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y}\,d\bar\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y),\\
 D^2[\mathbf f_i]_q(\boldsymbol\xi)[\mathbf v,\mathbf v']
 &=\int_D\sigma''(\boldsymbol\xi^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y})
   (\mathbf v^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y})
   (\mathbf v'^\top\widetilde{\mathbf y})
   \,d\bar\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y).
\end{align*}
Consequently, throughout \(\mathcal Z_R\),
\begin{equation*}
 \|\mathbf f_i\|_2\leq S_{0,R}\tau_i,\qquad
 \|D\mathbf f_i\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq S_{1,R}C_D\tau_i,
 \qquad
 \|D^2\mathbf f_i\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq S_{2,R}C_D^2\tau_i.
\end{equation*}
The gradient and Hessian of \(h_i\) have the block forms
\begin{equation*}
 \nabla h_i=
 \begin{pmatrix}(D\mathbf f_i)^\top\mathbf a\\ \mathbf f_i\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \nabla^2h_i=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  \sum_q a_qD^2[\mathbf f_i]_q&(D\mathbf f_i)^\top\\
  D\mathbf f_i&0
 \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
Bounding \(\|D\mathbf f_i\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) by its Frobenius norm, using
\(\|\nabla h_i\|_2\leq\|(D\mathbf f_i)^\top\mathbf a\|_2+\|\mathbf f_i\|_2\),
\(\|\sum_qa_qD^2[\mathbf f_i]_q\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\sum_q|a_q|\,S_{2,R}C_D^2\|\bar\nu_{iq}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\leq A_RS_{2,R}C_D^2\tau_i\) (Cauchy--Schwarz over \(q\)), and
\(
 \left\|\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B^\top\\B&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\)
gives~\cref{eqn:finite_measure_regularity_constants}. The mean-value
estimate on each convex radius-\(R\) ball then gives the required
Lipschitz-gradient bound. Finally,
\(
 \mathbb E[h_i\mid\boldsymbol\xi]
 =\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]^\top\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=0
\), proving the centering assertion.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:linearNTK}
For the network in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}, suppose
\Cref{assump:main} holds. Let
\(r_{\max}\) be the largest differential order among the finite collection of
strong-form differential constraints in~\Cref{def:linear_pde}. If
\(\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{r_{\max}+2}(\mathbb R)\), or more generally
\(\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{r_{\max}+1,1}(\mathbb R)\), then, for every
fixed \(0<R<\infty\), this family satisfies
\cref{eqn:predictionmap,eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} with radius \(R\) and
width-independent constants. In particular,
\cref{eqn:gd_row_condition} is then automatic for such constraints. If
\(\sigma\) is real analytic, each \(h_i\), hence every entry of
\(\boldsymbol\Psi\), is real analytic in \(z=(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)\).
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
\phantomsection
    \label{proof:linearNTK}
    For row $i$, set
    $t_m(\mathbf x_i)=\mathbf w_m^\top\mathbf x_i+\gamma b_m$. Applying
    each mixed derivative in~\cref{eqn:scalar_constraint_main} to one neuron
    gives
    \begin{equation}
      P_i(\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}h_i(\theta_m),
      \qquad
      h_i(\boldsymbol\xi_m,\mathbf a_m)
      =s_i\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\sum_{\alpha\in I_{iq}}
      a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x_i)(\mathbf a_m)_q
      \sigma^{(|\alpha|)}(t_m(\mathbf x_i))\mathbf w_m^\alpha.
      \label{eqn:classical_one_neuron_contribution}
    \end{equation}
    where \(a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x_i)\) are the operator coefficients
    of~\cref{eqn:scalar_constraint_main} and \((\mathbf a_m)_q\) the output
    weights. Thus, the representation in~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} holds with
    \begin{equation*}
      [\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi_m)]_q
      =s_i\sum_{\alpha\in I_{iq}}a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x_i)
      \sigma^{(|\alpha|)}(t_m(\mathbf x_i))\mathbf w_m^\alpha.
    \end{equation*}
    Each $h_i$ is a finite sum of products of hidden-weight monomials,
    output-weight coordinates, and derivatives of $\sigma$ of order at most
    $r_{\max}$. Hence $\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{r_{\max}+2}$ gives a
    continuously differentiable $h_i$ with locally Lipschitz gradient;
    the weaker condition
    $\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{r_{\max}+1,1}$ yields the same conclusion
    directly. The tube $\mathcal Z_R=\operatorname{supp}\mu+\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\mathbf0)$
    is compact and width independent, so $h_i$ and $\nabla h_i$ are uniformly
    bounded there, and, each ball $\overline{\mathbb B}_R(z_0)$ being convex,
    the mean-value inequality turns the uniform local Lipschitz constant of
    $\nabla h_i$ on $\mathcal Z_R$ into a Lipschitz constant on the ball. This
    proves~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}; explicit constants follow.
    Write $\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i=(\mathbf x_i,\gamma)$,
    $X_i=\|\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i\|_2$,
    $W_R=\max_{\mathcal Z_R}\max\{1,\|\mathbf w\|_2\}$,
    $A_R=\max_{\mathcal Z_R}\|\mathbf a\|_2$,
    $T_{\mathcal S,R}=\max_{i}\max_{\mathcal Z_R}
    |\boldsymbol\xi^\top\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i|$, and
    $S_j=\max_{|t|\leq T_{\mathcal S,R}}|\sigma^{(j)}(t)|$ for
    $j\leq r_{\max}+2$; in the $C^{r_{\max}+1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ case let
    $S_{r_{\max}+2}$ be the Lipschitz constant of $\sigma^{(r_{\max}+1)}$ on
    $[-T_{\mathcal S,R},T_{\mathcal S,R}]$. For
    $g_\alpha(\boldsymbol\xi)=\mathbf w^\alpha
    \sigma^{(|\alpha|)}(\boldsymbol\xi^\top\widetilde{\mathbf x}_i)$, the
    bounds $\|\nabla_{\mathbf w}\mathbf w^\alpha\|_2\leq|\alpha|W_R^{|\alpha|-1}$
    and $\|\nabla_{\mathbf w}^2\mathbf w^\alpha\|_{\mathrm{op}}
    \leq|\alpha|(|\alpha|-1)W_R^{|\alpha|-2}$ on $\mathcal Z_R$ and the
    product rule give, on $\mathcal Z_R$,
    \begin{align*}
     |g_\alpha|&\leq G_0(\alpha):=W_R^{|\alpha|}S_{|\alpha|},\\
     \|\nabla g_\alpha\|_2&\leq G_1(\alpha)
      :=W_R^{|\alpha|}\bigl(|\alpha|S_{|\alpha|}+X_iS_{|\alpha|+1}\bigr),\\
     \operatorname{Lip}(\nabla g_\alpha)&\leq G_2(\alpha)
      :=W_R^{|\alpha|}\bigl(|\alpha|(|\alpha|-1)S_{|\alpha|}
      +2|\alpha|X_iS_{|\alpha|+1}+X_i^2S_{|\alpha|+2}\bigr).
    \end{align*}
    With $F_{k,iq}=s_i\sum_{\alpha\in I_{iq}}|a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x_i)|\,
    G_k(\alpha)$ and $\mathbf F_{k,i}=(F_{k,iq})_{q\in[d_2]}$, the block
    computation in the proof of~\Cref{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity}
    yields the valid choices
    \begin{equation*}
     A_{0,i}=A_R\|\mathbf F_{0,i}\|_2,\qquad
     B_i=\|\mathbf F_{0,i}\|_2+A_R\|\mathbf F_{1,i}\|_2,\qquad
     L_i=\|\mathbf F_{1,i}\|_2+A_R\|\mathbf F_{2,i}\|_2,
    \end{equation*}
    all proportional to $s_i$ and independent of $d_1$. Finiteness of the
    sampled family makes the aggregate constants
    in~\cref{eqn:abstract_aggregate_constants} finite. If $\sigma$ is real
    analytic,~\cref{eqn:classical_one_neuron_contribution} is real analytic in
    the parameters of one neuron, and so is every entry of
    $\boldsymbol\Psi$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a real Banach space of \(\mathbb R^{d_2}\)-valued
functions embedded continuously in \(L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) as in clause
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}\), and let a loss-scaled bounded linear functional
\(\lambda_i\in\mathcal X^*\) induce a tested scalar constraint. Suppose the
complete one-neuron map
\(z\mapsto\mathbf a\,\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\cdot+\gamma b)\) is \(C^2\), or
more generally \(C^{1,1}\), as an \(\mathcal X\)-valued map on an open
neighborhood of the compact parameter tube \(\mathcal Z_R\). Then
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} verifies
\cref{eqn:predictionmap,eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}, with the explicit
constants in~\cref{eqn:bounded_functional_regularity_constants} (with
\(L_i=\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}M_{1,1}\) in the \(C^{1,1}\) case). In
particular, a continuous weak bilinear form with a fixed test function
satisfies the dual-norm estimate in
\cref{eqn:weak_functional_dual_norm_bound}; mixed weak-residual and bounded
boundary rows are covered when they act on one common trial space.
Finite-measure rows are the case \(\mathcal X=C(D;\mathbb R^{d_2})\) with
\(\|\lambda_i\|_{\mathcal X^*}\leq\sum_q\|\bar\nu_{iq}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\);
\Cref{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity} gives the sharper
constants~\cref{eqn:finite_measure_regularity_constants} for them directly
under \(\sigma\in C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}\). Fixed-node quadrature rules without
derivative evaluations are atomic finite-measure rows and fall under that
proposition; rules containing derivative evaluations are a special case here
whenever every evaluation used by the rule is bounded on the chosen trial
space. Singular
integral, fractional, and continuum weak constraints require this regularity
check; coefficient boundedness alone does not suffice.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:generallinearNTK}
    If the row-regularity condition in~\Cref{assump:general} holds, the
    deterministic-limit, finite-width concentration, and local stability
    statements in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK}
    hold, with bounded continuous parameter-derivative functions.
    For strong-form differential constraints of any fixed order, these
    functions are real analytic in the per-neuron parameters when \(\sigma\)
    is, by~\Cref{prop:linearNTK}.
    Weak or nonlocal cases require separate verification of this property.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
\phantomsection
        \label{proof:ntk_deterministic}
Order the coordinates of \(z=\theta_m\), and define the parameter-derivative functions
\begin{equation*}
 \psi_{i,p}(z)=\partial_{z_p}h_i(z),\qquad p\in[d_\theta].
\end{equation*}
Take one infinite i.i.d.\ sequence of per-neuron parameter vectors and construct
the width-\(d_1\) network from its first \(d_1\) vectors. Embedding these models in
a common probability space gives almost-sure convergence as
\(d_1\to\infty\); fresh independent resampling at each size gives
convergence in probability. The prediction components
and constraint design remain fixed, or one samples them independently of the
parameter sequence; in the latter case, the following limit is conditional on
the realized design. The sum over neurons in~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} gives,
exactly,
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}
 =\frac1{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\sum_{p=1}^{d_\theta}
 \psi_{i,p}(\theta_{m,(0)})\psi_{j,p}(\theta_{m,(0)}).
\end{equation*}
For fixed \(i,j,p\), these terms are i.i.d.\ by~\Cref{assump:main} and
bounded by~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}. The strong law therefore gives the
almost-sure deterministic limit
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{ij}
 =\sum_{p=1}^{d_\theta}\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}
   [\psi_{i,p}(z)\psi_{j,p}(z)].
\end{equation*}
Equivalently,
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}[\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\boldsymbol\Psi(z)^\top]\),
the population NTK of the main text. Among the \(d_\theta\) coordinates of
\(z\), \(d_2\) correspond to output weights and \(d_0+1\) to hidden affine
parameters. Each trainable coordinate \(p\in[d_\theta]\) contributes the
positive-semidefinite Gram matrix
\([\langle\Phi_i^{(p)},\Phi_j^{(p)}\rangle_{L^2(\mu)}]_{i,j\in[N]}\) of the
functions \(\Phi_i^{(p)}:=\psi_{i,p}\in L^2(\mu)\), so
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) is the positive-semidefinite sum of these
\(d_\theta\) matrices. These functions are bounded by \(B_i\) and Lipschitz
on every ball \(\overline{\mathbb B}_R(z_0)\), \(z_0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\),
by~\Cref{assump:general}, hence continuous on \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\); in particular
\(\psi_{i,p}\in L^2(\mu)\). For the strong-form differential rows
of~\Cref{prop:linearNTK} with real analytic \(\sigma\), they are analytic in
the parameters of a single neuron.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth}
    Suppose the condition in~\Cref{assump:general} holds and the fixed design has a
    positive-definiteness certificate as
    in~\Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate}, so
    \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0\), and let
    \(0<\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\) be a certified
    lower bound, and fix $0<\delta<1$. Set
    \begin{equation*}
    R_K:=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\sim\mu}
       \|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\|_2^2\leq B_*^2
    \quad\text{(by~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds})},
    \qquad
    c_{\mathrm{Ch}}:=\frac14+\frac34\log\frac34.
    \end{equation*}
    If
    \begin{equation*}
    d_1\geq \frac{R_K}{c_{\mathrm{Ch}}\lambda_0}
       \log\!\left(\frac{N}{\delta}\right),
    \end{equation*}
    then $\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\geq3\lambda_0/4$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
\phantomsection
    \label{proof:positive_definitenessfinitewidth}
Let $\mathbf J_{(0),m}\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_\theta}$ denote the
initialization-Jacobian block for neuron $m$, and define
\begin{equation*}
\boldsymbol\Psi_m=\sqrt{d_1}\,\mathbf J_{(0),m}
=\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{m,(0)}),
\qquad
\mathbf G_m=\boldsymbol\Psi_m\boldsymbol\Psi_m^\top.
\end{equation*}
The per-neuron parameter vectors are i.i.d., each $\mathbf G_m$ is positive semidefinite, and
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf K_{(0)}=\frac1{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\mathbf G_m,
\qquad
\mathbb E\mathbf G_m=\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty.
\end{equation*}
Because \(\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf G_m)=\|\boldsymbol\Psi_m\|_2^2\) and
\(\theta_{m,(0)}\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\) almost surely, the bounds
in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} give the almost-sure estimate
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf G_m)
 \leq R_K
 =\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\sim\mu}\|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\|_2^2
 \leq\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\sim\mu}
       \|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\|_F^2
 \leq B_*^2.
\end{equation*}

Apply the lower-tail matrix Chernoff
inequality~\citep[Corollary~5.2]{Tropp2012} to the independent summands
\(\mathbf X_m=\mathbf G_m/d_1\), which satisfy
\(\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf X_m)\leq R_K/d_1\) almost surely and
\(\mu_{\min}:=\lambda_{\min}(\sum_m\mathbb E\mathbf X_m)
=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\geq\lambda_0\). Since
\(\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\leq(1-\varepsilon)\lambda_0\}\subseteq
\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\leq(1-\varepsilon)\mu_{\min}\}\) and the
base \(e^{-\varepsilon}/(1-\varepsilon)^{1-\varepsilon}\) lies in \((0,1]\),
replacing \(\mu_{\min}\) by \(\lambda_0\) in the exponent only weakens the
bound, and we obtain, for $0\leq\varepsilon<1$,
\begin{equation*}
\Pr\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})
\leq(1-\varepsilon)\lambda_0\right\}
\leq N\left[
 \frac{e^{-\varepsilon}}{(1-\varepsilon)^{1-\varepsilon}}
 \right]^{d_1\lambda_0/R_K}.
\end{equation*}
Setting $\varepsilon=1/4$ gives the exponent $c_{\mathrm{Ch}}>0$
(so $c_{\mathrm{Ch}}^{-1}\approx29.207$) and yields
\begin{equation*}
\Pr\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})
\leq\frac34\lambda_0\right\}
\leq N\exp\!\left(-c_{\mathrm{Ch}}
                      \frac{d_1\lambda_0}{R_K}\right).
\end{equation*}
The stated width makes the right-hand side at most $\delta$, proving the claim.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The same argument can retain the population geometry. Define the
largest eigenvalue of a one-neuron Gram term in limiting-NTK coordinates:
\begin{equation*}
 \tau_K:=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\sim\mu}
 \lambda_{\max}\!\left(
   (\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)^{-1/2}
   \boldsymbol\Psi(z)\boldsymbol\Psi(z)^\top
   (\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)^{-1/2}\right).
\end{equation*}
The resulting whitened matrices have expectation \(\mathbf I_N\) and are bounded above
by \(\tau_K\mathbf I_N\). Matrix Chernoff therefore yields
\begin{equation*}
 \Pr\!\left\{\mathbf K_{(0)}\not\succeq
                   \frac34\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\right\}
 \leq N\exp\!\left(-c_{\mathrm{Ch}}d_1/\tau_K\right).
\end{equation*}
Indeed, the inequality first gives the good event for
\((\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)^{-1/2}\mathbf K_{(0)}
 (\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)^{-1/2}\), and congruence by
\((\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)^{1/2}\) gives the displayed matrix-order inequality.
Thus
\(d_1\geq c_{\mathrm{Ch}}^{-1}\tau_K\log(N/\delta)\) is an alternative
sufficient width for the event
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}\succeq\frac34\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\). Since
\(\tau_K\leq R_K/\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\), it is never larger
than the width in~\Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth} with
\(\lambda_0=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\), but it requires the
whitened quantity \(\tau_K\) rather than only \(R_K\) and a certified
\(\lambda_0\).
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
An entrywise Hoeffding alternative with $B_K$ an almost-sure upper bound on
the range of each scalar summand requires
$d_1=\Omega(B_K^2N^2\lambda_0^{-2}\log(N/\delta))$. It takes a union over
the $N^2$ entries and then uses the Frobenius norm. Matrix
Chernoff exploits positivity and controls the required lower eigenvalue directly.
Its sufficient width is
$d_1=\Omega(R_K\lambda_0^{-1}\log(N/\delta))$. With a fixed number of loss
groups and each row divided by the square root of its group's sample count,
$B_K=O(1/N)$ and $R_K=O(1)$, so the two widths are
$\Omega(\lambda_0^{-2}\log(N/\delta))$ and
$\Omega(\lambda_0^{-1}\log(N/\delta))$; without normalization $B_K=O(1)$ and
$R_K=O(N)$ generically, and they are
$\Omega(N^2\lambda_0^{-2}\log(N/\delta))$ and
$\Omega(N\lambda_0^{-1}\log(N/\delta))$. In both regimes the Chernoff width
is never larger, since, with $B_K=\max_iB_i^2$,
$\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\leq N^{-1}\sum_iB_i^2\leq B_K$
and $R_K\leq B_*^2\leq NB_K$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:positive_definiteness_via_parameters}
    Suppose the condition in~\Cref{assump:general} holds, let
    $\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}$, which holds almost surely
    under~\Cref{assump:main}, and let
    $\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$. Then
    $\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K(\theta))\leq B_*^2$ and
    \begin{equation}
    \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K(\theta))
    \geq\left(
      \sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})}
      -\frac{L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}
       \|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
    \right)_+^2;
    \label{eqn:direct_jacobian_stability_bound}
    \end{equation}
    for an iterate $\theta=\theta_{(k)}$ this bounds
    $\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(k)})$. In particular, if $0<\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}}<\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})$ and
    \begin{equation}
    \frac{L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}
      \|\theta_{(k)}-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
    \leq
      \sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})}-\sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}}},
    \label{eqn:direct_jacobian_stability_condition}
    \end{equation}
    then $\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\geq\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}}$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
\phantomsection
    \label{proof:positive_definiteness_via_parameters}
For any real matrix $\mathbf A$ with $N$ rows, write
\(\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf A):=
\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf A\mathbf A^\top)}\); this convention includes
the necessary zero singular values when $\mathbf A$ has fewer than $N$
columns.
Recall that
\(\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_\theta}\) satisfies
\([\boldsymbol\Psi(z)]_{ip}=\partial h_i(z)/\partial z_p\). Summing the row
bounds in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} over $i\in[N]$ and
using~\cref{eqn:abstract_aggregate_constants} together with
$\|\cdot\|_2\leq\|\cdot\|_F$ gives, for every $z_0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$ and all
$z,z'\in\overline{\mathbb B}_R(z_0)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\|_2\leq B_*,\qquad
 \|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)-\boldsymbol\Psi(z')\|_F^2
 =\sum_{i=1}^N\|\nabla h_i(z)-\nabla h_i(z')\|_2^2
 \leq L_*^2\|z-z'\|_2^2.
\end{equation*}
Fix $\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$. By~\cref{eqn:abstract_product_tube},
$\theta_m\in\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\theta_{m,(0)})$ for every $m$, and
$\theta_{m,(0)}\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$ by hypothesis, so the displayed bounds apply to
each pair $(z,z')=(\theta_m,\theta_{m,(0)})$ with $z_0=\theta_{m,(0)}$.
Write the full prediction Jacobian as a horizontal concatenation over neurons:
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf J(\theta)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}
 [\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_1)\ \cdots\ \boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{d_1})].
\end{equation*}
Then
\begin{align}
 \|\mathbf J(\theta)-\mathbf J(\theta_{(0)})\|_2^2
 &\leq \|\mathbf J(\theta)-\mathbf J(\theta_{(0)})\|_F^2
 =\frac1{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}
  \|\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_m)-\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{m,(0)})\|_F^2\nonumber\\
 &\leq \frac{L_*^2}{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\|\theta_m-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2^2
 =\frac{L_*^2}{d_1}\|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2^2,
 \label{eqn:direct_jacobian_perturbation}
\end{align}
so that
\(\|\mathbf J(\theta)-\mathbf J(\theta_{(0)})\|_2
\leq L_*\|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2/\sqrt{d_1}\).
Also, because \(\mathbf K(\theta)=\mathbf J(\theta)\mathbf J(\theta)^\top\), for
every \(\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\),
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K(\theta))
 \leq\frac1{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\|\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_m)\|_2^2
 \leq B_*^2.
\end{equation*}
Weyl's inequality for singular values,
\(|\sigma_N(\mathbf A)-\sigma_N(\mathbf B)|\leq\|\mathbf A-\mathbf B\|_2\),
and~\cref{eqn:direct_jacobian_perturbation} yield
\begin{align*}
 \sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J(\theta))
 &\geq \sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J(\theta_{(0)}))
       -\|\mathbf J(\theta)-\mathbf J(\theta_{(0)})\|_2\\
 &\geq \sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})}
       -\frac{L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}
        \|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2.
\end{align*}
Taking the positive part and using
\(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf J\mathbf J^\top)=\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J)^2\)
proves~\cref{eqn:direct_jacobian_stability_bound}. Under the condition
in~\cref{eqn:direct_jacobian_stability_condition}, the right-hand side
of~\cref{eqn:direct_jacobian_stability_bound} at \(\theta=\theta_{(k)}\) is
at least \(\lambda_{\mathrm{thr}}\), which establishes the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:jinwu_sigma_independence}
Let \(\sigma\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)\) be nonpolynomial, and let
\(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_M\in\mathbb R^{d_0}\) be pairwise distinct.
For each \(r\in[M]\), let \(J_r\subset\mathbb N_0^{d_0}\) be finite and
nonempty and let \((\kappa_{r,\alpha})_{\alpha\in J_r}\) be nonzero
coefficients. Define
\begin{equation}
Q_r(\mathbf w,v)
=\sum_{\alpha\in J_r}\kappa_{r,\alpha}
\sigma^{(|\alpha|)}(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_r+v)\mathbf w^\alpha.
\label{eqn:jinwu_specialized_polynomial}
\end{equation}
Then \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_M\) are linearly independent as functions on
\(\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\).
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Because \(J_r\) is a set, the monomials \(\mathbf w^\alpha\),
\(\alpha\in J_r\), are pairwise distinct,
so~\cref{eqn:jinwu_specialized_polynomial} contains no like terms; every
coefficient \(\kappa_{r,\alpha}\) is nonzero; and the derivative order
\(|\alpha|\) of every summand equals the degree of its monomial
\(\mathbf w^\alpha\). Hence every \(Q_r\) is orderly and nondegenerate, that
is, in the standard form of~\citet[Definition~2]{Jin2026}. Theorem~4
of~\citet{Jin2026} states that if a linear combination, with all coefficients
nonzero, of such standard-form expressions at pairwise distinct sites vanishes
identically on \(\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\), then \(\sigma\) is a polynomial. Suppose
\(\sum_{r=1}^Mc_rQ_r\equiv0\) with not all \(c_r\) zero. Omitting the indices
with \(c_r=0\) leaves a nonempty relation satisfying these hypotheses, which
would force \(\sigma\) to be a polynomial, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:quantitative_dntk_bound}
Use the two-layer network in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}, with its output
weights trainable, and let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N$ be any fixed linear
observations on a common function space containing the coordinate ridge
features. Set $P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))$ and write
\(\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)=\boldsymbol\Phi_{\mathrm{out}}(\boldsymbol\xi)
\in\mathbb R^{N\times d_2}\) for the output feature matrix of the main text,
\begin{equation*}
F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
=\lambda_i\!\left(\mathbf e_q\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}\right),
\qquad \boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b),\qquad
\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf x)=\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b).
\end{equation*}
Assume $F_{iq}\in L^2(\mu_h)$ for every $i,q$ and that the full limiting NTK
over all trainable parameters exists. The output-weight contribution is then
\(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\sim\mu_h}
[\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)^\top]\). Suppose there are
pairwise disjoint measurable sets \(E_1,\ldots,E_L\), parameter values
\(\boldsymbol\xi_\ell\), and numbers \(\beta>0\),
\(\varepsilon\geq0\)
such that
\begin{equation*}
\mu_h(E_\ell)\geq\beta,
\qquad
\sup_{\boldsymbol\xi\in E_\ell}
\|\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)-\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi_\ell)\|_2
\leq\varepsilon.
\end{equation*}
Let
\(\mathbf V=\left(\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi_1)^\top,\ldots,
\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi_L)^\top\right)^\top
\in\mathbb R^{Ld_2\times N}\), and assume
\(c_{\mathrm{sep}}:=\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf V)
=\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf V^\top\mathbf V)}>0\). Then
\begin{equation}
\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)
\geq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty)
\geq \frac{\beta c_{\mathrm{sep}}^2}{2}-\varepsilon^2.
\label{eqn:quantitative_dntk_bound}
\end{equation}
In particular, \(\varepsilon\leq c_{\mathrm{sep}}\sqrt\beta/2\) implies
\(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\geq\beta c_{\mathrm{sep}}^2/4\).

For the pointwise constraints of~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, this statement
specializes to
\begin{equation*}
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =s_i(\mathcal A_{iq}\sigma_{\mathbf w,b})(\mathbf x_i).
\end{equation*}
For the weak and nonlocal rows considered below, respectively, it specializes
to
\begin{equation*}
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =s_i a_i(\mathbf e_q\sigma_{\mathbf w,b},v_i),
 \qquad
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =s_i\int_D\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf y)\,d\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y).
\end{equation*}
Thus the same finite-witness lower bound applies to a combined
residual--boundary feature matrix in the pointwise, weak, or nonlocal setting. No
analyticity or density hypothesis is needed for this quantitative implication
once the displayed features and limiting kernels exist.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:fully_numerical_gd_certificate}
This example instantiates every constant in~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}
for one continuum nonlocal observation. It is a deliberately conservative
certificate, not a claim that the resulting width is necessary or practically
optimal. Let $d_0=d_2=1$, $\Omega=(-1,1)$, $D=\overline\Omega$, $\gamma=1$,
$\sigma=\tanh$, $s=1$, and
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda(f)=\frac12\int_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,dx,
 \qquad v_T=0.
\end{equation*}
Thus $N=1$ and, for $z=(w,b,a)$, the per-neuron prediction is
\begin{equation*}
 h(z)=aF(w,b),
 \qquad
 F(w,b)=\frac12\int_{-1}^{1}\tanh(wx+b)\,dx.
\end{equation*}
Initialize the neuron parameters independently across neurons, with mutually
independent coordinates
\begin{equation*}
 w\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-0.1,0.1],\qquad
 b\sim\operatorname{Unif}[1,2],\qquad
 a\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-0.1,0.1].
\end{equation*}
The law is width independent and compactly supported, its hidden marginal has
support with nonempty interior, and
$\mathbb E[a\mid w,b]=0$. Set $R=0.1$ and $\delta=0.05$.

We now verify the constants. At initialization, $wx+b\geq0.9$ for every
$x\in[-1,1]$. Since $\tanh$ is increasing,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)
 &=[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{11}
  =\mathbb E\|\nabla h(z)\|_2^2\\
 &\geq\mathbb E\bigl[(\partial_a h(z))^2\bigr]
  =\mathbb E[F(w,b)^2]
  \geq\tanh(0.9)^2=:\lambda_0>0.51308.
\end{aligned}
\label{eqn:numerical_certificate_gap}
\end{equation}
Writing subscripts for derivatives of $F$, differentiation under the integral
gives
\begin{equation*}
 |F|\leq1,\qquad |F_w|\leq\frac12,\qquad |F_b|\leq1.
\end{equation*}
Because
$\nabla h=(aF_w,aF_b,F)$, the initialization bound $|a|\leq0.1$ yields
\begin{equation}
 R_K\leq1+0.1^2\left(\frac14+1\right)=1.0125.
 \label{eqn:numerical_certificate_RK}
\end{equation}
Every point in a radius-$R$ per-neuron neighborhood satisfies $|a|\leq0.2$.
The same derivative bounds therefore give the valid local choice
\begin{equation}
 B_*^2=1.05.
 \label{eqn:numerical_certificate_B}
\end{equation}

For completeness, the gradient-Lipschitz bound follows from the Hessian rather
than from an unspecified smoothness constant. The sharp global bound
\begin{equation*}
 \|\tanh''\|_\infty=\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}=:c_2
\end{equation*}
implies
\begin{equation*}
 |F_{ww}|\leq\frac{c_2}{3},\qquad
 |F_{wb}|\leq\frac{c_2}{2},\qquad
 |F_{bb}|\leq c_2.
\end{equation*}
Since
\begin{equation*}
 \nabla^2h=
 \begin{pmatrix}
  aF_{ww}&aF_{wb}&F_w\\
  aF_{wb}&aF_{bb}&F_b\\
  F_w&F_b&0
 \end{pmatrix},
\end{equation*}
its operator norm is at most its Frobenius norm, and throughout the local
neighborhood
\begin{align}
 \|\nabla^2h\|_2^2
 &\leq0.2^2c_2^2
 \left(\frac19+\frac12+1\right)
 +2\left(\frac14+1\right)\notag\\
 &=\frac{30839}{12150}<2.5382.
 \label{eqn:numerical_certificate_L}
\end{align}
Hence $L_*^2=2.5382$ is valid. Finally, $A_{0,*}=0.1$ and independence of
$a$ and $(w,b)$ give
\begin{equation*}
 H_0^2=\mathbb E[h(z)^2]
 \leq\mathbb E[a^2]=\frac{0.1^2}{3}.
\end{equation*}
Consequently, the initialization-residual quantity at $\delta=0.05$ obeys
\begin{equation}
 \overline r_{0.05}
 \leq\frac{0.1}{\sqrt3}
 +0.1\sqrt{2\log40}
 =:\widehat r<0.32936.
 \label{eqn:numerical_certificate_rbar}
\end{equation}
Here $\widehat r$ denotes the exact expression on the left of the last
inequality; $0.32936$ is its display rounding, and the bounds below are
evaluated with the exact value (with the rounded value the second bound
would read $1356.02$ and the integer width below would become $1357$).

Substitution of
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_0=\tanh(0.9)^2,\quad
 R_K\leq1.0125,\quad \Lambda=B_*^2=1.05,\quad
 L_*^2=2.5382,\quad \overline r_{0.05}\leq\widehat r
\end{equation*}
into the three width terms
in~\cref{eqn:linear_pde_convergence_conditions} gives, using outward-rounded
interval evaluation and
$c_{\mathrm{Ch}}=\frac14+\frac34\log\frac34$,
\begin{align*}
 \frac{1.0125\log40}{c_{\mathrm{Ch}}\lambda_0}
 &<212.613,\\
 (320+128\sqrt6)
 \frac{2.5382(1.05)\widehat r^2}{\lambda_0^3}
 &<1355.980,\\
 \frac{16(1.05)\widehat r^2}
 {0.1^2\lambda_0^2}
 &<692.252,
\end{align*}
respectively. Therefore the integer width and step-size choices
\begin{equation}
 d_1\geq1356,\qquad 0<\eta\leq\frac{10}{21}
 \label{eqn:numerical_certificate_width_step}
\end{equation}
satisfy the theorem. With probability at least $0.95$, simultaneously for
every $k\geq0$,
\begin{align*}
 \max_{m\in[d_1]}\|\theta_{m,(k)}-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2&\leq0.1,\\
 \mathbf K_{(k)}&\succeq\frac{\tanh(0.9)^2}{2}\mathbf I_1,\\
 \mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})
 &\leq\bigl(1-\eta\tanh(0.9)^2\bigr)^k\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)}).
\end{align*}
This calculation is for the exact integral functional, not a quadrature
surrogate. Its purpose is to show that the theorem's sufficient conditions can
be evaluated end to end; the constants deliberately use elementary global
derivative bounds and are not optimized.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:positive_definiteness}
For $N$ sampled scalar rows, let \(\Phi_i\in L^2(\mu)\)
be real-valued parameter-derivative functions that are continuous on
\(\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\), and define
\([\mathbf K]_{ij}=\langle\Phi_i,\Phi_j\rangle_{L^2(\mu)}\).
Then \(\mathbf K\) is positive definite if and only if
\(\{\Phi_i\}_{i=1}^N\) is linearly independent in \(L^2(\mu)\), equivalently
on \(\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\).
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:positive_definiteness}
Given the limiting representation in the first item of~\Cref{thm:linearNTK}, let
\(\Phi_i^{(p)}\) denote the feature associated with constraint \(i\) in the
NTK contribution from coordinate \(p\), and
define its coordinate Gram matrix by
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}^{\infty,(p)}]_{ij}
 =\langle\Phi_i^{(p)},\Phi_j^{(p)}\rangle_{L^2(\mu)}.
\end{equation*}
Then \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) is positive definite if and only if the direct sums
of parameter-derivative functions
\begin{equation*}
\left(\Phi_i^{(1)},\ldots,\Phi_i^{(d_\theta)}\right),
\qquad i\in[N],
\end{equation*}
are linearly independent in \(L^2(\mu)^{d_\theta}\). Moreover,
\begin{equation*}
\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\bigcap_{p=1}^{d_\theta}\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^{\infty,(p)},
\qquad
\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigcap_{p=1}^{d_\theta}\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^{\infty,(p)}=\{0\}.
\end{equation*}
In particular, a positive-definite contribution from one coordinate
is sufficient but, in general, not necessary.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The claim follows by applying~\Cref{lem:direct_sum_feature_criterion} to the
summands in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:analytic_functional_rank}
For the two-layer network in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}, with its output
weights trainable, let
$P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))$, where the $\lambda_i$ are
linear on a common space containing all network realizations and all
single-neuron functions displayed below. Define
\begin{equation*}
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =\lambda_i\!\left(
 \mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)\right),
 \qquad \boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b).
\end{equation*}
Suppose every $F_{iq}$ is real analytic on $\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$, the hidden
law $\mu_h$ has compact support with nonempty interior, and the full limiting
NTK exists. Fix $\boldsymbol\xi_\star\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$. For
$K\in\mathbb N_0$, let
$\mathcal I_K=\{\boldsymbol\rho\in\mathbb N_0^{d_0+1}:
|\boldsymbol\rho|\leq K\}$, and define
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf C_K(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)
 =\left[
 \frac{1}{\boldsymbol\rho!}
 \partial_{\boldsymbol\xi}^{\boldsymbol\rho}
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)
 \right]_{\substack{i\in[N]\\(q,\boldsymbol\rho)\in[d_2]\times\mathcal I_K}}.
\end{equation*}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
 =\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\bigcap_{K\geq0}\ker\mathbf C_K(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)^\top.
 \label{eqn:analytic_coefficient_nullspace}
\end{equation}
Consequently, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$;
\item $\operatorname{rank}\mathbf C_K(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)=N$ for some finite $K$;
\item for some finite parameter set
$\Xi=\{\boldsymbol\xi^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol\xi^{(T)}\}$, the following
evaluation matrix has row rank $N$:
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf E_\Xi=\left[F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi^{(t)})\right]_{i,(t,q)}.
\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, $\Xi$ may be chosen within any prescribed nonempty open subset of
$\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For $\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N$, the output-weight Gram representation gives
