\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\mathbf c
 =\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int
 \left|\sum_{i=1}^Nc_iF_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)\right|^2
 \,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi).
\end{equation*}
If the quadratic form vanishes, continuity forces each such sum to be null on
$\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$.
Because this set contains an open subset, the identity theorem makes each
combination identically zero. This conclusion is equivalent to the vanishing of all Taylor
coefficients at $\boldsymbol\xi_\star$, proving the output-weight equality
in~\cref{eqn:analytic_coefficient_nullspace}.

The same relation among these features also gives, at every
finite width and parameter value,
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{i=1}^N c_iP_i(\theta)
 =\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}(\mathbf a_m)_q
 \sum_{i=1}^N c_iF_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi_m)=0.
\end{equation*}
Differentiation shows that $\mathbf c$ annihilates every gradient block.
Conversely, the output-weight kernel is a positive-semidefinite
summand of the full limiting kernel. The two implications prove the
identity in~\cref{eqn:analytic_coefficient_nullspace}.

The columns of the matrices $\mathbf C_K(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)$, $K\geq0$,
span $\mathbb R^N$ exactly when
$\bigcap_K\ker\mathbf C_K(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)^\top=\{0\}$. Since
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf C_K(\boldsymbol\xi_\star)$ is nondecreasing in $K$ and bounded
by $N$, it stabilizes, so full rank is reached at a finite $K$. Applying the
same left-nullspace
argument to the evaluation vectors proves assertion (iii). If their span were deficient on
a nonempty open set, a nonzero such combination would vanish there and
hence everywhere, contradicting condition (i).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:monomial_moment_rank}
In the setting of~\Cref{prop:analytic_functional_rank}, suppose that
$\sigma$ is real analytic and nonpolynomial and $\gamma>0$ (two conditions
not contained in clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$), and that the maps
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto
\mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)$ are analytic in a common
Banach trial space $\mathcal X$ on which every $\lambda_i$ is bounded and
whose norm convergence implies pointwise convergence along a subsequence,
almost everywhere on $\Omega$ for the $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$-embedded spaces of
clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and everywhere on $D$ for
$C(D;\mathbb R^{d_2})$ on a compact $D$. For
$p_\alpha(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^\alpha$, choose,
for each $\alpha$, an $r_\alpha\in\mathbb N_0$ such that
$\sigma^{(|\alpha|+r_\alpha)}(0)\neq0$. Banach-valued differentiation gives
\begin{equation*}
 \left.
 \partial_{\mathbf w}^{\alpha}\partial_b^{r_\alpha}
 \left[\mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)\right]
 \right|_{(\mathbf w,b)=(\mathbf0,0)}
 =\gamma^{r_\alpha}\sigma^{(|\alpha|+r_\alpha)}(0)
 \mathbf e_q p_\alpha\in\mathcal X.
\end{equation*}
Thus $\mathbf e_q p_\alpha\in\mathcal X$, and we may define
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf M_K=\left[\lambda_i(\mathbf e_q p_\alpha)\right]_
 {\substack{i\in[N]\\q\in[d_2],\ |\alpha|\leq K}}.
\end{equation*}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\bigcap_{K\geq0}\ker\mathbf M_K^\top,
 \qquad
 \mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf M_K=N\ \text{for some finite }K.
 \label{eqn:monomial_rank_equivalence}
\end{equation}
For weak functionals $\lambda_i(f)=s_i a_i(f,v_i)$ and integral observations,
respectively, the entries become
\begin{align}
 [\mathbf M_K^{\mathrm{weak}}]_{i,(q,\alpha)}
 &=s_i a_i(\mathbf e_q p_\alpha,v_i),
 \label{eqn:weak_monomial_matrix}\\
 [\mathbf M_K^{\mathrm{nl}}]_{i,(q,\alpha)}
 &=s_i\int_D p_\alpha(\mathbf y)\,d\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y).
 \label{eqn:nonlocal_moment_matrix}
\end{align}
On compact $D$, the loss-scaled measure tuples
$\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_1,\ldots,\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_N$ are linearly independent if
and only if $\mathbf M_K^{\mathrm{nl}}$ is surjective onto $\mathbb R^N$ for some finite $K$. If instead
every $\nu_{iq}$ is a combination of Dirac masses at a common finite set of
distinct nodes $\mathbf y_1,\ldots,\mathbf y_A$,
$\nu_{iq}=\sum_{a=1}^A m_{iqa}\delta_{\mathbf y_a}$, then independence of the
loss-scaled measure tuples is equivalent to
row rank $N$ of the Dirac-coefficient matrix
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf C^{\mathrm{Dirac}}=\left[s_im_{iqa}\right]_{i,(q,a)}.
 \label{eqn:nonlocal_dirac_coefficient_matrix}
\end{equation}
Include all residual and boundary rows jointly in these matrices.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
At $\boldsymbol\xi_\star=(\mathbf0,b_\star)$, boundedness of $\lambda_i$
and Banach-valued analyticity allow differentiation through the functional.
For every $r\in\mathbb N_0$,
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{\mathbf w}^{\alpha}\partial_b^rF_{iq}(\mathbf0,b_\star)
 =\gamma^r\sigma^{(|\alpha|+r)}(\gamma b_\star)
 \lambda_i(\mathbf e_q p_\alpha).
 \label{eqn:functional_feature_taylor_moment_identity}
\end{equation}
At every real center, a nonpolynomial analytic function has nonzero
derivatives of arbitrarily high order. Hence, for each $\alpha$, some
$r\in\mathbb N_0$ makes the prefactor
in~\cref{eqn:functional_feature_taylor_moment_identity} not vanish. The
Taylor-coefficient vectors and
$[\lambda_i(\mathbf e_q p_\alpha)]_{i=1}^N$ therefore span the same subspace of
$\mathbb R^N$. Equivalently, their common left nullspaces coincide.
\Cref{prop:analytic_functional_rank} then
proves~\cref{eqn:monomial_rank_equivalence} and the two displayed
specializations.

For compact $D$, the Stone--Weierstrass theorem makes polynomial restrictions
dense in $C(D)$, so a finite signed regular Borel measure that annihilates
all polynomials annihilates $C(D)$ and vanishes by Riesz uniqueness.
Thus the infinite moment matrix has row rank $N$ exactly when the loss-scaled
tuples $\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_1,\ldots,\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_N$ admit no nonzero
linear relation; finite dimensionality makes the rank
visible at some finite $K$. For the discrete measures above, distinct Dirac
masses are linearly independent,
giving~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_dirac_coefficient_matrix}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:ridge_density_sobolev}
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{d_0}\) be a bounded open set with the segment
property (for instance a bounded Lipschitz domain), \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), and
\(\mathcal X=H^k(\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\). Let \(\sigma\) be real analytic
and nonpolynomial and \(\gamma>0\). Then every map
\(\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}
=\mathbf e_q\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\!\cdot+\gamma b)\) is real analytic from
\(\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\) into \(\mathcal X\), and
\begin{equation*}
 \overline{\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}:
 \boldsymbol\xi\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1},\ q\in[d_2]\}}^{\mathcal X}
 =\mathcal X .
\end{equation*}
Consequently the analyticity and density conditions displayed in clause
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}\) of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} hold for this trial
space in every dimension \(d_0\); the remaining condition of
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}\), \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing\),
concerns \(\mu_h\) alone. Clause
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}\) is then verified for a given finite family of
rows by~\Cref{cor:weak_Hk_row_regularity} as soon as every row is bounded on
\(\mathcal X\).
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
\emph{Analyticity.} Fix \(\boldsymbol\xi_0=(\mathbf w_0,b_0)\). The arguments
\(t_0(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w_0^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b_0\), \(\mathbf x\in\overline\Omega\),
lie in a compact interval \(I\). A real analytic \(\sigma\) extends
holomorphically to a complex neighborhood of \(I\), so the Cauchy estimates
give \(\sup_{t\in I}|\sigma^{(n)}(t)|\leq C\,n!\,\rho^{-n}\) for some
\(C,\rho>0\) and all \(n\). For
\(\boldsymbol\xi=\boldsymbol\xi_0+\boldsymbol\delta\) with
\(\boldsymbol\delta=(\boldsymbol\delta_{\mathbf w},\delta_b)\), Taylor's
theorem in the scalar argument gives
\begin{equation*}
 \sigma(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b)
 =\sum_{n\geq0}\frac1{n!}\,\sigma^{(n)}(t_0(\mathbf x))
 \bigl(\boldsymbol\delta_{\mathbf w}^\top\mathbf x+\gamma\delta_b\bigr)^n .
\end{equation*}
The \(n\)-th term is a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(n\) in
\(\boldsymbol\delta\) with coefficients in \(C^k(\overline\Omega)\):
differentiating it \(j\leq k\) times in \(\mathbf x\) produces
\(\sigma^{(n+i)}(t_0(\mathbf x))\), \(i\leq j\), times polynomials in
\(\boldsymbol\delta_{\mathbf w}\) and in
\(\boldsymbol\delta_{\mathbf w}^\top\mathbf x+\gamma\delta_b\) of total degree
\(n\), so by the Cauchy estimates its \(C^k(\overline\Omega)\) norm is at
most \(C'(n+k)^k(\Lambda_\Omega\|\boldsymbol\delta\|_2/\rho)^n\) with
\(\Lambda_\Omega=\sup_{\mathbf x\in\overline\Omega}\|(\mathbf x,\gamma)\|_2\).
The series therefore converges absolutely in \(C^k(\overline\Omega)\), hence
in \(H^k(\Omega)\) on the bounded set \(\Omega\), for
\(\|\boldsymbol\delta\|_2<\rho/\Lambda_\Omega\), which is real analyticity
into \(\mathcal X\).

\emph{Density.} Let \(V\) be the closed linear span. Derivatives of a
Banach-space-valued analytic map at a point are limits of finite linear
combinations of its values, hence lie in \(V\). By the identity
in~\Cref{cor:monomial_moment_rank},
\(\partial_{\mathbf w}^{\alpha}\partial_b^{r_\alpha}\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}
|_{\boldsymbol\xi=\mathbf0}
=\gamma^{r_\alpha}\sigma^{(|\alpha|+r_\alpha)}(0)\,\mathbf e_q\mathbf x^\alpha\),
and because \(\sigma\) is nonpolynomial, for each \(\alpha\) some
\(r_\alpha\) has \(\sigma^{(|\alpha|+r_\alpha)}(0)\neq0\): otherwise the
Taylor series of \(\sigma\) at \(0\) would terminate and \(\sigma\) would be
a polynomial by analyticity. Thus \(V\) contains every vector monomial
\(\mathbf e_q\mathbf x^\alpha\), hence all \(\mathbb R^{d_2}\)-valued
polynomials. Polynomials are dense in \(H^k(\Omega)\): restrictions to
\(\Omega\) of functions in \(C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{d_0})\) are dense in
\(H^k(\Omega)\) for domains with the segment
property~\citep[Theorem~3.22]{Adams2003}, and any such function is
approximated in \(C^k\) on a compact box containing \(\overline\Omega\) by
polynomials (Weierstrass approximation of the function and its derivatives,
for instance by Bernstein polynomials), hence in \(H^k(\Omega)\). So
\(V=\mathcal X\).
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
For a quadrature-based weak loss, combine repetitions and enumerate the
resulting data as
$(q_a,\mathbf x_a,\alpha_a)\in[d_2]\times\overline\Omega\times
\mathbb N_0^{d_0}$, $a\in[A]$. Define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal Q_a(f)=\partial^{\alpha_a}f_{q_a}(\mathbf x_a),
 \qquad
 \mathbf B=[B_{ia}]\in\mathbb R^{N\times A},\qquad
 \lambda_i=\sum_{a=1}^A B_{ia}\mathcal Q_a.
 \label{eqn:quadrature_derivative_functionals}
\end{equation}
If $\{\mathcal Q_a\}_{a=1}^A$ is linearly independent in $\mathcal X^*$,
then
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \sum_{i=1}^N c_i\lambda_i=0\quad(\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N)
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbf c^\top\mathbf B=0,\\
 \{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^N\text{ is linearly independent}
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}\mathbf B=N.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eqn:quadrature_coefficient_rank}
\end{equation}
The stated equivalence relies on this property in $\mathcal X^*$; distinct
triples alone need not guarantee it for an arbitrary function space. For example, an architecture that
enforces exact boundary conditions can create linear relations among the
restrictions of the $\mathcal Q_a$ to the homogeneous-boundary tangent
subspace $\mathcal X_0$ of~\Cref{rem:derivative_hard_boundary}.
A symbolic nonzero $N\times N$ minor, or a rigorous interval bound containing
its determinant that excludes zero, proves full row rank; a floating-point
singular value is only a numerical diagnostic.
Rescaled orthogonal polynomials are preferable to raw monomials in computations.
Neither~\cref{eqn:monomial_rank_equivalence}
nor~\cref{eqn:quadrature_coefficient_rank} provides an a priori truncation degree or a mesh-uniform positive lower bound
on the smallest eigenvalue, and
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf B=N$ concerns the discretized functionals rather than the
continuum weak problem. A quantitative bound instead needs the finite-witness
data of~\Cref{prop:quantitative_dntk_bound}: pairwise disjoint sets of
$\mu_h$-measure at least $\beta>0$ on which the output feature matrix varies
by at most $\varepsilon$, and $c_{\mathrm{sep}}>0$. The resulting
estimate~\cref{eqn:quantitative_dntk_bound} depends on the design and is not
mesh-uniform either.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:weak_constraint_positivity}
Let \(\mathcal X\) be a Banach space over $\mathbb R$ of
\(\mathbb R^{d_2}\)-valued functions on \(\overline\Omega\), continuously
embedded in \(L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) as in clause \(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}\). For
\(i\in[N]\), let \(\mathcal V_i\) be normed over $\mathbb R$, let
\(a_i:\mathcal X\times\mathcal V_i\to\mathbb R\) be a continuous bilinear
form, fix \(v_i\in\mathcal V_i\), and define the weak prediction functional
and its loss-scaled version by
\begin{equation*}
\ell_i(f)=a_i(f,v_i),
\qquad
\lambda_i=s_i\ell_i\in\mathcal X^*,
\qquad s_i>0.
\end{equation*}
Use \(P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))\) with the network
in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}. Assume~\Cref{assump:main} and the weak
clauses of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} for this $\mathcal X$, the combined
family $\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^N$, and the ridge features
$\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$ of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}.
Define the space of exact relations among the weak constraints by
\begin{equation}
\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}
=\left\{\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N:
\sum_{i=1}^N c_i\lambda_i=0\ \text{in }\mathcal X^*\right\}.
\label{eqn:weak_functional_nullspace}
\end{equation}
Then \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) exists and
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) almost surely along nested widths
(in probability under fresh resampling). Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
=\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}},
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\}.
\label{eqn:weak_exact_ntk_nullspace}
\end{equation}
Consequently, this NTK is positive definite if and only if the
loss-scaled weak functionals are linearly independent in \(\mathcal X^*\).
In particular, suppose \(\mathcal V_i=\mathcal X\), all \(a_i=a\), and
\(a:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is coercive:
\(a(v,v)\geq c_a\|v\|_{\mathcal X}^2\) for some \(c_a>0\).
Then linearly independent test functions \(v_1,\ldots,v_N\) imply
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0\).
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}
Assume~\Cref{assump:main} and the weak clauses of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes} for the combined prediction vector. Let
\(\lambda_i^\Omega\in\mathcal X^*\), \(i\in[N_\Omega]\), be loss-scaled weak
PDE-residual functionals, and let
\(\beta_j^\partial\in\mathcal X^*\), \(j\in[N_\partial]\), be loss-scaled
boundary functionals on the same trial space. Set $N=N_\Omega+N_\partial$.
A boundary functional may be a
tested boundary-restriction (trace) functional or a strong-form pointwise
boundary observation, provided that it is bounded on \(\mathcal X\). Order
the residual rows before the others. Use the combined predictions
\(P_i^\Omega(\theta)=\lambda_i^\Omega(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))\) and
\(P_j^\partial(\theta)=\beta_j^\partial(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))\), and define
\begin{equation}
\mathcal N_{\Omega,\partial}^{\mathrm{weak}}
=\left\{(\mathbf c,\mathbf d)\in
\mathbb R^{N_\Omega}\times\mathbb R^{N_\partial}:
\sum_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}c_i\lambda_i^\Omega
+\sum_{j=1}^{N_\partial}d_j\beta_j^\partial=0
\ \text{in }\mathcal X^*\right\}.
\label{eqn:weak_boundary_joint_nullspace}
\end{equation}
We identify $(\mathbf c,\mathbf d)$ with its concatenation in
$\mathbb R^N$ when comparing the set with a kernel.
Then the mixed output-weight and full limiting NTKs obey
\begin{equation*}
\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
=\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\mathcal N_{\Omega,\partial}^{\mathrm{weak}},
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\dim\operatorname{span}\!\left(
\{\lambda_i^\Omega\}_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}
\cup\{\beta_j^\partial\}_{j=1}^{N_\partial}\right).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, this matrix is positive definite if and only if the
residual and boundary functionals are \emph{jointly} linearly independent.
Checking the two families individually is not sufficient in general.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Apply~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity} to the concatenated family
\(\{\lambda_i^\Omega\}_i\cup\{\beta_j^\partial\}_j\). Any functional
\(\beta\in\mathcal X^*\) not already written as \(s\,a(\cdot,v)\), in
particular each boundary functional, fits the theorem's bilinear notation by
taking \(\mathcal V=\mathbb R\), \(a(f,t)=t\beta(f)\), \(v=1\), and loss
scale one. The
nullspace in~\cref{eqn:weak_functional_nullspace} is then exactly the set
in~\cref{eqn:weak_boundary_joint_nullspace}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson}
Let $\Omega=(-1,1)$, let $\kappa\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfy
$0<\kappa_-\leq\kappa(x)\leq\kappa_+<\infty$ almost everywhere, and take
the common scalar trial space $\mathcal X=H^1(\Omega)$. Fix linearly
independent tests $v_1,\ldots,v_{N_\Omega}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and positive
row scales $s_i,t_-,t_+$. Define the continuum weak-residual and soft
Dirichlet prediction functionals by
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_i^\Omega(f)
 =s_i\int_{-1}^{1}\kappa(x)f'(x)v_i'(x)\,dx,
 \qquad
 \beta_-^\partial(f)=t_-f(-1),
 \qquad
 \beta_+^\partial(f)=t_+f(1).
 \label{eqn:continuum_weak_interface_rows}
\end{equation}
Use the biased scalar two-layer network in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}
with $\sigma=\tanh$ and $\gamma>0$, and assume~\Cref{assump:main} with
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$. Then the full
limiting NTK for the joint family
$\{\lambda_i^\Omega\}_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}\cup
\{\beta_-^\partial,\beta_+^\partial\}$ exists and is positive definite; the
independence proof below supplies its positive-definiteness certificate, and
the monomial procedure in~\Cref{sec:weak_positivity_certificate} gives an
alternative finite certificate for any given test family.
For every fixed localization radius $R>0$ the induced per-neuron prediction
maps satisfy $(\mathsf G_R)$ by~\Cref{cor:weak_H1_row_regularity}. Hence,
under the centering condition
$\mathbb E[a_m\mid w_m,b_m]=0$, for any fixed targets and
$0<\delta<1$, the explicit width and step-size conditions
in~\cref{eqn:linear_pde_convergence_conditions} imply, with probability at
least $1-\delta$, the all-iteration localization, kernel-gap preservation,
and geometric empirical-loss decay in~\cref{eqn:linear_convergence_main}.
In particular, the conclusion applies to the discontinuous
coefficient $\kappa=\mathbf1_{(-1,0)}+2\mathbf1_{[0,1)}$. For the equation
$-(\kappa u')'=g$ with $g\in L^2(\Omega)$ and prescribed endpoint values
$u(-1)=g_-$ and $u(1)=g_+$, the loss-scaled targets paired with
the rows in~\cref{eqn:continuum_weak_interface_rows} are
$s_i\int_{-1}^{1}g(x)v_i(x)\,dx$, $t_-g_-$, and $t_+g_+$, respectively.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The bilinear form
\begin{equation*}
 a(f,v)=\int_{-1}^{1}\kappa(x)f'(x)v'(x)\,dx,
 \qquad (f,v)\in H^1(\Omega)\times H_0^1(\Omega),
\end{equation*}
is continuous by Cauchy--Schwarz, and endpoint evaluation is bounded on
$H^1(\Omega)$ by the one-dimensional trace theorem. Thus all rows
in~\cref{eqn:continuum_weak_interface_rows} belong to $\mathcal X^*$.

For each $(w,b)\in\mathbb R^2$, the ridge $x\mapsto\tanh(wx+\gamma b)$
belongs to $H^1(\Omega)$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 (w,b)\longmapsto\tanh(w\,\cdot+\gamma b)
 \label{eqn:tanh_H1_analytic_map}
\end{equation}
is real analytic as an $H^1(\Omega)$-valued map. Indeed, at any real
$(w_0,b_0)$, the holomorphic extension of $\tanh$ has no pole on the compact
segment $w_0[-1,1]+\gamma b_0$; a sufficiently small complex neighborhood
of $(w_0,b_0)$ therefore gives a holomorphic map into
$C^1([-1,1];\mathbb C)$, and the embedding $C^1([-1,1])\hookrightarrow
H^1(\Omega)$ is continuous.

The span of the ridge functions $\{\tanh(w\,\cdot+\gamma b):(w,b)\in\mathbb R^2\}$
is dense in $H^1(\Omega)$. To see this without invoking a
Sobolev universal-approximation theorem, fix $n\in\mathbb N_0$. Since
$\tanh$ is analytic and nonpolynomial, $\tanh^{(n)}$ is not identically
zero; choose $b_n$ with $\tanh^{(n)}(\gamma b_n)\neq0$. Banach-valued
differentiation of~\cref{eqn:tanh_H1_analytic_map} gives
\begin{equation*}
 \left.\partial_w^n\tanh(wx+\gamma b_n)\right|_{w=0}
 =\tanh^{(n)}(\gamma b_n)x^n.
\end{equation*}
This derivative is an $H^1$ limit of finite linear combinations of ridge
features, so every monomial, and hence every polynomial, lies in the closure
of their span. Polynomials are dense in $H^1(-1,1)$: approximate the weak
derivative of an $H^1$ function in $L^2$ by a polynomial and integrate that
polynomial, matching one endpoint value. Thus the Banach-valued analyticity
and ridge-density requirements in clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes} hold; its hidden-support requirement is assumed in
the statement.
For any fixed $R$, the closed radius-$R$ neighborhood of the compact
initialization support is compact. The complete one-neuron map
$(w,b,a)\mapsto a\tanh(w\,\cdot+\gamma b)$ is $C^\infty$ into
$H^1(\Omega)$, so boundedness of the finitely many rows makes every induced
scalar prediction map $C^{1,1}$ there. Hence clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ also holds, and
\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank} gives existence of the population NTK. Once
joint independence is established below, conditional centering and
\Cref{cor:functional_gd_convergence} give the stated GD conclusion.

It remains to verify joint independence. Suppose, for every $f\in H^1(\Omega)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}c_i\lambda_i^\Omega(f)
 +d_-\beta_-^\partial(f)+d_+\beta_+^\partial(f)=0,
\end{equation*}
and set $v=\sum_i c_i s_i v_i\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Restricting to
$f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ and then choosing $f=v$ yields
$\int_{-1}^{1}\kappa|v'|^2=0$. Coercivity and the zero trace imply $v=0$;
linear independence of the $v_i$ and positivity of the $s_i$ give $c_i=0$
for every $i$. The remaining relation is
$d_-t_-f(-1)+d_+t_+f(1)=0$. Testing with the two affine endpoint cardinal
functions gives $d_-=d_+=0$. The joint criterion
in~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity} now supplies the claimed
positive-definiteness certificate.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:weak_poisson_2d}
Let $\Omega=(-1,1)^2$, let $\kappa\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfy
$0<\kappa_-\leq\kappa\leq\kappa_+<\infty$ almost everywhere, and take the
scalar trial space $\mathcal X=H^1(\Omega)$. Fix linearly independent
polynomial tests $v_1,\ldots,v_{N_\Omega}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, for instance
the products $(1-x_1^2)(1-x_2^2)\mathbf x^\alpha$ with distinct
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^2$,
linearly independent boundary test
functions $\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_{N_\partial}\in L^2(\partial\Omega)$, and
positive row scales $s_i,t_j$. Define
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_i^\Omega(f)=s_i\int_\Omega\kappa\,\nabla f\cdot\nabla v_i\,d\mathbf x,
 \qquad
 \beta_j^\partial(f)=t_j\int_{\partial\Omega}(\operatorname{Tr}f)\,\psi_j\,dS.
\end{equation*}
Use the biased scalar two-layer network of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}
with a real analytic nonpolynomial $\sigma$ and $\gamma>0$, and
assume~\Cref{assump:main} with $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$. Then the full limiting NTK of the joint family
$\{\lambda_i^\Omega\}_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}\cup\{\beta_j^\partial\}_{j=1}^{N_\partial}$
exists and is positive definite, and for every $R>0$ the rows satisfy
$(\mathsf G_R)$; if moreover
$\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0$, then
\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} applies with
$\lambda_0=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)$ and its width and
step-size conditions. The same conclusions hold with the boundary rows replaced by
pointwise Dirichlet rows $\beta_j^\partial(f)=t_jf(\mathbf x_j)$ at distinct
points $\mathbf x_j\in\partial\Omega$, provided the trial space is
$\mathcal X=H^2(\Omega)$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
$\Omega$ is a bounded Lipschitz domain. The bilinear form
$a(f,v)=\int_\Omega\kappa\nabla f\cdot\nabla v$ is continuous on
$H^1(\Omega)\times H_0^1(\Omega)$ by Cauchy--Schwarz, and the trace
$\operatorname{Tr}:H^1(\Omega)\to L^2(\partial\Omega)$ is bounded, so every
row lies in $\mathcal X^*$. \Cref{lem:ridge_density_sobolev} with $k=1$
gives the analyticity and density clauses of $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$, and
\Cref{cor:weak_Hk_row_regularity} with $k=1$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and hence $(\mathsf G_R)$; the interior-support
clause is assumed. For joint independence, suppose
$\sum_ic_i\lambda_i^\Omega+\sum_jd_j\beta_j^\partial=0$ on $\mathcal X$.
Every $f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ has zero trace, so
$\sum_ic_is_i\,a(f,v_i)=0$ for all $f\in H_0^1(\Omega)$; taking
$f=v:=\sum_ic_is_iv_i\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ gives $a(v,v)=0$, and coercivity of
$a$ on $H_0^1(\Omega)$ (from $\kappa\geq\kappa_-$ and the Poincar\'e
inequality) forces $v=0$, hence $\mathbf c=\mathbf0$ because the $v_i$ are
independent and $s_i>0$. Then $\sum_jd_jt_j\int_{\partial\Omega}
(\operatorname{Tr}f)\psi_j\,dS=0$ for all $f\in H^1(\Omega)$; since the
trace map has range $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$, which is dense in
$L^2(\partial\Omega)$, the function $\sum_jd_jt_j\psi_j$ is orthogonal to a
dense subspace and vanishes in $L^2(\partial\Omega)$; independence of the
$\psi_j$ and $t_j>0$ give $\mathbf d=\mathbf0$. Thus the set
$\mathcal N_{\Omega,\partial}^{\mathrm{weak}}$
in~\cref{eqn:weak_boundary_joint_nullspace} is trivial,
\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity} gives
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$, and \Cref{cor:classwise_gd_convergence}
applies. For pointwise boundary rows on $H^2(\Omega)$:
\Cref{cor:weak_Hk_row_regularity} with $k=2$ (admissible since a real
analytic $\sigma$ lies in $C^4_{\mathrm{loc}}$) gives the $C^2$ regularity of
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ into $H^2(\Omega)$, hence $(\mathsf G_R)$, and,
since $k=2>d_0/2$ on the Lipschitz domain $\Omega$, bounded point evaluation;
\Cref{lem:ridge_density_sobolev} with $k=2$ gives the analyticity and density
clauses of $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ in $H^2(\Omega)$; and the residual rows
remain bounded on $H^2(\Omega)\hookrightarrow H^1(\Omega)$.
In the independence argument, test first on $f\in H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$,
which contains the polynomial tests $v_i$ and on which every pointwise
boundary row vanishes, since such $f$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega$ and
its trace is its restriction to $\partial\Omega$; this gives
$\mathbf c=\mathbf0$ as before. Then $\sum_jd_jt_jf(\mathbf x_j)=0$ for all
$f\in H^2(\Omega)$, and
a polynomial taking prescribed values at the distinct points $\mathbf x_j$
gives $\mathbf d=\mathbf0$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}
Let \(D\subseteq\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{d_0}\) be compact and set
$\mathcal X=C(D;\mathbb R^{d_2})$. For every
\(i\in[N]\) and \(q\in[d_2]\), let \(\nu_{iq}\) be a finite signed regular
Borel measure on \(D\), and define
\begin{equation*}
\ell_i(f)=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int_D f_q(\mathbf y)\,d\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y),
\qquad
\lambda_i=s_i\ell_i\in\mathcal X^*,\qquad
P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)),
\qquad s_i>0.
\end{equation*}
Assume~\Cref{assump:main} and the nonlocal clauses of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes}. Set
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}
=\left\{\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N:
\sum_{i=1}^N c_i s_i\nu_{iq}=0
\ \text{as a signed measure for every }q\in[d_2]\right\}.
\end{equation*}
Then \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) exists and
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) almost surely along nested widths
(in probability under fresh resampling). Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
=\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}},
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\dim\operatorname{span}
\left\{\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_i:i\in[N]\right\}.
\label{eqn:nonlocal_exact_ntk_nullspace}
\end{equation}
Consequently, \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0\) if and only if the loss-scaled
tuples \(\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_i=s_i(\nu_{i1},\ldots,\nu_{id_2})\),
\(i\in[N]\), are linearly independent in
\(\mathcal M(D)^{d_2}\), where \(\mathcal M(D)=C(D)^*\) is the space of finite
signed regular Borel measures on \(D\).
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:nonlocal_boundary_joint_positivity}
Assume~\Cref{assump:main} and the nonlocal clauses of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes} for the combined prediction map.
For \(i\in[N_\Omega]\), let
\(\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_i=s_i(\nu_{i1},\ldots,\nu_{id_2})\) define a nonlocal
PDE-residual row. For \(j\in[N_\partial]\), let
\(\bar{\boldsymbol\omega}_j=t_j(\omega_{j1},\ldots,\omega_{jd_2})\), \(t_j>0\), be a
vector of finite signed regular Borel measures on \(D\), typically supported
on \(D\cap\partial\Omega\), defining another constraint. Set
$N=N_\Omega+N_\partial$ and order the residual rows before the boundary rows.
The corresponding predictions are
\[
P_i^\Omega(\theta)=s_i\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int_Du_q(\mathbf y;\theta)\,d\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y),
\qquad
P_j^\partial(\theta)=t_j\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int_Du_q(\mathbf y;\theta)\,d\omega_{jq}(\mathbf y).
\]
Set
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal N_{\Omega,\partial}^{\mathrm{nl}}
=\left\{(\mathbf c,\mathbf d)\right.&\in
\mathbb R^{N_\Omega}\times\mathbb R^{N_\partial}:\\
&\sum_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}c_i s_i\nu_{iq}
+\sum_{j=1}^{N_\partial}d_j t_j\omega_{jq}=0\\[-0.2em]
&\left.\text{as a signed measure for every }q\in[d_2]\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
We identify $(\mathbf c,\mathbf d)$ with its concatenation in
$\mathbb R^N$.
Then
\begin{equation*}
\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
=\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\mathcal N_{\Omega,\partial}^{\mathrm{nl}},
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\dim\operatorname{span}\!\left(
\{\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_i\}_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}
\cup\{\bar{\boldsymbol\omega}_j\}_{j=1}^{N_\partial}\right).
\end{equation*}
Thus the mixed limiting NTK is positive definite exactly when the combined
family of residual and boundary measure tuples is linearly independent.
Taking \(\omega_{jq}=b_{jq}\delta_{\mathbf x_j}\) with \(\mathbf x_j\in D\) and
\(b_{jq}\in\mathbb R\) gives the order-zero pointwise row
\(t_j\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}b_{jq}f_q(\mathbf x_j)\). When
\(\mathbf x_j\in D\cap\partial\Omega\), \(b_{jq_0}=1\), and \(b_{jq}=0\) for
\(q\neq q_0\), this is a Dirichlet row for component \(q_0\); when
\(\mathbf x_j\in D\cap\Omega\), the same functional is interior point data.

Suppose additionally that a positive regular Borel measure \(\rho\) on \(D\)
satisfies \(\nu_{iq}\ll\rho\) (absolute continuity with respect to \(\rho\))
and \(\omega_{jq}\perp\rho\) (mutual singularity with \(\rho\)) for every
index.
Then the combined family is linearly independent if and only if the residual
family \(\{\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_i\}_i\) and boundary family
\(\{\bar{\boldsymbol\omega}_j\}_j\) are each linearly independent. Hence separate
checks suffice under this mutual-singularity condition.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Apply~\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity} to the concatenated collection of
measure tuples. For the final assertion, in each output coordinate \(q\) the
residual part \(\zeta_q^\Omega=\sum_ic_is_i\nu_{iq}\) of a null combination is
absolutely continuous with respect to \(\rho\) and the boundary part
\(\zeta_q^\partial=\sum_jd_jt_j\omega_{jq}\) is singular with respect to
\(\rho\). Since \(\zeta_q^\Omega=-\zeta_q^\partial\) is both, it vanishes: a
Borel set \(E\) with \(\rho(E)=0\) carries all of \(|\zeta_q^\partial|\), and
absolute continuity gives \(|\zeta_q^\Omega|(E)=0\). Hence both parts vanish
separately, after which within-family independence makes every coefficient
zero. The converse is immediate.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:derivative_hard_boundary}
A Dirichlet evaluation is integration against a Dirac mass and therefore
falls under~\Cref{cor:nonlocal_boundary_joint_positivity}. In contrast, a
Neumann or Robin normal-derivative term is a distributional derivative, not a
finite measure acting on \(C(D)\). Combined with finite-measure residual
rows, such a row falls instead under~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}
on a common space \(\mathcal X\) of functions on \(\overline\Omega\), for instance
\(C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^{d_2})\) for bounded \(\Omega\), with measures on
\(D\subseteq\overline\Omega\) extended by zero, on
which both the measure rows and the boundary derivative are bounded; combined
with pointwise residual rows it is covered directly by the pointwise clauses
of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}. The single-neuron
features must also belong to $\mathcal X$ and satisfy the stated Banach-valued
analyticity and density hypotheses. The weak formulation may
alternatively incorporate tested Neumann or Robin data.

If the architecture enforces an essential boundary condition \emph{hard}
rather than penalizing boundary-loss rows, one may write the constrained
model as $\mathbf g+\mathcal E\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)$, where the network
$\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)$ of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} is regarded as an
element of a Banach space $\widetilde{\mathcal X}$, and the predictions are the
residual rows
$P_i^\Omega(\theta)=\lambda_i^\Omega\bigl(\mathbf g+\mathcal E\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)\bigr)$,
$i\in[N_\Omega]$, with loss-scaled $\lambda_i^\Omega\in\mathcal X^*$. Here
$\mathbf g\in\mathcal X$ is a fixed lifting satisfying the inhomogeneous
data. A bounded linear operator
$\mathcal E:\widetilde{\mathcal X}\to\mathcal X_0$ maps into a closed
homogeneous-boundary tangent subspace $\mathcal X_0\subseteq\mathcal X$ with
the inherited norm. No additional penalty rows are present. The
tangent features become $\mathcal E\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$, and the exact
criterion concerns the restrictions of the residual functionals to
$\mathcal X_0$:
\begin{equation*}
\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
=\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
=\left\{\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^{N_\Omega}:
\left.\sum_{i=1}^{N_\Omega}c_i\lambda_i^\Omega\right|_{\mathcal X_0}=0
\ \text{in }\mathcal X_0^*\right\},
\end{equation*}
provided that \Cref{assump:main} holds with
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$, that the raw features
$\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$ belong to $\widetilde{\mathcal X}$ and depend
real-analytically on their parameters in that space (with boundedness of
$\mathcal E$ this gives the $C^2$ regularity of clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ for the adapted one-neuron map, hence
$(\mathsf G_R)$ by \Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity}), and that the
adapted family $\mathcal E\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$ has dense span in
$\mathcal X_0$.
The fixed lifting changes the target but
not the NTK. The density hypothesis concerns the adapted family itself:
unconstrained single-neuron features generally do
not belong to a zero-boundary-value trial space, so one cannot simply reuse a
density result for the unconstrained features in a hard-boundary construction.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{ex:ridge_density_obstruction}
Delete from clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} only
the ridge-density requirement
\begin{equation*}
 \overline{\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}:
 \boldsymbol\xi\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1},\ q\in[d_2]\}}^{\mathcal X}
 =\mathcal X,
\end{equation*}
and keep every other hypothesis
of~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank,thm:weak_constraint_positivity}. Let
$\Omega=(0,1)$, so $\overline\Omega=[0,1]$, let $d_0=d_2=1$, and let
$\mathcal X=C([0,1])$ with the supremum norm. Use the network
of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} with the linear activation $\sigma(z)=z$,
bias scale $\gamma=1$, and i.i.d.\ per-neuron initialization
$\theta_m=(w_m,b_m,a_m)\sim\operatorname{Unif}([-1,1]^3)$. Take the $N=3$ unit-scaled
evaluation rows
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_i(f)=f(x_i),
 \qquad
 (x_1,x_2,x_3)=(0,1,\tfrac12),
\end{equation*}
which lie in $\mathcal X^*$ and are therefore admissible
in~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity} through the reduction
$\mathcal V_i=\mathbb R$, $v_i=s_i=1$, $a_i(f,t)=t\lambda_i(f)$ used in the
proof of~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}. Positive loss scales $s_i$ would
only replace the null vector $\mathbf c$ below by $(c_i/s_i)_{i=1}^3$.

Every retained clause holds. The embedding
$\mathcal X\hookrightarrow L^1(0,1)$ is continuous, each
$\lambda_i\in\mathcal X^*$, and the one-neuron map
$\mathcal G(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)=a(w\,\cdot+\gamma b)$ is a quadratic
polynomial map $\mathbb R^3\to\mathcal X$, hence $C^\infty$ and real analytic
on all of $\mathbb R^3$; clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and the
feature-analyticity part of $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ therefore hold. The law
$\mu$ is width independent and compactly supported, so~\Cref{assump:main}
holds; $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)=(-1,1)^2\neq\varnothing$, so the
support part of $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ holds; and
$\mathbb E[a_m\mid w_m,b_m]=0$, so the conditional output-weight centering
that~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} imposes for gradient descent holds as well.
Only density fails, and it fails by a definite margin: with $d_2=1$ the single
coordinate feature is $\varphi_{(w,b)}=w\,\cdot+\gamma b$, so
$\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}:\boldsymbol\xi\in\mathbb R^2\}
=\operatorname{span}\{1,x\}=:\mathcal P_1$, a two-dimensional and therefore closed proper
subspace of $\mathcal X$.

The three rows are linearly independent in $\mathcal X^*$: testing
$\sum_ic_i\lambda_i=0$ against continuous hat functions $f_j$ with $f_j(x_j)=1$
and $f_j(x_k)=0$ for $k\neq j$ gives $c_j=0$ for each $j$. Independence
notwithstanding, $\mathbf c=(1,1,-2)^\top$ and
$\lambda_{\mathbf c}=\lambda_1+\lambda_2-2\lambda_3$ satisfy
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_{\mathbf c}(\alpha+\beta x)
 =\alpha+(\alpha+\beta)-2\left(\alpha+\tfrac{\beta}{2}\right)=0
 \qquad\text{for all }\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R,
\end{equation*}
so the nonzero functional $\lambda_{\mathbf c}$ annihilates $\mathcal P_1$ and
hence every ridge feature. The same vector quantifies the failure of density:
$\lambda_{\mathbf c}(x^2)=\tfrac12$ and
$\|\lambda_{\mathbf c}\|_{\mathcal X^*}=4$ give
$\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_1}\|x^2-p\|_{\mathcal X}\geq\tfrac18$, which is exactly
the Chebyshev distance attained by $x-\tfrac18$.

Because $\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)\in\mathcal P_1$ at every width and every
parameter value,
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{i=1}^3c_iP_i(\theta)
 =\lambda_{\mathbf c}(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))=0,
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 \mathbf J(\theta)^\top\mathbf c=\mathbf0,
 \quad
 \mathbf K(\theta)\mathbf c=\mathbf0 .
\end{equation*}
That is the one-line reason. Explicitly, with
$h_i(w,b,a)=a(wx_i+\gamma b)$ in~\cref{eqn:predictionmap}, the Gram
representation in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} gives
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{ij}
 =\mathbb E\!\left[a^2\right]\!\left(x_ix_j+\gamma^2\right)
 +\mathbb E\!\left[(wx_i+\gamma b)(wx_j+\gamma b)\right]
 =\tfrac23\left(1+x_ix_j\right),
\end{equation*}
using $\mathbb E[a^2]=\mathbb E[w^2]=\mathbb E[b^2]=\tfrac13$ and
$\mathbb E[wb]=0$. Writing $\mathbf V_{i,:}=(1,x_i)$, this says
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\tfrac23\mathbf V\mathbf V^\top,
 \qquad
 \mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty=\tfrac13\mathbf V\mathbf V^\top,
\end{equation*}
so both matrices have rank $2$ and kernel $\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,-2)^\top\}$.

The weakened statement therefore fails. The relation space
in~\cref{eqn:weak_functional_nullspace} is
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}=\{\mathbf0\}$, whereas
$\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty=\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\neq\{\mathbf0\}$
and $\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=2$, which is smaller than
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\}=3$. Both identities
in~\cref{eqn:weak_exact_ntk_nullspace} fail; equivalently, the rows are
linearly independent while $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\not\succ0$. The clause as
actually stated excludes the construction, since $\mathcal P_1$ is not dense in
$\mathcal X$, so~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank,thm:weak_constraint_positivity}
are untouched.

Three scoping remarks. First, only one inclusion is lost. Density is consumed
exactly once, in the step
$\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}$. The
opposite inclusion
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}\subseteq\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ follows by
differentiating $\sum_ic_iP_i(\theta)=0$ and, for
$\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty$, is immediate
from~\cref{eqn:weak_output_quadratic}; it survives the deletion, as do the
resulting bound
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\leq\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_i\}_{i=1}^N$ and the
existence and convergence conclusions, which use only clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Second, the rows are not at fault. Replacing
$\sigma$ by $\tanh$ with $\gamma>0$ restores density by the ridge-monomial
argument in the proof of~\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson} together
with the Weierstrass theorem, and the same three rows then give
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ by~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank}, as they also
do by~\Cref{prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank}, since the Dirac measures at
$x_1,x_2,x_3$ are linearly independent. Third, the mechanism is not tied to an
affine activation. For any polynomial $\sigma$ of degree $p$ on this
one-dimensional domain the closed ridge span lies in the polynomials of degree
at most $p$, so any $p+2$ distinct evaluation rows are independent in
$\mathcal X^*$ yet dependent on that span. For $\sigma=\tanh$ with the
bias-free scale $\gamma=0$ permitted by~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} every
ridge vanishes at $x=0$, so the closed span lies in
$\{f\in\mathcal X:f(0)=0\}$ and the single row $\lambda_1$, which is nonzero
and hence trivially independent, already yields $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=0$
for an analytic nonpolynomial activation. Clauses $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ and
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$ exclude such configurations by explicitly requiring a
nonpolynomial $\sigma$ and $\gamma>0$; clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ states
neither requirement, and its density clause is precisely what does that work on
a general trial space.

What the example does not show: it establishes only that the clause cannot be
deleted outright, not that density is the weakest usable replacement, and it is
purely qualitative, since a feature family whose span is dense but poorly
conditioned still yields a positive definite kernel whose smallest eigenvalue
requires~\Cref{prop:quantitative_dntk_bound}. It also says nothing about the
pointwise or nonlocal classes. Like~\Cref{ex:compatible_singular_ntk}, which
restricts the model space by a polynomial activation for strong-form rows, the
construction is degenerate by design; the point here is the identification of
the single weak-class clause that rules such degeneracies out.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
\label{ex:gamma_zero_parity_obstruction}
Take $d_0=d_2=1$, $\Omega=(-1,1)$, and $D=\overline\Omega=[-1,1]$, so that
$\mathcal X=C([-1,1])$. Use~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} with the bias-free
scale $\gamma=0$ and the activation $\sigma=\cosh$,
\begin{equation*}
 u_\theta(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}a_m\cosh(w_mx),
\end{equation*}
and initialize every coordinate of $(w_m,b_m,a_m)$ i.i.d.\ from
$\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]$. As in~\Cref{ex:compatible_singular_ntk}, the formal hidden
biases $b_m$ do not enter the prediction when $\gamma=0$, so their Jacobian
columns vanish. Impose the two nonlocal rows
of~\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity} with $s_1=s_2=1$ and
\begin{equation*}
 \nu_1=\delta_{1},\qquad \nu_2=\delta_{-1},
 \qquad
 P_1(\theta)=u_\theta(1),\qquad P_2(\theta)=u_\theta(-1).
\end{equation*}
Every clause of $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$
in~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} holds except one: the rows are finite signed
regular Borel measures on the compact set $D$, the law $\mu$
of~\Cref{assump:main} is compactly supported,
$\cosh\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^2(\mathbb R)$ is real analytic and nonpolynomial,
and $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)=(-1,1)^2\neq\varnothing$. Only the clause
$\gamma>0$ is deleted, and \Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} admits $\gamma=0$.

The deleted clause is exactly what the conclusion needs. Testing the identity
$c_1\delta_1+c_2\delta_{-1}=0$ on the Borel sets $\{1\}$ and $\{-1\}$ gives
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}=\{\mathbf0\}$ and
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_1,\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_2\}=2$, so the
weakened forms of~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_exact_ntk_nullspace}
and~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_rank_main} would assert
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=2$. It is instead $1$. Because $\cosh$ is even
and $\gamma=0$, every ridge $y\mapsto\cosh(wy)$ is even, hence
$u_\theta(-x)=u_\theta(x)$ for every $\theta$ and every width, and
$P_1-P_2\equiv0$ as a function of $\theta$. Equivalently, the per-neuron
Jacobian $\boldsymbol\Psi$ defined before~\cref{eqn:full_output_hidden_decomposition},
evaluated at $z=(w,b,a)$ with columns ordered as
$(\partial_w,\partial_b,\partial_a)$, has two identical rows,
\begin{equation*}
 \boldsymbol\Psi(z)
 =\begin{bmatrix}
 a\sinh w&0&\cosh w\\
 a\sinh w&0&\cosh w
 \end{bmatrix},
\end{equation*}
since $\cosh(-w)=\cosh w$ and $(-1)\sinh(-w)=\sinh w$. Taking the expectation
in $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}[\boldsymbol\Psi(z)
\boldsymbol\Psi(z)^\top]$ and using
$\mathbb E[\cosh^2w]=\tfrac14(2+\sinh2)$,
$\mathbb E[\sinh^2w]=\tfrac14(\sinh2-2)$, and $\mathbb E[a^2]=\tfrac13$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\frac{1+\sinh 2}{3}
 \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1)^\top\},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=1.
 \label{eqn:gamma_zero_singular_ntk}
\end{equation}
Both summands of~\cref{eqn:full_output_hidden_decomposition} are separately
singular here, with every entry of $\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty$ equal to
$\tfrac14(2+\sinh2)$ and every entry of $\mathbf K_{\mathrm{hid}}^\infty$ equal
to $\tfrac1{12}(\sinh2-2)$.

The failure is localized to a single step of the proof
of~\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}, where $\gamma>0$ makes the
shifts $\gamma b$ exhaust $\mathbb R$ and thereby licenses the uniform
universal-approximation theorem for a nonpolynomial activation \emph{with a
bias}~\citep{Leshno1993}. When $\gamma=0$ the available features are
$\{y\mapsto\cosh(wy):w\in\mathbb R\}$, whose closed span in $C([-1,1])$
consists of even functions only, so it is a proper closed subspace and the
Riesz--Markov step is unavailable. Concretely,
$\zeta=\delta_1-\delta_{-1}$ satisfies
$\int_D\cosh(wy)\,d\zeta(y)=\cosh(w)-\cosh(-w)=0$ for every $w$ while
$\zeta\neq0$, so~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_all_ridges_annihilated} no longer forces
the corresponding signed measure to vanish. The degeneracy is exactly one
dimensional: $c_1\delta_1+c_2\delta_{-1}$ annihilates every even continuous
function precisely when $c_1+c_2=0$,
matching~\cref{eqn:gamma_zero_singular_ntk}.

Restoring $\gamma>0$ repairs the same two rows. With $\gamma=1$ and the same
law, the output-weight features
$[\boldsymbol\Phi_{\mathrm{out}}(\boldsymbol\xi)]_{i,:}
=\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi)^\top$
of~\cref{eqn:full_output_hidden_decomposition} are
$\mathbf f_1(w,b)=\cosh(w+b)$ and $\mathbf f_2(w,b)=\cosh(w-b)$, so
$\mathbb E[\mathbf f_1\mathbf f_2]
=\tfrac12\mathbb E[\cosh2w+\cosh2b]=\tfrac12\sinh2$ and
$\mathbb E[\mathbf f_1^2]=\mathbb E[\mathbf f_2^2]
=\tfrac12+\tfrac18\sinh^22$, whence
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
 =\frac18\begin{bmatrix}
 4+\sinh^22&4\sinh 2\\
 4\sinh 2&4+\sinh^22
 \end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{spec}(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty)
 =\left\{\frac{(\sinh 2+2)^2}{8},\frac{(\sinh 2-2)^2}{8}\right\},
\end{equation*}
approximately $\{3.958,0.331\}$ with eigenvectors $(1,\pm1)^\top$. Both
eigenvalues are positive because $\sinh2\neq2$, so
$\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\succ0$ and therefore
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ by~\cref{eqn:block_pd_certificate_bound}: an
exact certificate in the sense
of~\Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate}, agreeing
with~\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}. The mechanism is general. For
any $\gamma>0$ and any $\mu_h$ whose support has nonempty interior,
$\mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\mathbf c=0$ forces the
real-analytic function
$g_{\mathbf c}(w,b)=(c_1+c_2)\cosh w\cosh(\gamma b)
+(c_1-c_2)\sinh w\sinh(\gamma b)$
to vanish on $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)$, hence on all of $\mathbb R^2$
by the identity theorem; setting $b=0$ gives $c_1+c_2=0$ because
$\cosh\geq1$, and then $(w,b)=(1,1/\gamma)$ gives $c_1=c_2$. The bias is what
breaks the parity.

Two limitations are worth stating. First, the construction leaves the
existence half of~\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity} intact:
\Cref{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity} imposes no condition on $\gamma$, so
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ still exists and
$\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ at $\gamma=0$. Only the nullspace
and rank identity in~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_exact_ntk_nullspace} fails. Second,
the example isolates the hypothesis rather than the architecture: with
$\gamma=0$ and the also real-analytic nonpolynomial $\sigma=\exp$, the
identity $\int_De^{wy}\,d\zeta(y)=0$ for all $w\in\mathbb R$ continues
analytically to the Fourier transform of $\zeta$ and still forces $\zeta=0$,
so the conclusion survives for that instance. What the construction shows is
that the weakened hypothesis set admits false instances, not that every
$\gamma=0$ model is degenerate.

The same pair also settles the pointwise class. Since $\delta_{\pm1}$ are
order-zero rows of~\Cref{def:linear_pde} at the distinct sites
$\mathbf x=\pm1\in\overline\Omega$ with local coefficient vectors
$\mathbf b_1(1)=\mathbf b_2(-1)=(1)$, the weakened form
of~\cref{eqn:exact_dntk_rank} would likewise predict
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=1+1=2$, and $\cosh$ satisfies
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$ for $r_{\max}=0$. So $\gamma>0$ is load-bearing in
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ for~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} exactly as it is
in $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$
for~\Cref{prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank,thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}. The
example is distinct from~\Cref{ex:compatible_singular_ntk}, which also sets
$\gamma=0$ but additionally violates the nonpolynomiality clause; here
analyticity and nonpolynomiality are retained and only $\gamma>0$ is removed.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
\label{ex:weak_analyticity_necessity}
Delete from clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} only
the requirement that every $\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$ be
real analytic into $\mathcal X$, keeping
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$, the ridge-density clause, and
all of $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Both identities
in~\cref{eqn:weak_exact_ntk_nullspace} then fail, and with them the
positive-definiteness criteria
of~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank,cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}.

Take the row family of~\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson} with
$d_0=d_2=1$, $\Omega=(-1,1)$, $\mathcal X=H^1(\Omega)$, $\kappa\equiv1$,
$\gamma=1$, unit row scales, the single test function
$v_1(x)=1-x^2\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, and the network
of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}; only the activation will be changed. The
$N=3$ rows
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda_1^\Omega(f)=\int_{-1}^{1}f'(x)v_1'(x)\,dx,
 \qquad
 \beta_-^\partial(f)=f(-1),
 \qquad
 \beta_+^\partial(f)=f(1)
\end{equation*}
are bounded on $\mathcal X$ by Cauchy--Schwarz and the one-dimensional trace
theorem, and they are linearly independent in $\mathcal X^*$: testing a
vanishing combination against $v_1$, then against $x\mapsto(1-x)/2$, then
against the constant function $1$ forces its three coefficients to vanish in
that order. Hence $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}=\{\mathbf0\}$
in~\cref{eqn:weak_functional_nullspace}, and the weakened statement would
assert $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$ with rank $3$. For $\sigma=\tanh$ this is
exactly what~\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson} proves.

Replace $\tanh$ by
\begin{equation*}
 \sigma_\star(z)=z+\chi\!\left(\tfrac12-z\right),
 \qquad
 \chi(t)=e^{-1/t}\mathbf 1_{\{t>0\}},
\end{equation*}
and let $\mu=\operatorname{Unif}([1,2]\times[3,4])\otimes\operatorname{Unif}([-1,1])$. Then
$\sigma_\star\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$, it agrees with the identity on
$[\tfrac12,\infty)$, and it is neither polynomial nor real analytic, because
$\sigma_\star(0)=e^{-2}\neq0$ while any polynomial, or any real-analytic
function, that agrees with $z$ on a half-line equals $z$ everywhere. The law
$\mu$ is width independent, compactly supported, and sampled i.i.d., with
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)=(1,2)\times(3,4)\neq\varnothing$ and
$\mathbb E[a_m\mid\boldsymbol\xi_m]=0$, so~\Cref{assump:main} holds.

On the open cone $Q=\{\boldsymbol\xi=(w,b):\gamma b-|w|>\tfrac12\}$ every
preactivation seen on the domain lies in the affine piece of $\sigma_\star$:
for $x\in\overline\Omega$,
\begin{equation*}
 wx+\gamma b\geq\gamma b-|w|>\tfrac12,
 \qquad\text{so}\qquad
 \varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}=w\,p_1+\gamma b\,p_0
 \quad\text{exactly on }\overline\Omega,
\end{equation*}
where $p_0=1$ and $p_1=x$. Moreover $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h\subset Q$, because
$b-|w|\geq3-2=1$ there; any $\gamma>0$ works after rescaling the bias support
to $[3/\gamma,4/\gamma]$. Thus
$\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}:\boldsymbol\xi\in Q\}
=\operatorname{span}\{p_0,p_1\}$ is two-dimensional, although the full ridge family over
$\mathbb R^2$ is dense. Writing
$F_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=\lambda_i(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi})$ for the three rows in
the order above, and using that $v_1\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ makes
$\int_{-1}^{1}v_1'=0$, so that $\lambda_1^\Omega$ annihilates every affine
function, we obtain on $Q$
\begin{equation*}
 F_1\equiv0,
 \qquad
 F_2=\gamma b-w,
 \qquad
 F_3=\gamma b+w,
 \qquad
 \nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}F_2=(-1,\gamma),
 \qquad
 \nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}F_3=(1,\gamma).
\end{equation*}
The Gram representation in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK}, applied to the per-neuron maps
$h_i(z)=aF_i(\boldsymbol\xi)$ supplied
by~\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} for $z=(\boldsymbol\xi,a)$,
gives for every $\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^3$
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\mathbf c
 =\mathbb E_{\mu_h}\!\left[
 \big((c_3-c_2)w+(c_2+c_3)\gamma b\big)^2\right]
 +\tfrac13\left\|\big(c_3-c_2,\
 \gamma(c_2+c_3)\big)\right\|_2^2,
\end{equation*}
since $\mathbb E[a^2]=\tfrac13$ and $a$ is independent of $\boldsymbol\xi$. The
second term vanishes precisely when $c_3-c_2=0$ and $c_2+c_3=0$, that is, when
$c_2=c_3=0$; the first term then vanishes as well, and $c_1$ is unconstrained,
so
\begin{equation*}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0)^\top\}
 \neq\{\mathbf0\}=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=2<3
 =\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1^\Omega,\beta_-^\partial,\beta_+^\partial\}.
\end{equation*}
The annihilating functional is explicit: $\lambda_1^\Omega$ is nonzero on
$\mathcal X$, since $\lambda_1^\Omega(v_1)=\int_{-1}^{1}4x^2\,dx=\tfrac83$, yet
it kills every $\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}$ with $\boldsymbol\xi\in Q$. The
degeneracy is not an infinite-width artifact: $F_1\equiv0$ on the open set $Q$
and $\boldsymbol\xi_m\in\operatorname{supp}\mu_h\subset Q$ almost surely, so
$\nabla_\theta P_1(\theta_{(0)})=\mathbf0$ almost surely and the first row and
column of $\mathbf K_{(0)}$ vanish at every width, while the target
$\int_{-1}^{1}gv_1$ of that row is generically nonzero.

Analyticity is the only clause that fails. Clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$
holds in full, because the rows lie in $\mathcal X^*$ and
$\sigma_\star\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^3(\mathbb R)$, so
\Cref{cor:weak_H1_row_regularity} makes $\mathcal G$ a $C^2$ map into
$H^1(\Omega)$ on an open neighborhood of every fixed parameter tube; the
existence and convergence half of~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank} is therefore
intact and only its positive-definiteness half fails. The hidden support has
nonempty interior. The ridge-density clause also holds: for each
$n\in\mathbb N_0$, nonpolynomiality gives $b_n$ with
$\sigma_\star^{(n)}(\gamma b_n)\neq0$, and
$\partial_w^n\sigma_\star(wx+\gamma b_n)|_{w=0}
=\sigma_\star^{(n)}(\gamma b_n)x^n$ is an $H^1$ limit of finite combinations of
ridge features, so the monomials, and hence the $H^1(-1,1)$-dense polynomials,
lie in the closed span, exactly as in the proof
of~\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson}. Only Banach-valued analyticity
fails, and visibly so: $\varphi_{(0,b)}=\sigma_\star(\gamma b)p_0$ is not a
real-analytic function of $b$.

The failure occurs at exactly the step the proof needs. In the proof
of~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity}, analyticity is used once: a
combination of the $F_{iq}$ that vanishes $\mu_h$-almost surely vanishes on
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)$ by continuity, and the identity theorem
propagates this to all of $\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$, where the density clause turns
it into $\sum_ic_i\lambda_i=0$ in $\mathcal X^*$; the same step appears
in~\Cref{prop:analytic_functional_rank}. Here the propagation is the only
thing that fails: the relation $F_1\equiv0$ holds on $Q$ and stops there, while
the density clause quantifies over all of $\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$, so the two
clauses never meet. The reverse inclusion
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}\subseteq\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ uses only
linearity and still holds. The example also shows that the clause must be read
globally in $\boldsymbol\xi$: here
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}$ is real analytic on a
neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$, indeed affine there, and that is not enough.

Two remarks delimit the claim. First, $\sigma=\operatorname{ReLU}$ with the same $\mu$
produces the identical collapse, because $\gamma b-|w|\geq1>0$ on $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$
places the kink $x=-\gamma b/w\leq-\tfrac32$ outside $\overline\Omega$;
however, $\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}$ is then not
differentiable into $H^1(\Omega)$ once the kink enters $\Omega$, so $\operatorname{ReLU}$
also violates $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ on parameter tubes of radius at least
$1/\sqrt2$ and is not a single-clause counterexample. The smooth
$\sigma_\star$ shows that neither smoothness nor nonpolynomiality substitutes
for analyticity. Second, the example does not claim that non-analytic
activations give degenerate kernels in general: the collapse is a property of
the pair $(\sigma,\mu_h)$, and a hidden support over which the affine piece of
$\sigma_\star$ fails to cover $\overline\Omega$ produces a far richer feature
family. Nor is analyticity the weakest possible clause; density of
$\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}:\boldsymbol\xi\in\operatorname{supp}\mu_h\}$ would
suffice, and analyticity is the checkable condition that transports the stated
density clause from $\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$ to $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$.

The same device applies to the other two classes with $\sigma_\star$, whose
smoothness already gives $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$. On $Q$ the strong-form row $u\mapsto u''(0)$ and
the nonlocal row $f\mapsto\int f\,d\nu$ with
$\nu=\delta_{-1}-2\delta_0+\delta_1$ both annihilate $\operatorname{span}\{p_0,p_1\}$ and
give an identically zero limiting NTK, although each row is nonzero and its
local coefficient vector, respectively measure tuple, is nonzero. The
analyticity requirements in $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ and
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$, used
by~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank,prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank}, are load-bearing for
the same reason. Unlike~\Cref{ex:relu3_fourth_order_obstruction}, where the
obstruction is a mismatch between activation smoothness and differential order,
the activation here may be taken as smooth as desired and the obstruction is
purely the loss of analytic continuation.
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
\label{ex:compact_support_analyticity_obstruction}
This example weakens exactly one clause of the hypotheses
of~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity}: in clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, replace ``every
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}$ is real analytic into
$\mathcal X$'' by ``$C^\infty$ into $\mathcal X$'', and keep every other
requirement verbatim, including~\Cref{assump:main}, clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$, $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$,
and density of the ridge span over all
$\boldsymbol\xi\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$. The weakened statement is false, and
with it the weakened forms of~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank}
and~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}. It is the same clause as
in~\Cref{ex:weak_analyticity_necessity}, broken by a different mechanism:
there the features are locally affine on the region the row observes, here
they are locally zero.

Take $d_0=d_2=1$, $\Omega=(-1,1)$, $\mathcal X=H^1(-1,1)$, and $\gamma=1$
in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}, with the standard bump activation
\begin{equation*}
 \sigma(z)=
 \begin{cases}
  \exp\!\big((z^2-1)^{-1}\big),&|z|<1,\\[2pt]
  0,&|z|\geq1,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \sigma\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\sigma=[-1,1].
\end{equation*}
Initialize $(w_m,b_m)\sim\operatorname{Unif}\!\left([1,2]\times[1,\tfrac32]\right)$ and
$a_m\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{\pm1\}$ independently, so $\mu$ is compactly supported and
width independent, $\mathbb E[a_m\mid w_m,b_m]=0$, and
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)=(1,2)\times(1,\tfrac32)\neq\varnothing$.
Impose the single ($N=1$) weak residual row generated by the $H^1$ inner
product, that is, the weak form of $-u''+u$ tested against a fixed
$v_1\in C_c^\infty\!\left((\tfrac12,1)\right)$ with $v_1\geq0$ and
$v_1\not\equiv0$:
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal V_1=\mathcal X,
 \qquad
 a(f,v)=\int_{-1}^{1}\big(f'v'+fv\big)\,dx=\langle f,v\rangle_{H^1},
 \qquad
 \lambda_1=a(\cdot,v_1),\qquad s_1=1.
\end{equation*}
Write $\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}(x)=\sigma(wx+b)$ and
$F_1(\boldsymbol\xi)=\lambda_1(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi})$ for
$\boldsymbol\xi=(w,b)$.

The weakened hypotheses hold. Since
$\sigma\in C^\infty\subset C_{\mathrm{loc}}^3$,
\Cref{cor:weak_H1_row_regularity} gives the required $C^2$ map into
$\mathcal X$ on a neighborhood of every radius-$R$ parameter tube, and $a$ is
continuous and bilinear with $\lambda_1\in\mathcal X^*$,
$\|\lambda_1\|_{\mathcal X^*}=\|v_1\|_{H^1}$; clause
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ therefore holds. All derivatives of $\sigma$ are
bounded and uniformly continuous, so
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}$ is $C^\infty$ into
$C^1([-1,1])\hookrightarrow H^1(-1,1)$. The ridge span is dense: by the
Banach-valued differentiation argument in the proof
of~\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson},
$\partial_w^n\sigma(wx+b)\big|_{w=0}=\sigma^{(n)}(b)\,x^n$ is an $H^1$ limit of
finite linear combinations of features $\varphi_{(w,b)}$ with $b$ fixed, and
$\sigma^{(n)}\not\equiv0$ for every $n$, since otherwise $\sigma$ would be a
polynomial vanishing on $[1,\infty)$, hence identically zero, contradicting
$\sigma(0)=e^{-1}$. Choosing $b_n$ with $\sigma^{(n)}(b_n)\neq0$ puts every
monomial, and hence every polynomial, in the closed span, and polynomials are
dense in $H^1(-1,1)$. Finally $a$ is coercive with $c_a=1$ and $\{v_1\}$ is
linearly independent, so~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity} in its weakened
form, and likewise its coercive special case, would assert
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0$.

The conclusion fails. Let
$U=\{(w,b):w>0,\ \tfrac w2+b>1\}$, an open set containing
$\operatorname{supp}\mu_h=[1,2]\times[1,\tfrac32]$, where $\tfrac w2+b\geq\tfrac32$. For
$\boldsymbol\xi\in U$ and $x\geq\tfrac12$ we have $wx+b\geq\tfrac w2+b>1$, and
$\{x:wx+b>1\}=\big((1-b)/w,\infty\big)$ with $(1-b)/w<\tfrac12$; hence
$\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}$ and all of its $x$-derivatives vanish on a
neighborhood of $[\tfrac12,1]$ in $\overline\Omega$, which contains
$\operatorname{supp} v_1$. Therefore
\begin{equation*}
 F_1(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =\int_{1/2}^{1}\big(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}'v_1'
 +\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}v_1\big)\,dx=0
 \qquad\text{for every }\boldsymbol\xi\in U,
\end{equation*}
and, $U$ being open, every partial derivative of $F_1$ vanishes on $U$ as
well. This is consistent with the density just established: $F_1$ is nonzero
off $U$, for instance $F_1(0,0)=e^{-1}\int_{1/2}^{1}v_1>0$. Because
$P_1(\theta)=d_1^{-1/2}\sum_m a_mF_1(\boldsymbol\xi_m)$, both
$\partial P_1/\partial a_m=d_1^{-1/2}F_1(\boldsymbol\xi_m)$ and
$\partial P_1/\partial\boldsymbol\xi_m
=d_1^{-1/2}a_m\nabla F_1(\boldsymbol\xi_m)$ vanish, so
$\nabla_\theta P_1(\theta)=\mathbf0$ at every parameter vector whose neuron
blocks lie in $\operatorname{supp}\mu$. Hence $\mathbf K_{(0)}=\mathbf0$ almost surely at
every width and $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\mathbf0$. Yet
$\lambda_1(v_1)=\|v_1\|_{H^1}^2>0$, so $\lambda_1\neq0$ and
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}=\{0\}$. Therefore
\begin{equation*}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\mathbb R\neq\{0\}=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=0<1=\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1\},
\end{equation*}
contradicting~\cref{eqn:weak_exact_ntk_nullspace}. Since
$\nabla_\theta\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)})=\mathbf0$, gradient descent is
stationary at every width and step size, and by~\Cref{def:pinn_loss} with
$s_1=1$ the loss is frozen at $\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)})=y_1^2$.

The kernel need not collapse to zero. Append the boundary row
$\lambda_2=\delta_{-1}$, that is, $\lambda_2(f)=f(-1)$, which is bounded on
$H^1(-1,1)$ by the one-dimensional trace theorem and enters
\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity} through the device
$\mathcal V_2=\mathbb R$, $a_2(f,t)=tf(-1)$, $v_2=s_2=1$ used in the proof
of~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}. Then
$F_2(\boldsymbol\xi)=\sigma(b-w)$, and $b-w\in[-1,\tfrac12]$ on $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$,
so $F_2>0$ $\mu_h$-almost everywhere, with $F_2(1,1)=\sigma(0)=e^{-1}$;
consequently $[\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty]_{22}=\int F_2^2\,d\mu_h>0$, and
the full kernel dominates the output-weight block
by~\cref{eqn:block_pd_certificate_bound}. The rows are independent, since
$c_1\lambda_1+c_2\lambda_2=0$ applied to $v_1$ gives
$c_1\|v_1\|_{H^1}^2=0$ because $v_1(-1)=0$, and applying the relation to the
constant function $1$ then gives $c_2=0$. The first row of
$\mathbf J(\theta)$ still vanishes identically, so the first row and column of
the kernel vanish and
\begin{equation*}
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf e_1\}\neq\{0\},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=1<2=\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2\}.
\end{equation*}
This is a weak residual row together with a boundary row on a common trial
space, so the weakened form of~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity} fails
as well.

The one-line reason: the proof of~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity}
concludes from $F_1\equiv0$ on $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$ that $F_1\equiv0$ on
$\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$ by the identity theorem; a $C^\infty$ map can be flat, so
that step, and only that step, is what the weakening removes. The hypothesis
as written excludes the example: $\sigma$ vanishes on $|z|\geq1$ while
$\sigma(0)=e^{-1}\neq0$, so it is not real analytic, and since
$\delta_0\in H^1(-1,1)^*$, real analyticity of
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}$ into $\mathcal X$ would force
$b\mapsto\sigma(b)$ to be real analytic. The degeneracy is a different
mechanism from~\Cref{ex:relu3_fourth_order_obstruction}: there the activation
violates the regularity clause and each feature is locally a nonzero
polynomial that a high-order derivative row annihilates, an order mismatch,
whereas here regularity is amply satisfied, the row is a bounded first-order
weak row, and the features are locally \emph{zero} on the region the row
observes, a support mismatch. The example does not break the existence half of
the theorem: clause $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$ still holds, so the first
conclusion of~\Cref{prop:functional_ntk_rank} still yields existence of
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ and convergence of $\mathbf K_{(0)}$, here trivially.
Nor does it show that analyticity is the only possible hypothesis: density
over all $\boldsymbol\xi$ does hold, and what fails is that
$\operatorname{span}\{\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi}:\boldsymbol\xi\in\operatorname{supp}\mu_h\}$ lies in the
proper closed subspace $\{f\in\mathcal X:f|_{[1/2,1]}=0\}$, so requiring
density of the features indexed by $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)$ alone would
restore the conclusion. What is shown is that the analyticity clause cannot
simply be downgraded to $C^\infty$ while the density clause is quantified over
all of $\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$, and that the obstruction is a mismatch between
$\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$ and the region a row observes rather than a defect of compactly
supported activations as such.
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\label{ex:empty_interior_support}
Delete the clause $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$ from
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{pd}}$ and $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$
in~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} and retain every other hypothesis. The following
system then satisfies all remaining clauses and has linearly independent rows,
yet its limiting NTK is singular.

Let $d_0=d_2=1$, $\Omega=(-\pi,\pi)$, $D=\overline\Omega=[-\pi,\pi]$,
$\sigma=\sin$, and $\gamma>0$. Use the network
of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization},
\begin{equation*}
 u_\theta(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{d_1}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}a_m\sin(w_mx+\gamma b_m),
\end{equation*}
with the three unit-scaled evaluation rows $\nu_i=\delta_{x_i}$ at
$(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(-\pi,0,\pi)$ and $s_i=1$, so that $P_i(\theta)=u_\theta(x_i)$:
two Dirichlet boundary rows and one interior measurement. Initialize the
neurons i.i.d.\ with independent coordinates
\begin{equation*}
 w_m\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{-1,1\},\qquad
 b_m\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1],\qquad
 a_m\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{-1,1\},
\end{equation*}
so that $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h=\{-1,1\}\times[-1,1]$ is compact with empty interior in
$\mathbb R^2$; for $d_0=1$ this is the unit-norm hidden-weight sphere with a
free bias. Every other hypothesis holds. The law $\mu$ is compactly supported
and width independent as in~\Cref{assump:main}; $\sin$ is real analytic,
nonpolynomial, and smooth; $\gamma>0$; $D$ is compact and the rows are finite
signed regular Borel measures, giving $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Reading the
same rows as $\lambda_i(f)=f(x_i)$ on $\mathcal X=C(D)$ gives
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$, since $C(D)$ embeds continuously in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, point evaluations are bounded on it, and
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\sin(w\,\cdot+\gamma b)$ is $C^2$ (indeed analytic)
into $C(D)$; such rows are
covered by~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity} on taking
$\mathcal V_i=\mathbb R$, $v_i=s_i=1$, and $a_i(f,t)=t\lambda_i(f)$, exactly as
in the proof of~\Cref{cor:weak_boundary_joint_positivity}. The remaining clauses of
$\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}$ hold as well:
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,1}=\sin(w\,\cdot+\gamma b)$ is
real analytic into $C(D)$ because $D$ is compact, and the ridge span is dense
by~\citet{Leshno1993}. Finally $\mathbb E[a_m\mid w_m,b_m]=0$, so the
output-weight centering used for GD also holds.

Take $\mathbf c=(1,2,1)^\top$. The associated single-neuron feature
combination is
\begin{equation*}
 H(w,b)=\sum_{i=1}^3c_i\sin(wx_i+\gamma b)
 =\sin(\gamma b-\pi w)+2\sin(\gamma b)+\sin(\gamma b+\pi w)
 =4\sin(\gamma b)\cos^2\!\left(\tfrac{\pi w}{2}\right),
\end{equation*}
by the sum-to-product identity followed by $1+\cos t=2\cos^2(t/2)$. The squared
factor is the whole point: $\cos^2(\pi w/2)$ has a \emph{double} zero at every
odd integer, so the per-neuron map $h_{\mathbf c}(w,b,a)=aH(w,b)$, which
satisfies $\sum_ic_iP_i(\theta)=d_1^{-1/2}\sum_mh_{\mathbf c}(\theta_m)$, has
gradient
\begin{equation*}
 \nabla h_{\mathbf c}
 =\left(
 -4\pi a\sin(\gamma b)\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi w}{2}\right)
 \cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi w}{2}\right),\;
 4a\gamma\cos(\gamma b)\cos^2\!\left(\tfrac{\pi w}{2}\right),\;
 4\sin(\gamma b)\cos^2\!\left(\tfrac{\pi w}{2}\right)
 \right),
\end{equation*}
in the coordinates $(w,b,a)$. Every component retains a factor
$\cos(\pi w/2)$, so $\nabla h_{\mathbf c}$ vanishes identically on
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$. Hence $\mathbf J(\theta_{(0)})^\top\mathbf c=\mathbf0$ almost
surely at every width, so $\mathbf K_{(0)}\mathbf c=\mathbf0$ and
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\mathbf c=\mathbf0$. Explicitly, the limit exists by
$\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} and equals the per-neuron
gradient expectation; writing $\mathbf f_1=(-1,1,-1)^\top$ and
$\mathbf f_2=(1,0,-1)^\top$, both signs $w=\pm1$ give
$(\sin(wx_i+\gamma b))_i=\sin(\gamma b)\mathbf f_1$,
$(\partial_w\sin(wx_i+\gamma b))_i=\pi\cos(\gamma b)\mathbf f_2$, and
$(\partial_b\sin(wx_i+\gamma b))_i=\gamma\cos(\gamma b)\mathbf f_1$, so that,
with $a^2\equiv1$ and $b\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]$,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =\underbrace{\left(\mathbb E[\sin^2(\gamma b)]
 +\gamma^2\mathbb E[\cos^2(\gamma b)]\right)}_{=:A}
 \mathbf f_1\mathbf f_1^\top
 +\underbrace{\pi^2\mathbb E[\cos^2(\gamma b)]}_{=:B}\,
 \mathbf f_2\mathbf f_2^\top.
\end{equation*}
Here $A\geq\min(1,\gamma^2)>0$ because $\sin^2+\cos^2=1$, and $B>0$ because
$\cos(\gamma b)$ vanishes at only finitely many $b\in[-1,1]$. Since
$\mathbf f_1$ and $\mathbf f_2$ are independent,
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=2,
 \qquad
 \ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,1)^\top\},
\end{equation*}
the null direction being the one orthogonal to both $\mathbf f_1$ and
$\mathbf f_2$. A referee may check this in one line from the entries
$[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{11}=[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{33}=A+B$,
$[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{12}=[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{23}=-A$,
$[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{13}=A-B$, and
$[\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{22}=A$: the determinant is zero while the leading
$2\times2$ minor equals $AB>0$.

Distinct Dirac masses are linearly independent, so
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}=\{0\}$ and
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_1,\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_2,
\bar{\boldsymbol\nu}_3\}=3$. The weakened
\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity,prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank} would
therefore assert $\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\{0\}$ and
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=3$; both fail, and with them the implication
from independence of the measure tuples to positive definiteness. Reading the
same three rows in $C(D)^*$ breaks the weakened
\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity,prop:functional_ntk_rank} identically, and
reading them as order-zero pointwise rows at distinct sites breaks the weakened
\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank}, whose local coefficient families
$\mathbf b_i(x_i)=(1)$ are independent. The finite-dimensional witnesses fail
with them: the moment matrix
$[\mathbf M_2^{\mathrm{nl}}]_{i,(1,\alpha)}=x_i^\alpha$
of~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_moment_matrix} is a Vandermonde matrix at the nodes
$-\pi,0,\pi$, with determinant $(0+\pi)(\pi+\pi)(\pi-0)=2\pi^3\neq0$,
so~\Cref{cor:monomial_moment_rank,prop:analytic_functional_rank} would certify
positive definiteness from a rank-$3$ test.

The deleted clause is exactly what licenses the analytic-continuation step. The
proofs
of~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity,thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}
pass from $\mathbf c\in\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty$ to vanishing of the
analytic function $G_{\mathbf c,1}$ on $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$ --- here
$G_{\mathbf c,1}=H$ --- invoke the identity theorem because that support
contains a nonempty open set, and only then apply ridge density as
in~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_all_ridges_annihilated}. In this example $H$ does vanish
on $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$, because $\operatorname{supp}\mu_h$ lies inside the zero set
$\{w\in2\mathbb Z+1\}\cup\{\gamma b\in\pi\mathbb Z\}$, and that zero set has
empty interior; there is therefore no open set to continue from, and the
density step is never reached. No repair is available within the argument: it
is the conclusion, not only the proof, that fails. The failure is also neither
an artifact of the row count nor of a knife-edge law. Appending further rows of
any class keeps $(\mathbf c,\mathbf0)$ in the kernel, because
$\nabla h_{\mathbf c}$ still vanishes on all of $\operatorname{supp}\mu$, and \emph{every}
law carried by $\{|w|=1\}$, with any bias marginal, produces the same null
vector.

Four caveats. First, only the ``pd'' conclusions break: the deleted clause
appears nowhere in $\mathsf N_{\mathrm{reg}}$ or $\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}$, so
existence of $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ and the convergence
$\mathbf K_{(0)}\to\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ still hold here, and we used them.
Second, the example shows that the clause cannot be \emph{deleted}; it does not
show that the clause is the weakest available hypothesis. A nontrivial
real-analytic function has a Lebesgue-null zero set, so the strictly weaker
requirement $|\operatorname{supp}\mu_h|>0$ already suffices for the same proof. The exact
condition under which the conclusion holds is that $\mu_h$ charge the
complement of the zero set of every feature combination attached to a vector
outside the relation space, but that condition is a restatement of the
conclusion rather than a checkable design criterion, which is why a geometric
sufficient condition is assumed instead. Third, the statement concerns the
kernel at initialization, which is what these theorems characterize and what
the spectral premise of~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} requires; the hidden
weights leave $\{-1,1\}$ under GD, and we make no claim about
$\mathbf K_{(k)}$ for $k\geq1$. Fourth, only the positive-dimensional support
uses the periodicity of $\sin$. For an arbitrary real-analytic nonpolynomial
$\sigma$, any $\gamma>0$, and any $d_0$, take $\mu_h=\delta_{\boldsymbol\xi_0}$
and $N\geq d_0+3$ Dirac rows at distinct sites: the limiting NTK is then a sum
of the $d_\theta=d_0+2$ rank-one Gram terms generated by the single parameter
value $\boldsymbol\xi_0$, so $\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\leq d_0+2<N$ while
the rows remain independent. Empty interior, not the choice of activation, is
what the construction exploits.
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
\label{ex:heavy_tail_no_deterministic_limit}
The initialization clause of~\Cref{assump:main} asks three things of the
per-neuron law $\mu$: that it be i.i.d.\ across neurons, width independent,
and compactly supported. Delete only the third, so that $\mu$ is an arbitrary
width-independent law on $\mathbb R^{d_\theta}$, and retain every clause
of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}. The existence half
of~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank}, equivalently statement one
of~\Cref{thm:linearNTK}, then fails already for a single value row.

Take $d_0=d_2=1$, $\gamma=1$, $\Omega=(0,1)$, and the one Dirichlet row
of~\Cref{def:linear_pde} with $\mathbf x_1=1$, $I_{11}=\{0\}$, coefficient
$a_{11\alpha}\equiv1$ at $\alpha=0$, and $s_1=1$, so that $N=1$,
$r_{\max}=0$ and $P_1(\theta)=u_\theta(1)$. Let $\sigma(z)=\exp(z^4)$ and
\begin{equation*}
 \theta_{m,(0)}=(w_m,b_m,a_m)
 \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,\mathbf I_3),
 \qquad
 t_m=w_m\mathbf x_1+\gamma b_m=w_m+b_m\sim\mathcal N(0,2).
\end{equation*}
