Every hypothesis other than compact support holds: $\sigma$ is real analytic
on $\mathbb R$, hence lies in $C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{r_{\max}+1,1}(\mathbb R)$, and
is nonpolynomial; $\gamma>0$;
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)=\mathbb R^2\neq\varnothing$; and $\mu$ is
i.i.d.\ across neurons and width independent. Thus $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$
and $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ both hold, as does the structural centering
requirement $\mathbb E[a_m\mid\boldsymbol\xi_m]=0$ imposed for gradient
descent, since $a_m$ has mean zero and is independent of $\boldsymbol\xi_m$.
Only $\operatorname{supp}\mu=\mathbb R^3$ is noncompact.

By~\cref{eqn:classical_one_neuron_contribution} the per-neuron map
of~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} is $h_1(\boldsymbol\xi,a)=a\,\sigma(w+\gamma b)$,
so the output-weight entry of the single-neuron Jacobian $\boldsymbol\Psi$
defined in~\Cref{assump:general} is $\partial_ah_1=\sigma(t)$. Since $N=1$,
discarding the nonnegative contributions of the two hidden coordinates gives
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{11}
 =\frac1{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}
 \bigl\|\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{m,(0)})\bigr\|_F^2
 \;\geq\;\frac1{d_1}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}X_m,
 \qquad X_m=\exp\!\left(2t_m^4\right).
\end{equation*}
These i.i.d.\ nonnegative summands are not integrable: since $t^2\leq t^4$ for
$|t|\geq1$,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E X_1
 =\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}
   \exp\!\left(2t^4-\tfrac{t^2}4\right)\,dt
 \geq\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi}}\int_{|t|\geq1}
   \exp\!\left(\tfrac74t^4\right)\,dt
 =\infty,
\end{equation*}
the last integrand being at least $e^{7/4}$ on an unbounded set. Truncation
gives the one-line failure. For each $K\in\mathbb N$ the variables
$\min\{X_m,K\}$ are i.i.d.\ and bounded, so the strong law yields
$\liminf_{d_1\to\infty}[\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{11}\geq\mathbb E\min\{X_1,K\}$
almost surely for every $K$ simultaneously, while
$\mathbb E\min\{X_1,K\}\uparrow\mathbb E X_1=\infty$ by monotone convergence.
Hence $[\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{11}\to\infty$ almost surely along one coupled
i.i.d.\ sequence, and the same truncation with the weak law gives
$\Pr\{[\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{11}\leq M\}\to0$ for every $M$ under separate
resampling at each width, so both convergence modes asserted in statement one
fail. Moreover $\mathbb E[\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{11}=\infty$ at every finite width,
so no deterministic $\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$ exists and the Gram
representation in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} is undefined.

Compact support is used at exactly one point in this chain. Statement one is
proved by~\Cref{thm:generallinearNTK} under the row bounds
of~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}, equivalently $(\mathsf G_R)$
in~\cref{eqn:gd_row_condition}, and for the pointwise class those bounds are
not assumed but derived: the proof of~\Cref{prop:linearNTK} extracts them from
compactness of $\operatorname{supp}\mu+\overline{\mathbb B}_R(0)$. Here
$\sup_{z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu}|h_1(z)|=\infty$, so the constant $A_{0,1}$ does not exist
and the derivation has no substitute, the conclusion itself being false. Note
that the divergence comes from the output-weight coordinate alone, which
involves no derivative of $\sigma$ and no differential order, so it is not an
artifact of activation smoothness or of high-order rows.

This sharpens~\Cref{ex:gaussian_moment_obstruction}, which records the
infinite population moment for the same activation: the point here is that the
empirical kernel itself diverges, so the conclusion fails and not merely its
proof, and that every remaining clause has been checked. Three limits should
be stated plainly. First, this is an existence failure and says nothing about
positive definiteness; the rank criteria of~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} are
never reached because there is no limiting matrix to test. For the same reason
the identity $\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}h_1(z)=0$ delivered by conditional centering
is vacuous here, $h_1$ not being $\mu$-integrable; this is a symptom of the
same nonintegrability rather than a second failed hypothesis. Second, the
example shows that the compact-support clause cannot be deleted, not that
compactness is necessary:
$\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}\|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\|_F^2<\infty$ would already suffice
for the deterministic limit, which is the relaxation
that~\Cref{ex:example1d} exploits. Compact support is retained because it
additionally supplies the essential-supremum constant $R_K$ for the
finite-width Chernoff bound and the uniform gradient-Lipschitz constant $L_*$
for the local stability bound, neither of which follows from moments alone.
Third, the obstruction is a joint incompatibility between the tail of $\mu$ and
the growth of $\sigma$, not a defect of Gaussian initialization: a Gaussian
$\mu$ with $\tanh$, or with any activation whose relevant derivatives grow
polynomially, leaves the per-neuron terms integrable and the limit intact.
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
\label{ex:example1d}
Consider the following \(\gamma=0\) specialization
of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}:
\[
u(x,\theta)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_1}}
\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}a_m\tanh(w_mx).
\]
Assume the marginal initialization law of
\(w_m\) has compact support containing an open neighborhood of zero (for
example, a compactly supported density that is positive near zero). Also take
the per-neuron parameter vectors to be i.i.d.\ and the output weights to
have finite second moment. These conditions ensure that the full
 limiting NTK exists; compact initialization as in~\Cref{assump:main} is
 sufficient. Use the PINN loss
in~\Cref{def:pinn_loss}
with inputs \(x=1,2,3,4,5\) for the one-dimensional Poisson problem
\begin{align*}
-\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}&=f(x),\quad x\in\Omega=(1,5),\\
u(1)&=0,\quad u(5)=0.
\end{align*}
In this bias-free model the scalar inputs are all multiples of one another,
so the distinct-direction condition of bias-free positivity results, which
requires that no two inputs be parallel, fails. Nevertheless,
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) is positive definite because an analytic
power-series coefficient calculation proves that the parameter-derivative
functions in the output-weight contribution are linearly independent. This is
the example-specific positive-definiteness certificate described in the pointwise
procedure of~\Cref{sec:pointwise_positivity_certificate}; see also
\hyperref[proof:example1d]{the detailed derivation}.
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
\label{ex:compatible_singular_ntk}
Let \(\Omega=(-1,1)\) and use the network
in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} with one-dimensional output and analytic
activation \(\sigma(z)=z+z^2\):
\begin{equation*}
u_\theta(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_1}}
\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}a_m\sigma(w_mx).
\end{equation*}
Because $\gamma=0$, the formal hidden-bias parameters $b_m$ do not affect
the predictions; their Jacobian columns are zero, so we omit them below.
Initialize \(a_m\) and \(w_m\) independently from the uniform distribution
\(\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]\). This deliberately polynomial activation
violates the activation clause used by the differential-NTK positivity result.
More decisively, its limiting NTK is singular, so it admits no positive-definiteness
certificate and does not satisfy the corresponding premise of the convergence
theorem. Place one PDE collocation
point at \(x_D=0\) and the two Dirichlet points at \(x_-=-1\) and \(x_+=1\).
Every network output has the form \(A_\theta x+B_\theta x^2\), and therefore
\begin{equation}
u_\theta''(0)=u_\theta(-1)+u_\theta(1).
\label{eqn:compatible_feature_identity}
\end{equation}
Differentiate the identity in~\cref{eqn:compatible_feature_identity} with
respect to every trainable parameter and define
\[
\boldsymbol\Phi_D:=\nabla_\theta u_\theta''(0),\qquad
\boldsymbol\Phi_-:=\nabla_\theta u_\theta(-1),\qquad
\boldsymbol\Phi_+:=\nabla_\theta u_\theta(1).
\]
These gradients obey the relation
\[
\boldsymbol\Phi_D=\boldsymbol\Phi_-+\boldsymbol\Phi_+.
\]
Thus the NTK is singular despite the distinct physical points and the linear
independence of the two boundary parameter-derivative functions.
The data can obey exactly the same relation in the following well-posed
problem:
\[
u''(x)=2,\qquad u(-1)=u(1)=1.
\]
The unique solution is \(u^*(x)=x^2\), which the network represents
for every even \(d_1\), and its unweighted target vector \((2,1,1)^\top\) is
orthogonal to the NTK null vector \((1,-1,-1)^\top\). Consequently, the
fixed-kernel dynamics attain zero limiting loss despite singularity. The
sample-group normalization in~\Cref{def:pde} rescales both prediction
components and data and preserves rank and orthogonality to the
nullspace. This construction uses \(\gamma=0\) and a polynomial activation
to restrict the model and tangent spaces, so it lies
outside~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} and the positive-definiteness-certificate premise
of~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}.
See~\cref{sec:compatible_singular_ntk_calculation} for the full calculation.
<!-- end example-15 -->
<!-- example-16: body_md -->
\label{ex:pointwise_coefficient_certificate}
Assume the network and initialization hypotheses of~ 
\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank}; for example, use a biased tanh network with
$\gamma=1$, i.i.d.\ compactly supported per-neuron initialization whose hidden
marginal support has nonempty interior, and bounded conditionally centered
output weights.
For this scalar network on $(0,1)$, place two marked pointwise rows at $x=0$:
\begin{equation*}
 \ell_1(f)=f(0)+f'(0),\qquad
 \ell_2(f)=f(0)-f'(0).
\end{equation*}
The second row can, for example, be read as a Robin boundary observation; the
first may be a co-located residual observation.  With unit row scales and
columns ordered as $(f(0),f'(0))$,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf A_0=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det\mathbf A_0=-2\neq0.
\end{equation*}
Thus the two co-located rows are jointly independent and
\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} proves that their limiting NTK is positive
definite.  Replacing the second row by a copy of the first makes the same
matrix rank one and produces the exact null vector $(1,-1)^\top$.
<!-- end example-16 -->
<!-- example-17: body_md -->
\label{ex:weak_mixed_monomial_certificate}
Let $\mathcal X=H^1(-1,1)$, take
$v(x)=1-x^2\in H_0^1(-1,1)$, and define one weak residual and two soft
Dirichlet rows by
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda^\Omega(f)=\int_{-1}^1 f'(x)v'(x)\,dx,
 \qquad \beta_-^\partial(f)=f(-1),
 \qquad \beta_+^\partial(f)=f(1).
\end{equation*}
For $p_0=1$, $p_1=x$, and $p_2=x^2$, the degree-two matrix in
\cref{eqn:weak_mixed_monomial_certificate} is
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf M_2^{\mathrm{weak,mix}}
 =\begin{pmatrix}
  0&0&-8/3\\
  1&-1&1\\
  1&1&1
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det\mathbf M_2^{\mathrm{weak,mix}}=-\frac{16}{3}\neq0.
\end{equation*}
Endpoint evaluation is bounded on $H^1(-1,1)$, and the weak row is bounded by
Cauchy--Schwarz. Take the biased tanh network and compact initialization
specified in~\Cref{cor:continuum_weak_interface_poisson}. The explicit
$H^1$-valued analyticity and polynomial-density argument in the proof of that
corollary, together with the boundedness just checked, verifies the feature
hypotheses used here. The exact minor above and
\Cref{cor:monomial_moment_rank} therefore provide a positive-definiteness certificate
for the joint three-row limiting NTK without appealing to the
positive-definiteness conclusion of that corollary.
<!-- end example-17 -->
<!-- example-18: body_md -->
\label{ex:nonlocal_mixed_moment_certificate}
Let $D=[-1,1]$, $d_2=1$, and use the nonlocal residual and Dirichlet rows
\begin{equation*}
 \lambda^\Omega(f)=f(0)-\frac12\int_{-1}^1f(y)\,dy,
 \qquad \beta_-^\partial(f)=f(-1),
 \qquad \beta_+^\partial(f)=f(1).
\end{equation*}
Their scaled measures, with unit scales, are
$\delta_0-\tfrac12\mathrm{Leb}|_{[-1,1]}$, $\delta_{-1}$, and $\delta_1$.
Against $p_0=1$, $p_1=y$, and $p_2=y^2$,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf M_2^{\mathrm{nl,mix}}
 =\begin{pmatrix}
  0&0&-1/3\\
  1&-1&1\\
  1&1&1
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det\mathbf M_2^{\mathrm{nl,mix}}=-\frac{2}{3}\neq0.
\end{equation*}
Thus the three measure rows are jointly independent. Under the activation
and initialization hypotheses of~\Cref{thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity},
the displayed nonzero minor is a positive-definiteness certificate for the joint
limiting NTK.
<!-- end example-18 -->
<!-- example-19: body_md -->
\label{ex:vectorvalued}
Let \(\mathbf u=(u_1,u_2)^\top\) on \([0,1]^2\) satisfy
\begin{align*}
 \partial_t u_1+v_{\text{adv}}\partial_x u_1&=f_1, &
 \partial_t u_2-\nu_{\text{diff}}\partial_{xx}u_2-c_{\text{coup}}u_1&=f_2,
\end{align*}
where $v_{\text{adv}},c_{\text{coup}}\in\mathbb R$ and
$\nu_{\text{diff}}>0$.
Impose also initial conditions \(u_1(x,0),u_2(x,0)\) and noncorner side conditions
\(u_1(0,t),u_2(1,t)\), and sample each of the six scalar row families (the two residual rows, the two initial rows, and the two side rows) at pairwise distinct points; a point repeated within one family repeats a row, and the resulting parallel pair gives an exact null vector of \(\mathbf K_{(0)}\) at every width and of \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) (\Cref{ex:duplicate_active_subspace}). In coordinates
\((u_1,\partial_x u_1,\partial_t u_1,\partial_{xx}u_2,\partial_t u_2)\), the
two interior rows at the same site are
\((0,v_{\text{adv}},1,0,0)\) and
\((-c_{\text{coup}},0,0,-\nu_{\text{diff}},1)\), and they are independent for
every admissible coefficient triple. At a shared physical location, the initial
constraints are the standard basis vectors in \((u_1,u_2)\), and each side
constraint is nonzero. \Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} asks for independence
of the joint family at each site, not of the interior, initial, and side
families separately. At a site carrying interior and data rows, the rows present match distinct members of the four-row family below, and each $\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)$ is $s_i>0$ times its member restricted to $\mathcal C_{\mathbf x}$, which drops only coordinates on which every row present vanishes; neither operation affects linear independence, so it suffices to check that family. Its common
coordinates are
\((u_1,\partial_xu_1,\partial_tu_1,u_2,\partial_{xx}u_2,\partial_tu_2)\) and
the rows \((0,v_{\text{adv}},1,0,0,0)\),
\((-c_{\text{coup}},0,0,0,-\nu_{\text{diff}},1)\), \((1,0,0,0,0,0)\), and
\((0,0,0,1,0,0)\) are independent: on the columns $(\partial_tu_1,\partial_tu_2,u_1,u_2)$ they form the unit upper triangular matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&1&-c_{\text{coup}}&0\\0&0&1&0\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so for every admissible coefficient triple the corresponding $4\times4$ minor of $\mathbf A_{\mathbf x}$, whose rows carry the loss scales, equals the product of the four positive scales $s_i$ and is the nonzero minor required by step~3 of the certificate procedure; the
word ``noncorner'' excludes exactly the corner sites at which an initial row
and a side row of the same component would coincide and be dependent. Thus
the local coefficient vectors are independent at
every site. Under~\Cref{assump:main} and the pointwise clauses of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, the rank result
in~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} gives \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\succ0\). The
sitewise procedure in~\Cref{sec:pointwise_positivity_certificate} is therefore
an explicit positive-definiteness certificate for the sampled rows of this coupled pointwise PDE system. It neither requires nor establishes well-posedness of the continuum problem, which as stated is not well posed: \(u_2\) carries a side condition only at \(x=1\), so the problem does not determine \(u_2\) uniquely, and \(u_1(0,t)\) is an inflow condition only when \(v_{\text{adv}}>0\).
More generally, the same criterion applies to vector-valued pointwise
systems. Their limiting NTKs are positive definite exactly when the local
coefficient vectors $\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)$ are linearly independent at every
sampled physical location; at a location carrying a single row this means only
that its coefficient vector is nonzero.
<!-- end example-19 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
\phantomsection
\label{proof:positive_definiteness}
For every \(\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N\), the Gram representation gives
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K\mathbf c
 =\int\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i\Phi_i(z)\right)^2d\mu(z)
 =\left\|\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i\Phi_i\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2.
\end{equation*}
Thus \(\mathbf K\succ0\) exactly when the \(\Phi_i\) are independent in
\(L^2(\mu)\). To obtain the support formulation, let
\(g_{\mathbf c}=\sum_i c_i\Phi_i\). If the continuous function
\(g_{\mathbf c}\) is nonzero at a point of \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\), it remains nonzero
on a neighborhood. By definition of the support, this open set has
positive \(\mu\)-measure. Hence \(g_{\mathbf c}=0\) almost surely if and only if it
vanishes on \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\).
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:direct_sum_feature_criterion}
Let
\(\mathbf K=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbf K^{(\ell)}\), where every
\(\mathbf K^{(\ell)}\) is a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix with
parameter-derivative functions \(\Phi_i^{(\ell)}\), indexed by the constraints, in a
Hilbert space \(\mathcal H_\ell\). Then
\begin{equation}
 \ker(\mathbf K)
 =\bigcap_{\ell=1}^{L}\ker(\mathbf K^{(\ell)})
 =\left\{\mathbf c:
   \sum_{i=1}^{N}c_i\Phi_i^{(\ell)}=0
   \text{ for every }\ell\right\}.
 \label{eqn:direct_sum_kernel_intersection}
\end{equation}
Consequently, \(\mathbf K\) is positive definite if and only if the
combined feature tuples
\(\left(\Phi_i^{(1)},\ldots,\Phi_i^{(L)}\right)\) are linearly independent
in \(\bigoplus_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathcal H_\ell\), equivalently if and only if
the intersection in~\cref{eqn:direct_sum_kernel_intersection} is trivial;
requiring one positive-semidefinite contribution \(\mathbf K^{(\ell)}\) to
be positive definite is sufficient but not necessary.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
For every \(\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N\),
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K\mathbf c
 =\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
   \left\|\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_i\Phi_i^{(\ell)}\right\|_{\mathcal H_\ell}^{2}.
\end{equation*}
All summands are nonnegative, so the sum is zero exactly when every summand
is zero, that is, exactly when \(\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_i\Phi_i^{(\ell)}=0\) for
every \(\ell\). For a positive-semidefinite matrix \(\mathbf M\),
\(\mathbf c^\top\mathbf M\mathbf c=\|\mathbf M^{1/2}\mathbf c\|_2^2\) vanishes
if and only if \(\mathbf M\mathbf c=\mathbf 0\); applied to \(\mathbf K\) and
to each \(\mathbf K^{(\ell)}\), whose quadratic form is the \(\ell\)th
summand, this gives both equalities
in~\cref{eqn:direct_sum_kernel_intersection}. Since \(\mathbf K\) is the Gram
matrix of the tuples \((\Phi_i^{(1)},\ldots,\Phi_i^{(L)})\) in
\(\bigoplus_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathcal H_\ell\) with the inner product
\(\sum_{\ell}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal H_\ell}\),
\(\mathbf K\succ0\) exactly when these tuples are linearly independent,
equivalently when the intersection is trivial, and
\(\mathbf K\succeq\mathbf K^{(\ell)}\) shows that one positive-definite
contribution suffices. It is not necessary: for \(N=L=2\),
\(\mathcal H_1=\mathcal H_2=\mathbb R\), \(\Phi_1^{(1)}=\Phi_2^{(2)}=1\), and
\(\Phi_2^{(1)}=\Phi_1^{(2)}=0\), both \(\mathbf K^{(1)}=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\)
and \(\mathbf K^{(2)}=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\) are singular, while
\(\mathbf K=\mathbf I_2\).
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
\phantomsection
\label{proof:quantitative_dntk_bound}
Fix \(\|\mathbf c\|_2=1\). Recall that
\begin{gather*}
 \mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty
 =\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\sim\mu_h}
 [\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)^\top],\\
 \|\mathbf p+\mathbf p'\|_2^2\geq\tfrac12\|\mathbf p\|_2^2-\|\mathbf p'\|_2^2
 \quad\text{for all }\mathbf p,\mathbf p'\in\mathbb R^{d_2}.
\end{gather*}
Because the sets \(E_\ell\) are disjoint, these facts give
\begin{align*}
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\mathbf c
 &\geq\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\int_{E_\ell}
   \|\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)^\top\mathbf c\|_2^2\,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi)\nonumber\\
 &\geq\frac12\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mu_h(E_\ell)
   \|\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi_\ell)^\top\mathbf c\|_2^2
   -\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\int_{E_\ell}
   \|(\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi)-\mathbf F(\boldsymbol\xi_\ell))^\top\mathbf c\|_2^2
   \,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi)\nonumber\\
 &\geq\frac{\beta}{2}\|\mathbf V\mathbf c\|_2^2
   -\varepsilon^2\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mu_h(E_\ell)
 \geq\frac{\beta c_{\mathrm{sep}}^2}{2}-\varepsilon^2.
\end{align*}
Taking the infimum over unit \(\mathbf c\), and using that the limiting NTK
contributions from the remaining trainable parameter groups are positive
semidefinite, proves~ 
\cref{eqn:quantitative_dntk_bound}. The final claim follows by substitution.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:exact_dntk_nullspace}
Use the network and pointwise constraints in~ 
\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization,def:scalar_collocation_constraints}.
Assume~\Cref{assump:main} and the pointwise clauses of
\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, but do not assume that the evaluated operator
coefficient vectors at each location are linearly independent. Let
$\mathcal S=\{\mathbf x_i:i\in[N]\}$. For every \(\mathbf x\in\mathcal S\), let
\(I_{\mathbf x}=\{i:\mathbf x_i=\mathbf x\}\), and define the coordinate
index set
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal C_{\mathbf x}
 =\left\{(q,\alpha):q\in[d_2],
   \alpha\in\bigcup_{i\in I_{\mathbf x}}I_{iq}\right\},
\end{equation*}
assigning zero to entries absent from an individual constraint on
\(\mathcal C_{\mathbf x}\). Define
\[
\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)
=\bigl(s_i a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x)\bigr)_
{(q,\alpha)\in\mathcal C_{\mathbf x}},
\qquad
\mathcal N_{\mathbf x}
=\left\{\mathbf c_{\mathbf x}:
\sum_{i\in I_{\mathbf x}}c_i\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)=\mathbf0\right\}.
\]
The partition
$[N]=\bigsqcup_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}I_{\mathbf x}$ canonically identifies
$\mathbb R^N$ with
$\bigoplus_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}\mathbb R^{I_{\mathbf x}}$.
Then the output-weight Gram block is well defined and
\begin{equation}
 \ker(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty)
 =\bigoplus_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}\mathcal N_{\mathbf x},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty)
 =\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}
 \dim\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x):i\in I_{\mathbf x}\}.
 \label{eqn:exact_output_dntk_nullspace}
\end{equation}
The full limiting NTK \(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\), formed from all trainable
parameters, exists and has exactly the same nullspace and rank:
\begin{equation}
 \ker(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)
 =\ker(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)
 =\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}
 \dim\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x):i\in I_{\mathbf x}\}.
 \label{eqn:exact_full_dntk_nullspace}
\end{equation}
Thus, under these hypotheses, linear
independence of the evaluated operator coefficient vectors at every location
is necessary and sufficient for both Gram matrices to be positive definite.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For scalar constraint row $i$, output component $q$, and one hidden affine
parameter $\boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b)\sim\mu_h$, the parameter-derivative
function associated with the output-weight coordinate $a_q$ is the entry
$F_{iq}$ of the output feature matrix $\mathbf F=\boldsymbol\Phi_{\mathrm{out}}$:
\begin{equation*}
F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
=[\mathbf f_i(\boldsymbol\xi)]_q
=s_i(\mathcal A_{iq}\sigma_{\mathbf w,b})(\mathbf x_i),
\qquad
\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf x)=\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b).
\end{equation*}
The $d_2$ output-weight families occupy disjoint coordinate blocks. Their
contribution to the limiting NTK is therefore
\begin{equation*}
[\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty]_{ij}
=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}
\langle F_{iq},F_{jq}\rangle_{L^2(\mu_h)},
\end{equation*}
and, for every $\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N$,
\begin{equation}
\mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\mathbf c
=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}
\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N c_iF_{iq}\right\|_{L^2(\mu_h)}^2.
\label{eqn:dntk_output_quadratic}
\end{equation}

The compact hidden support makes these parameter-derivative functions square-integrable,
so the display also proves existence of this block.
Suppose the quadratic form in~ 
\cref{eqn:dntk_output_quadratic} is zero. For every output coordinate
$q$, define the real-analytic function
\begin{equation*}
G_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf w,b)=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i s_i
(\mathcal A_{iq}\sigma_{\mathbf w,b})(\mathbf x_i).
\end{equation*}
It vanishes $\mu_h$-almost surely. Continuity
extends this equality to $\operatorname{supp}(\mu_h)$, which contains a nonempty open
subset. Hence the
identity theorem for real-analytic functions
gives $G_{\mathbf c,q}\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^{d_0+1}$. Because $\gamma>0$, the change of
variable $v=\gamma b$ ranges over all $v\in\mathbb R$.

Group the scalar constraints by their distinct physical sites. At a fixed
$\mathbf x$, the corresponding part of $G_{\mathbf c,q}$ is the following finite
sum of activation derivatives multiplied by monomials in the hidden weights:
\begin{equation*}
G_{\mathbf c,q,\mathbf x}(\mathbf w,v)
=\sum_{i:\,\mathbf x_i=\mathbf x}c_i s_i
\sum_{\alpha\in I_{iq}}a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x)
\sigma^{(|\alpha|)}(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+v)\mathbf w^\alpha.
\end{equation*}
After combining like terms, every formally nonzero $G_{\mathbf c,q,\mathbf x}$ is in
the standard form of~\citet{Jin2026}. Omitting trivial groups,
the independence lemma in~\Cref{lem:jinwu_sigma_independence} applies across
the remaining distinct sites. Since
\(\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}G_{\mathbf c,q,\mathbf x}(\mathbf w,v)
=G_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf w,v/\gamma)=0\) for all
\((\mathbf w,v)\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\), and the omitted groups are formally
zero, the remaining groups satisfy a linear relation with all coefficients
equal to one; the lemma excludes such a relation unless no group remains.
Thus every grouped polynomial is formally zero, which means that, for every
$q$, $\alpha$, and $\mathbf x\in\mathcal S$,
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{i:\,\mathbf x_i=\mathbf x}c_i s_i
a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x)=0.
\end{equation*}
Equivalently, \(\mathbf c_{\mathbf x}\in\mathcal N_{\mathbf x}\) for every
\(\mathbf x\in\mathcal S\).
Conversely, by~\cref{eqn:dntk_output_quadratic} and
\(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\succeq0\),
\(\mathbf c\in\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\) as soon as every
\(G_{\mathbf c,q}\) vanishes, and, through the grouped expansion
\(G_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf w,b)
=\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}G_{\mathbf c,q,\mathbf x}(\mathbf w,\gamma b)\),
these local coefficient cancellations make every \(G_{\mathbf c,q}\) vanish
identically.
The equivalence proves the first nullspace equality
in~\cref{eqn:exact_output_dntk_nullspace}. Rank--nullity supplies its rank
expression.

\Cref{prop:linearNTK,thm:generallinearNTK} give existence of the full limiting
NTK.
It remains to check that the other parameter coordinates neither remove nor
create dependencies caused by local operator coefficient relations. If
\(\mathbf c\in\bigoplus_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}\mathcal N_{\mathbf x}\), then for every
vector-valued function \(\mathbf u\) sufficiently differentiable through the
largest differential order among the constraints, and hence for every
network realization,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{i=1}^{N}c_iP_i(\theta)
 =\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal S}
 \sum_{(q,\alpha)\in\mathcal C_{\mathbf x}}
 \left(\sum_{i\in I_{\mathbf x}}c_i s_i
 a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x)\right)
 \partial^\alpha u_q(\mathbf x;\theta)=0.
 \label{eqn:local_operator_relation_predictions}
\end{equation}
Differentiating gives \(\mathbf J(\theta)^\top\mathbf c=0\) at every finite
width and every parameter value. Thus such a \(\mathbf c\) also belongs to
the kernel of the full limiting NTK whenever it exists.
Conversely, that matrix is the output-weight contribution plus
positive-semidefinite terms from the remaining trainable coordinates. Hence
its kernel is contained in
\(\ker(\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty)\). This argument establishes~ 
\cref{eqn:exact_full_dntk_nullspace}. The final assertion follows because a
finite family is linearly independent exactly when its relation space is zero.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
\phantomsection
\label{proof:limiting_ntk_rank}
\Cref{prop:linearNTK,thm:generallinearNTK} give existence and empirical
convergence.
Under clause $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$, apply
\Cref{prop:exact_dntk_nullspace}. Its local relation spaces and span dimensions
give~\cref{eqn:exact_dntk_rank}; the positive-definiteness criterion follows
by rank--nullity.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
\phantomsection
\label{proof:weak_constraint_positivity}
The complete one-neuron map
\[
\mathcal G(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)
=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}a_q\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}
\]
is real analytic into \(\mathcal X\), being a finite sum of the coordinates
\(a_q\) times the analytic maps
\(\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}\) of clause
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}\); for this step the \(C^2\) regularity of clause
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{reg}}\) already suffices. Compact initialization and
\Cref{lem:bounded_functional_row_regularity} therefore verify the condition
in~\Cref{assump:general}; \Cref{thm:generallinearNTK} proves existence of
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) and the stated empirical convergence.

Recall the relation map
\(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c
=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i\lambda_i\in\mathcal X^*\) of the main text.
For the derivative with respect to output coordinate \(q\) of one neuron's
output weight, define
\begin{equation*}
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =\lambda_i(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}).
\end{equation*}
Linearity of \(\lambda_i\) and the network parameterization give
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{\partial P_i(\theta)}
 {\partial (\mathbf a_m)_q}
 =\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_1}}F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi_m).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, the limiting output-weight contribution satisfies
\begin{align}
 [\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty]_{ij}
 &=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)F_{jq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 \,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi),
 \label{eqn:weak_output_kernel}\\
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\mathbf c
 &=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int
 \left|(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c)
 (\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q})\right|^2
 \,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi).
 \label{eqn:weak_output_quadratic}
\end{align}
In particular, this matrix is positive semidefinite without any
independence assumption.

Suppose first that
\(\mathbf c\in\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\). Every nonnegative term in~ 
\cref{eqn:weak_output_quadratic} is then zero, so, for every \(q\),
\begin{equation}
 g_{\mathbf c,q}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c)(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q})=0
 \qquad\mu_h\text{-almost surely}.
 \label{eqn:weak_feature_relation_ae}
\end{equation}
The map into \(\mathcal X\) is real analytic by assumption, and composition
with the bounded functional \(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c\) shows that
\(g_{\mathbf c,q}\) is a real-analytic scalar function. In particular it
is continuous. If it were nonzero at a point of
\(\operatorname{supp}(\mu_h)\), it would remain nonzero on a
neighborhood having positive \(\mu_h\)-measure, contradicting~ 
\cref{eqn:weak_feature_relation_ae}. It therefore vanishes on the support,
and hence, since \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing\) by clause
\(\mathsf W_{\mathrm{pd}}\), on a nonempty open set. The identity theorem for
real-analytic
functions gives
\begin{equation*}
 (\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c)(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q})=0
 \qquad
 \text{for every }\boldsymbol\xi\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1}
 \text{ and }q\in[d_2].
\end{equation*}
Thus \(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c\) vanishes on the linear span of all coordinate
ridge features. This set is dense in \(\mathcal X\), so continuity of
\(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c\) implies \(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c=0\) on
\(\mathcal X\). This approximation argument proves
\(\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}\).
The reverse inclusion follows immediately from~ 
\cref{eqn:weak_output_quadratic}; hence
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}.
 \label{eqn:weak_output_kernel_nullspace}
\end{equation}

It remains to compare the output-weight block with the total NTK.
The full limiting matrix equals this contribution plus positive-semidefinite
terms from the other coordinates.
Therefore
\(\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\subseteq
\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\).
Conversely, if \(\mathbf c\in\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}\), then at every finite
width and every parameter value,
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{i=1}^N c_iP_i(\theta)
 =(\mathcal R_\lambda\mathbf c)(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))=0.
\end{equation*}
Differentiating this relation gives
\(\mathbf J(\theta)^\top\mathbf c=0\), so \(\mathbf c\) lies in the empirical
full NTK's kernel and hence in the kernel of its population limit.
Together with~\cref{eqn:weak_output_kernel_nullspace}, this argument proves both
nullspace identities in~\cref{eqn:weak_exact_ntk_nullspace}. Rank--nullity
then supplies
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty
 =N-\dim\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}
 =\dim\operatorname{span}\{\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\}.
\end{equation*}

Finally, in the coercive special case, a relation among the weak
functionals implies, with
\(v_{\mathbf c}=\sum_i c_i s_i v_i\),
\begin{equation*}
 a(u,v_{\mathbf c})=0\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal X.
\end{equation*}
Taking \(u=v_{\mathbf c}\) and using coercivity yields
\(c_a\|v_{\mathbf c}\|_{\mathcal X}^2\leq0\), so
\(v_{\mathbf c}=0\). Linear independence of the \(v_i\), together with
\(s_i>0\), gives \(\mathbf c=0\). Thus
\(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{weak}}=\{0\}\), which proves the final assertion.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
\phantomsection
\label{proof:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}
Because analyticity implies \(\sigma\in C_{\mathrm{loc}}^2\),
\Cref{prop:finite_measure_row_regularity} verifies the condition in
\Cref{assump:general}; \Cref{thm:generallinearNTK} proves existence of
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\) and the stated empirical convergence.

For \(\boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b)\), use the scalar ridge feature
\(\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf y)
=\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf y+\gamma b)\)
of~\Cref{prop:quantitative_dntk_bound}, so that
\(\varphi_{\boldsymbol\xi,q}=\mathbf e_q\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}\)
in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}, and define the output-weight features
\begin{equation*}
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =s_i\int_D\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf y)
 \,d\nu_{iq}(\mathbf y).
\end{equation*}
 Because \(D\) is compact and each measure has finite total variation, the
 integrals are finite. We next justify that
 \(\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)\) is real analytic. Fix
 \(\boldsymbol\xi_0=(\mathbf w_0,b_0)\). The affine arguments
 \(\mathbf w_0^\top\mathbf y+\gamma b_0\), \(\mathbf y\in D\), lie in a compact
 interval \(I\). A real-analytic function
 on \(\mathbb R\) has compatible local holomorphic extensions, and compactness
 gives a holomorphic extension \(\widetilde\sigma\) to an open set
 \(U\subset\mathbb C\) containing \(I\). There is then a neighborhood
 \(V\subset\mathbb C^{d_0+1}\) of \(\boldsymbol\xi_0\) such that every affine
 argument for \(\boldsymbol\xi\in V\) and \(\mathbf y\in D\) lies in \(U\).
 The resulting integrand is holomorphic in \(\boldsymbol\xi\) and uniformly
 bounded on compact subsets of \(V\). Dominated integration against the
 finite total-variation measure (alternatively, Fubini's theorem with Morera's
 theorem in each complex variable) preserves
 holomorphy near \(\boldsymbol\xi_0\). Restriction to real arguments proves
 the asserted analyticity. Because
 \(\boldsymbol\xi_0\) was arbitrary, the conclusion holds on all of
 \(\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\).

As in~\cref{eqn:weak_output_kernel}, differentiation with respect to the
output weights gives
\begin{align}
 [\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty]_{ij}
 &=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int
 F_{iq}(\boldsymbol\xi)F_{jq}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 \,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi),\nonumber\\
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\mathbf c
 &=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int
 \left|\int_D\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf y)
 \,d\zeta_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf y)\right|^2
 \,d\mu_h(\boldsymbol\xi),
 \label{eqn:nonlocal_output_quadratic}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
 \zeta_{\mathbf c,q}=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i s_i\nu_{iq}.
 \label{eqn:combined_nonlocal_measure}
\end{equation}
Thus this Gram matrix is always positive semidefinite.

Suppose \(\mathbf c\in\ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty\). For each \(q\),
define the real-analytic function
\begin{equation*}
 G_{\mathbf c,q}(\boldsymbol\xi)
 =\int_D\sigma_{\mathbf w,b}(\mathbf y)
 \,d\zeta_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf y).
\end{equation*}
It vanishes \(\mu_h\)-almost surely by~ 
\cref{eqn:nonlocal_output_quadratic}. Continuity extends this equality to
\(\operatorname{supp}(\mu_h)\), and the support contains a nonempty open
set. The real-analytic identity theorem therefore gives
\begin{equation}
 \int_D\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf y+\gamma b)
 \,d\zeta_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf y)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }(\mathbf w,b)\in\mathbb R^{d_0+1}.
 \label{eqn:nonlocal_all_ridges_annihilated}
\end{equation}
Because \(\gamma>0\), the shifts \(\gamma b\) range over all real numbers.
The uniform universal-approximation theorem for a nonpolynomial activation
with a bias~\citep{Leshno1993} says that the linear span of the functions in~ 
\cref{eqn:nonlocal_all_ridges_annihilated} is dense in \(C(D)\). Integration
against the finite signed measure \(\zeta_{\mathbf c,q}\) defines a bounded
functional on that space. It therefore vanishes on all of \(C(D)\), and
uniqueness in the Riesz--Markov representation theorem yields
\(\zeta_{\mathbf c,q}=0\). The conclusion holds for every \(q\), proving
\(\mathbf c\in\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}\). Conversely, if
\(\mathbf c\in\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}\), every combined measure in~ 
\cref{eqn:combined_nonlocal_measure} is zero, and the quadratic form in~ 
\cref{eqn:nonlocal_output_quadratic} is zero. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K_{\mathrm{out}}^\infty=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}.
 \label{eqn:nonlocal_output_kernel_nullspace}
\end{equation}

The full limiting NTK is a sum of positive-semidefinite parameter-coordinate
contributions, so its kernel is contained in the output-weight kernel. In
the reverse direction, \(\mathbf c\in\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}\) implies, at
every finite width and every parameter value \(\theta\),
\begin{equation*}
 \sum_{i=1}^N c_iP_i(\theta)
 =\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\int_D u_q(\mathbf y;\theta)
 \,d\zeta_{\mathbf c,q}(\mathbf y)=0.
\end{equation*}
Differentiating gives \(\mathbf J(\theta)^\top\mathbf c=0\). Thus
\(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{nl}}\subseteq\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\), and~ 
\cref{eqn:nonlocal_output_kernel_nullspace} proves the two nullspace
identities in~\cref{eqn:nonlocal_exact_ntk_nullspace}. Rank--nullity yields
the displayed rank formula, and the positive-definiteness criterion follows.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Before the normalization assigned to each loss group in~ 
\Cref{def:pde}, set
$\widetilde P_D(\theta)=u_\theta''(0)$,
$\widetilde P_-(\theta)=u_\theta(-1)$, and
$\widetilde P_+(\theta)=u_\theta(1)$. For a scalar-output neuron with weights
$(a_m,w_m)$, define its width-rescaled parameter-gradient
blocks by
$\boldsymbol\phi_\bullet(a_m,w_m)
:=\sqrt{d_1}\,\nabla_{(a_m,w_m)}\widetilde P_\bullet(\theta)$.
The hidden-bias derivative is zero because $\gamma=0$, so we omit that
coordinate below. Writing a generic block as $(a,w)$ gives
\begin{align*}
\boldsymbol\phi_D(a,w)&=(2w^2,4aw),\\
\boldsymbol\phi_-(a,w)&=(-w+w^2,a(-1+2w)),\\
\boldsymbol\phi_+(a,w)&=(w+w^2,a(1+2w)).
\end{align*}
Hence $\boldsymbol\phi_D=\boldsymbol\phi_-+\boldsymbol\phi_+$ pointwise for
every $(a,w)$, separately for the
output-weight and hidden-weight coordinates. This identity is therefore a linear
dependence among the full parameter-gradient vectors used by the NTK, rather
than a dependence confined to the contribution from one parameter group.

For independent $a,w\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]$, direct integration gives, in
the order $(D,-,+)$, the unweighted population Gram matrix
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{\mathbf K}_{(0)}^\infty=\frac{1}{45}
\begin{pmatrix}
116&58&58\\
58&59&-1\\
58&-1&59
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}
Its eigenvalues are $0$, $4/3$, and $58/15$, and its nullspace is spanned by
$\mathbf n=(1,-1,-1)^\top$. In particular, the two boundary parameter-gradient
vectors are linearly independent, and the displayed identity is the only
dependence among the three parameter-gradient vectors.
The target $\widetilde{\mathbf v}_T=(2,1,1)^\top$ satisfies
$\mathbf n^\top\widetilde{\mathbf v}_T=0$. Every network prediction obeys the
same identity, so every initial error is also orthogonal to $\mathbf n$ and
belongs to $\operatorname{Range}(\widetilde{\mathbf K}_{(0)}^\infty)$; the loss dynamics with
the kernel held fixed at $\widetilde{\mathbf K}_{(0)}^\infty$ therefore contract to zero for
a suitable step size.

The continuum compatibility is not merely a relation among the three target
entries. The Dirichlet problem has the unique solution $u^*(x)=x^2$. For every
even width, the network represents it exactly by taking half of the hidden weights
equal to $1$, half equal to $-1$, and all output weights equal to
$d_1^{-1/2}$, because
\begin{equation*}
\frac12\left(\sigma(x)+\sigma(-x)\right)=x^2.
\end{equation*}
Finally, the residual group has $N_r=1$ row and the boundary group has two
rows, so the normalization in~ 
\Cref{def:pde} multiplies the last two prediction components and targets
by $1/\sqrt2$. Define the rescaled features by
$\boldsymbol\phi_D^{\mathrm{norm}}:=\boldsymbol\phi_D$ and
$\boldsymbol\phi_\pm^{\mathrm{norm}}:=\boldsymbol\phi_\pm/\sqrt2$, so
$\boldsymbol\phi_D^{\mathrm{norm}}
=\sqrt2(\boldsymbol\phi_-^{\mathrm{norm}}
+\boldsymbol\phi_+^{\mathrm{norm}})$. The null
vector becomes $(1,-\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)^\top$, while both the normalized target
and every normalized prediction remain orthogonal to it.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:output_linear_target_projection}
For the network in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization} and linear prediction
components under the applicable ``reg'' clause
of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, which makes the Jacobian and the tangent Gram
matrix defined at every parameter value, let \(\mathbf J_{\mathrm{out}}(\theta)\) be the columns of the full
Jacobian associated with the output weights, and set
$\mathbf a_{\mathrm{stack}}=(\mathbf a_1^\top,\ldots,
\mathbf a_{d_1}^\top)^\top$. At every finite width and
parameter value,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf v_P(\theta)
 =\mathbf J_{\mathrm{out}}(\theta)\mathbf a_{\mathrm{stack}},
 \qquad
 \mathbf v_P(\theta)\in\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf K(\theta)).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, let \(\Pi_{\ker\mathbf K(\theta)}\) denote the orthogonal
projector onto \(\ker\mathbf K(\theta)\); then
\begin{equation}
 \Pi_{\ker\mathbf K(\theta)}
   \left(\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta)\right)
 =\Pi_{\ker\mathbf K(\theta)}\mathbf v_T.
 \label{eqn:target_residual_projection_identity}
\end{equation}
For a limiting-kernel nullspace generated by the local operator coefficient
relations in~ 
\Cref{prop:exact_dntk_nullspace}, the same conclusion holds because~ 
\cref{eqn:local_operator_relation_predictions} annihilates every network prediction.
Without either structural guarantee, the generally valid formula projects the
initial training error rather than the target alone.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Linearity of every prediction component
in the network output makes the prediction vector homogeneous and linear in
$\mathbf a_{\mathrm{stack}}$; its coefficient matrix is
exactly \(\mathbf J_{\mathrm{out}}(\theta)\). Moreover,
\(\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf J(\theta))=
\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf J(\theta)\mathbf J(\theta)^\top)=
\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf K(\theta))\). Hence the prediction has zero
projection onto \(\ker\mathbf K(\theta)\), which proves~ 
\cref{eqn:target_residual_projection_identity}. The claim for a limiting
nullspace forced by local operator relations follows directly from~ 
\cref{eqn:local_operator_relation_predictions}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
\phantomsection
    \label{proof:example1d}
    The stated marginal-law hypothesis covers the Gram contribution studied
    below. To establish the full limiting NTK using
    all trainable parameters, use the example's further hypotheses that the
    per-neuron parameter vectors are i.i.d.\ across neurons and that the output
    weights have finite second moment;~\Cref{assump:main} is one sufficient
    choice. These hypotheses
    make every individual Gram contribution integrable, so the strong-law
    argument in the \hyperref[proof:ntk_deterministic]{deterministic-NTK proof}
    gives existence.
    We study the parameter-derivative functions associated with $a_m$, whose
    linear independence follows from the invertibility
    of the coefficient matrix constructed from their Taylor coefficients.
    Because nonzero row scaling preserves this property, divide by the
    positive loss-row scales and multiply the three Poisson-residual features
    by $-1$. Denote $w=w_m$. The resulting derivatives fall into two groups.
    The boundary pair is \(g_1(w)=\tanh(w)\) and \(g_2(w)=\tanh(5w)\) on the
    support of the hidden-weight law. For the interior constraints, define
    \(\chi_x(w)=w^2\tanh^{(2)}(xw)\), where \(\tanh^{(2)}\) is the second
    derivative of the hyperbolic tangent. The three collocation sites then
    give \(g_3=\chi_2\), \(g_4=\chi_3\), and \(g_5=\chi_4\) on the support of
    the hidden-weight law.
    
    All five parameter-derivative functions are analytic in \(w\).
  Because, by the assumption in~\Cref{ex:example1d}, the support of the
  hidden-weight law contains an open neighborhood of $w=0$, if a linear
  combination \(\sum_{i=1}^5c_ig_i\) vanishes on the support, then every
  coefficient of its power series at \(w=0\) vanishes. The two boundary-feature series are
  \begin{align*}
    \tanh(w) &= w - \frac{w^3}{3} + \frac{2w^5}{15} - \frac{17w^7}{315} + \frac{62w^9}{2835} + O(w^{11}), \\
    \tanh(5w) &= 5w - \frac{125w^3}{3} + \frac{6250w^5}{15} - \frac{1328125w^7}{315} + \frac{121093750w^9}{2835} + O(w^{11}).
  \end{align*}
  The corresponding interior expansions are
  \begin{align*}
    \chi_2(w) &= -4w^3 + \frac{64w^5}{3} - \frac{1088w^7}{15} + \frac{63488w^9}{315} + O(w^{11}), \\
    \chi_3(w) &= -6w^3 + 72w^5 - \frac{2754w^7}{5} + \frac{120528w^9}{35} + O(w^{11}), \\
    \chi_4(w) &= -8w^3 + \frac{512w^5}{3} - \frac{34816w^7}{15} + \frac{8126464w^9}{315} + O(w^{11}).
  \end{align*}
  Setting to zero the coefficients of \(w,w^3,w^5,w^7,w^9\) in
  \(\sum_{i=1}^5c_ig_i\) (every even coefficient vanishes because each
  \(g_i\) is odd) produces a five-equation system. The
  coefficients of $w$ and $w^3$ give
  \begin{align*}
      c_1 + 5c_2 &= 0, \\
      -\frac{c_1}{3} - \frac{125c_2}{3} - 4c_3 - 6c_4 - 8c_5 &= 0.
  \end{align*}
  The remaining powers yield
  \begin{align*}
      \frac{2c_1}{15} + \frac{6250c_2}{15} + \frac{64c_3}{3} + 72c_4 + \frac{512c_5}{3} &= 0, \\
      -\frac{17c_1}{315} - \frac{1328125c_2}{315} - \frac{1088c_3}{15} - \frac{2754c_4}{5} - \frac{34816c_5}{15} &= 0, \\
      \frac{62c_1}{2835} + \frac{121093750c_2}{2835} + \frac{63488c_3}{315} + \frac{120528c_4}{35} + \frac{8126464c_5}{315} &= 0.
  \end{align*}
  The coefficient matrix of the combined system has determinant
  $6976569344/135\neq0$. Therefore it has the unique solution
  $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf0$, and the five
  parameter-derivative functions are linearly independent as functions of $w$.
  Hence the population output-weight contribution is nonsingular. Under the
  finite-moment condition above, the full limiting NTK
  exists and is positive definite because it is the sum of this block and
  positive-semidefinite terms from the other parameters.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:initial_residual_bound}
Under~\Cref{assump:main}, suppose $(\mathsf G_R)$ holds and
\(\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0\), set
\(\mathbf h(z)=(h_i(z))_{i=1}^N\),
\(H_0^2=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}\|\mathbf h(z)\|_2^2\leq A_{0,*}^2\), and
\(\mathbf r_{(0)}=\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})\). Every initialization
realization whose per-neuron parameter vectors lie in the initialization
support (and hence almost every realization) satisfies
\begin{equation}
\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
\leq \|\mathbf v_T\|_2+\sqrt{d_1}\,A_{0,*}.
\label{eqn:deterministic_r0_bound}
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every \(0<\varepsilon<1\),
\begin{equation*}
\Pr\!\left\{
\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
\leq \|\mathbf v_T\|_2
+H_0+A_{0,*}\sqrt{2\log\frac1\varepsilon}
\right\}\geq1-\varepsilon.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:structural_spaces_compatibility}
For the pointwise, weak, and finite-measure classes, let
$\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}$ be, respectively,
$C^{r_{\max}}(\mathbb R^{d_0};\mathbb R^{d_2})$, the stated trial space
$\mathcal X$, or $C(D;\mathbb R^{d_2})$, and let
$\lambda_i:\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}\to\mathbb R$ denote the $i$th
loss-scaled linear row, so that $P_i(\theta)=\lambda_i(\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta))$
(for weak and finite-measure rows this is $\lambda_i$
of~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, that is, $s_i\ell_i$ in the notation
of~\Cref{thm:weak_constraint_positivity,thm:nonlocal_constraint_positivity}).
Define
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal O&:\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}\to\mathbb R^N,
 & [\mathcal O f]_i&=\lambda_i(f),\\
 \mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}
 &=\left\{\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N:
 \sum_{i=1}^Nc_i\lambda_i=0\text{ on }\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}\right\},
 & \mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}&=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}^\perp.
\end{align*}
A target is \emph{compatible} if
$\mathbf v_T\in\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}$, equivalently if it is orthogonal to
every exact row relation. A \emph{structural-nullspace certificate} proves
$\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}$. For a nonzero
prescribed active subspace $\mathcal U$ with orthonormal basis matrix
$\mathbf U$, a \emph{compressed positive-definiteness certificate} verifies
\mbox{$\mathbf U^\top\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\mathbf U\succ0$}.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:structural_compatibility_compression}
For the structural spaces in~\Cref{def:structural_spaces_compatibility},
under the applicable ``reg'' clause of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, so that
$\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}$ for every $\theta$,
$\operatorname{Range}(\mathcal O)=\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}$. In particular, if one
admissible field $f_\star\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}$ generates all targets,
$\mathbf v_T=\mathcal O f_\star$, then the target is compatible. Moreover,
every network prediction lies in $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}$ and
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}\subseteq\ker\mathbf K(\theta)
 \qquad\text{for every }\theta.
\end{equation*}
If a structural-nullspace certificate holds,
$\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}\neq\{\mathbf0\}$, and $\mathbf U$ is an orthonormal
basis matrix for $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}$, then
$\mathbf U^\top\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\mathbf U\succ0$, with smallest
eigenvalue equal to the smallest positive eigenvalue of
$\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$. Whether or not a structural-nullspace certificate
holds, for every target, every $\theta$, and every orthonormal basis matrix
$\mathbf U$ of $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}$, the loss decomposes exactly as
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal L(\theta)
 =\|\mathbf U^\top(\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta))\|_2^2
  +\|\Pi_{\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}}\mathbf v_T\|_2^2,
 \qquad
 \mathbf K_{\mathcal U}(\theta)
 =\mathbf U^\top\mathbf K(\theta)\mathbf U.
 \label{eqn:structural_loss_compression}
\end{equation}
The second term is an irreducible constant and vanishes exactly for compatible
targets. Hence, for a compatible target, the full residual belongs to
$\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}$ and the original loss is exactly the compressed
loss; for an incompatible target, gradient descent still optimizes the same
active loss but cannot remove the nullspace term.
If $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{str}}=\{\mathbf0\}$, the loss decomposition still
holds, but there is no positive active eigenvalue and no nontrivial compressed
GD problem.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The definition of $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}$ gives
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}=\operatorname{Range}(\mathcal O)^\perp$; the range is a subspace
of finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$ and hence is closed, proving the first
identity. Taking $f=f_\star$ proves compatibility of a jointly generated
target, while taking $f=\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)$ proves that every prediction
is active. Differentiating
$\mathbf c^\top\mathbf v_P(\theta)=0$ gives
$\mathbf J(\theta)^\top\mathbf c=0$, and hence the empirical-kernel
inclusion. If the population kernel has kernel
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}$, its quadratic form is strictly positive on the
orthogonal complement, which proves compressed positive definiteness. The
spectral assertion follows by restricting the eigendecomposition to the
positive eigenspace. Since every prediction is active, orthogonal decomposition
of the residual gives~\cref{eqn:structural_loss_compression}; its nullspace
component is $\Pi_{\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}}\mathbf v_T$. Finally, the
compressed Jacobian is $\mathbf U^\top\mathbf J(\theta)$, giving the final
kernel identity.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:active_subspace_convergence}
Fix \(0<\delta<1\). Let \(\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^N\) be a fixed
\(r\)-dimensional subspace, where $1\leq r\leq N$, and let
\(\mathbf U\in\mathbb R^{N\times r}\) have orthonormal columns that span
\(\mathcal U\). Suppose
\begin{equation}
\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta)\in\mathcal U
\qquad\text{for every }\theta\text{ in an open neighborhood of }
\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)}).
\label{eqn:fixed_compatible_subspace}
\end{equation}
Set \(\mathbf v_{T,\mathcal U}=\mathbf U^\top\mathbf v_T\), assume
\Cref{assump:main} and
\(\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0\), and require
$(\mathsf G_R)$ for the compressed prediction
\(\mathbf U^\top\mathbf v_P\). Form its per-neuron regularity constants and
the corresponding initial-residual bound \(\overline r_{\delta,\mathcal U}\),
with target \(\mathbf v_{T,\mathcal U}\), as in~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}.
Also define
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal U}^\infty=\mathbf U^\top\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\mathbf U\)
and require a compressed positive-definiteness certificate as in
\Cref{def:structural_spaces_compatibility}, namely
\(\lambda_{\mathcal U}=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{\mathcal U}^\infty)>0\).
In the width and step-size conditions of~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence},
replace
\(\lambda_0,\Lambda,R_K,A_{0,*},H_0,B_*,L_*\) by their compressed
counterparts, \(\overline r_\delta\) by
\(\overline r_{\delta,\mathcal U}\), and \(N\) by \(r\) in the Chernoff
logarithm. Assume that the resulting inequalities hold. Then, with probability at least
\(1-\delta\), every iterate lies in
\(\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\) and, for every \(k\in\mathbb N_0\),
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})
\leq(1-\eta\lambda_{\mathcal U})^k\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)}).
\end{equation*}
The full \(N\times N\) kernel may be singular. In particular, let
$\mathcal N=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}$ and assume the applicable ``pd''
clause of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, so that
$\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty=\mathcal N$, a structural-nullspace certificate:
the relation set in each kernel identity
of~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank,prop:functional_ntk_rank,prop:nonlocal_ntk_rank}
lies in $\mathcal N$, and
$\mathcal N\subseteq\ker\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty$
by~\Cref{lem:structural_compatibility_compression}. Choose
$\mathcal U=\mathcal N^\perp$. If $\dim\mathcal U\geq1$, then
\Cref{lem:structural_compatibility_compression} verifies
\cref{eqn:fixed_compatible_subspace} and the compressed certificate for every
compatible target; it also shows that targets generated jointly by one
admissible exact field are compatible automatically. If
$\mathcal U=\{\mathbf0\}$, every compatible residual is identically zero, so
there is no nontrivial optimization statement. If instead $\dim\mathcal U\geq1$
and $\mathbf v_T$ is incompatible, then $\Pi_{\mathcal U}\mathbf v_T$ is
compatible and has the same $\mathbf v_{T,\mathcal U}$, hence the same
$\overline r_{\delta,\mathcal U}$; by~\cref{eqn:structural_loss_compression}
the two losses differ by the constant $\|\Pi_{\mathcal N}\mathbf v_T\|_2^2$,
so they have the same gradient and generate the same GD path. The displayed
bound for $\Pi_{\mathcal U}\mathbf v_T$ therefore gives, on the same event and
for every $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})-\|\Pi_{\mathcal N}\mathbf v_T\|_2^2
\leq(1-\eta\lambda_{\mathcal U})^k
\bigl(\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)})-\|\Pi_{\mathcal N}\mathbf v_T\|_2^2\bigr)$.
Requiring subspace membership only at initialization, without such a global
relation, is not sufficient for this corollary.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Under~\cref{eqn:fixed_compatible_subspace},
\(\|\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta)\|_2^2
=\|\mathbf U^\top(\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta))\|_2^2\) throughout the parameter
neighborhood. Therefore the original objective and gradient are exactly those
of the compressed prediction map, whose NTK is
\(\mathbf U^\top\mathbf K(\theta)\mathbf U\). Starting from the same initialization, the
two update paths consequently coincide up to
the first possible exit from the neighborhood. Apply~ 
\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} to this compressed system; its
localization induction rules out leaving that set.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:necessary_conditions}
Let the rows be as in~\Cref{def:linear_pde} and satisfy the applicable
``reg'' clause of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, so that
$\mathbf u(\cdot;\theta)\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{row}}$ for every $\theta$, and
let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}$ be the structural nullspace
of~\Cref{def:structural_spaces_compatibility}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{Structural loss floor.} For every $\theta$,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal L(\theta)\geq\|\Pi_{\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}}\mathbf v_T\|_2^2 .
\end{equation*}
Hence, for an incompatible target, no parameter sequence, whether produced by
gradient descent at any width and step size or by any other method, drives
the loss below this positive constant.
\item \emph{Counting bound.} Let $\mathcal W\subset\mathbb R^{d_1d_\theta}$ be
bounded and suppose $\theta\mapsto\mathbf v_P(\theta)$ is Lipschitz on
$\overline{\mathcal W}$; under $(\mathsf G_R)$ this holds, with constant
$B_*$, for the closed radius-$R$ tube $\mathcal W=\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$
whenever $\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}$, which holds almost surely
under~\Cref{assump:main}. If $N>d_1d_\theta$, then
$\mathbf v_P(\overline{\mathcal W})$ is a compact Lebesgue-null subset of
$\mathbb R^N$, so for Lebesgue-almost every target $\mathbf v_T\in\mathbb R^N$,
\begin{equation*}
 \inf_{\theta\in\mathcal W}\mathcal L(\theta)>0 .
\end{equation*}
In particular, for every fixed initialization
$\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}$ and Lebesgue-almost every target, no
trajectory that remains in $\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$ satisfies
$\mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})\to0$. When $d_1<N/d_\theta$, the conclusion
of~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} fails for every target and every
initialization, because $\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K(\theta)=\operatorname{rank}\mathbf J(\theta)
\leq d_1d_\theta<N$ for every $\theta$ rules out
$\mathbf K_{(k)}\succeq\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N$. Its localization and
decay parts fail as well: Fubini's theorem applied to the $\sigma$-compact set
$\{(\theta_{(0)},\mathbf v_T):\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1},\
\mathbf v_T\in\mathbf v_P(\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)}))\}$ shows that, for almost
every target, localization in $\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$ together with
$\mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})\to0$ has probability zero over the initialization.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Part (i) is the decomposition~\cref{eqn:structural_loss_compression}, whose
second term does not depend on $\theta$. For part (ii), a map that is
Lipschitz on a subset of $\mathbb R^{d_1d_\theta}$ does not increase Hausdorff
dimension, so $\mathbf v_P(\overline{\mathcal W})$ has Hausdorff dimension at
most $d_1d_\theta<N$ and therefore Lebesgue measure zero in $\mathbb R^N$; the
image is compact because $\overline{\mathcal W}$ is compact and the map is
continuous. For $\mathbf v_T$ outside this null set,
$\mathbf v_T\neq\mathbf v_P(\theta)$ for every
$\theta\in\overline{\mathcal W}$, so the continuous function
$\theta\mapsto\mathcal L(\theta)$ attains a positive minimum on
$\overline{\mathcal W}$, which bounds the infimum over $\mathcal W$ from
below. A trajectory confined to $\mathcal W$ with
$\mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})\to0$ would contradict this bound. When
$\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}$, $(\mathsf G_R)$ bounds the gradient of
every $h_i$ by $B_i$ on each ball $\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\theta_{m,(0)})$ of
the tube, so the mean-value inequality on the convex set
$\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$ and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality over the
neurons make $\mathbf v_P$ Lipschitz there with constant $B_*$. The Fubini
step uses that the set in question is the continuous image of the closed set
$\{(\theta_{(0)},\theta):\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1},\
\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\}$, that each $\theta_{(0)}$-section of it
is Lebesgue-null by the Lipschitz bound above, and that $(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}$ has
full probability under~\Cref{assump:main}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- example-20: body_md -->
\label{ex:vector_dependency_floor}
Let $d_2=2$ and prescribe at one point $\mathbf x_0$ the two rows
$u_1+u_2=y_1$ and $2u_1+2u_2=y_2$ with loss scales $s_1,s_2>0$, so that
$P_1(\theta)=s_1(u_1+u_2)(\mathbf x_0;\theta)$ and
$P_2(\theta)=2s_2(u_1+u_2)(\mathbf x_0;\theta)$. The local coefficient
vectors $s_1(1,1)$ and $2s_2(1,1)$ are dependent, so
$\operatorname{rank}\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty\leq1$, with equality under clause
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ by~\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank}, and the
sitewise certificate of~\Cref{sec:pointwise_positivity_certificate} fails
before any training. Indeed $2s_2P_1(\theta)-s_1P_2(\theta)=0$ for every
$\theta$, so $\mathbf c=(2s_2,-s_1)^\top\in\mathcal N_{\mathrm{str}}$, and
with $\mathbf v_T=(s_1y_1,s_2y_2)^\top$ part~(i) of
\Cref{prop:necessary_conditions} gives, for every width and every $\theta$,
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal L(\theta)\geq
 \frac{(\mathbf c^\top\mathbf v_T)^2}{\|\mathbf c\|_2^2}
 =\frac{s_1^2s_2^2(2y_1-y_2)^2}{4s_2^2+s_1^2},
\end{equation*}
which is positive whenever $y_2\neq2y_1$. For the compatible data $y_2=2y_1$
the floor vanishes, the active subspace is one-dimensional, and, under clause
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$, conditional centering
$\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]=\mathbf0$, and the compressed width
and step-size conditions, \Cref{cor:active_subspace_convergence} applies to
the compressed single-row problem.
<!-- end example-20 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Let
\(\mathbf h_m=(h_1(\theta_{m,(0)}),\ldots,
h_N(\theta_{m,(0)}))^\top\). Then
\(\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})=d_1^{-1/2}\sum_m\mathbf h_m\) and
\(\|\mathbf h_m\|_2\leq A_{0,*}\), which proves~ 
\cref{eqn:deterministic_r0_bound} by the triangle inequality. The
conditional-centering condition gives \(\mathbb E\mathbf h_m=0\); with
independence of the per-neuron parameter vectors, this yields
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\|\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})\|_2^2
 =\mathbb E\|\mathbf h_1\|_2^2=H_0^2\leq A_{0,*}^2,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\|\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})\|_2\leq H_0.
\end{equation*}
If \(A_{0,*}=0\), the prediction is zero almost surely and the claim is immediate.
Suppose \(A_{0,*}>0\). Changing one per-neuron parameter vector changes
\(\|d_1^{-1/2}\sum_m\mathbf h_m\|_2\) by at most
\(2A_{0,*}/\sqrt{d_1}\). McDiarmid's inequality therefore gives
\begin{equation*}
 \Pr\!\left\{
 \|\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})\|_2
 >H_0+t\right\}
 \leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2A_{0,*}^2}\right).
\end{equation*}
Set \(t=A_{0,*}\sqrt{2\log(1/\varepsilon)}\) and use
\(\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\leq\|\mathbf v_T\|_2+
\|\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})\|_2\).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
For a fixed number of loss groups, divide each row by the square root of its
group's sample count. If the unnormalized per-neuron contributions and target
values are uniformly bounded, \(A_{0,*}\) and \(\|\mathbf v_T\|_2\) are
\(O(1)\), uniformly in the group sample counts. Hence the initial-residual estimate in~ 
\Cref{lem:initial_residual_bound} gives width- and sample-count-independent
high-probability control of \(\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\). Without per-constraint
normalization,
the corresponding aggregate quantities can grow with \(N\).
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:generalconvergence}
Suppose the condition in~\Cref{assump:general} holds and use gradient descent
as in~\Cref{def:gradient_descent}.
  Require a positive-definiteness certificate as in
  \Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate}, and let
  $0<\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^{\infty})$ be a certified
  lower bound. Set
  $\mathbf r_{(0)}=\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})$. Define the squared
  operator-norm envelope for one neuron's initialization Jacobian contribution by
  \[
   R_K:=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{z\sim\mu}\|\boldsymbol\Psi(z)\|_2^2
   \leq B_*^2.
  \]
  Also set
  \begin{equation*}
    c_{\mathrm{Ch}}
    :=\frac14+\frac34\log\frac34>0
    \qquad
    (c_{\mathrm{Ch}}^{-1}\approx29.207).
  \end{equation*}
  Let $\Lambda\geq\lambda_0$ be a deterministic upper bound on
  $\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K(\theta))$ throughout the per-neuron parameter
  neighborhood in~ 
  \Cref{assump:general}, and let $0<\delta<1$. If
\begin{equation*}
  d_1\geq \frac{R_K}{c_{\mathrm{Ch}}\lambda_0}
  \log\frac{N}{\delta},
\end{equation*}
then the matrix-Chernoff initialization event
$\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\geq3\lambda_0/4\}$
of~\Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth} has probability at least $1-\delta$.
On this event, suppose additionally that the realized initialization satisfies
\(\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}\), which holds almost surely
under~\Cref{assump:main}, and
\begin{equation*}
d_1\geq\max\!\left\{
  (320+128\sqrt6)\frac{L_*^2\Lambda\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2^2}
    {\lambda_0^3},
  \frac{16B_*^2\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2^2}{R^2\lambda_0^2}
\right\}.
\end{equation*}
If $0<\eta\Lambda\leq1/2$, every iterate remains in the fixed parameter set
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})
 :=\left\{\theta:\max_{m\in[d_1]}
 \|\theta_m-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2\leq R\right\},
\end{equation*}
and, for every $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
\[
 \mathbf K_{(k)}\succeq\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N,
 \qquad
 \mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})
 \leq(1-\eta\lambda_0)^k\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)}).
\]
One may take $\Lambda=B_*^2$
by~\Cref{prop:positive_definiteness_via_parameters}; since
$\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\leq R_K\leq B_*^2$, this
choice also gives
$\lambda_0\leq\Lambda$, so the contraction factor is positive. The
Jacobian-perturbation width condition also implies the Taylor-remainder
condition
\begin{equation*}
 d_1\geq(3+2\sqrt2)\frac{L_*^2\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2^2}
 {\lambda_0^2}.
\end{equation*}
Indeed, $\Lambda\geq\lambda_0$ and
$320+128\sqrt6>3+2\sqrt2$. For a fixed collection of PINN loss groups, divide each
row by the square root of its group's sample count. Then $B_*$ and $L_*$ are
independent of the number of points when the corresponding unnormalized
constraint-wise bounds are uniform.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Apply~\Cref{lem:initial_residual_bound} with
\(\varepsilon=\delta/2\). On the resulting event,
\(\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\leq\overline r_\delta\). Invoke~ 
\Cref{thm:generalconvergence} with its initialization failure probability set
to \(\delta/2\), \(\Lambda=B_*^2\), the squared operator-norm envelope
\(R_K\) of the single-neuron Jacobian, and the deterministic envelope \(\overline r_\delta\) in every
condition that depends on the initial training error. The union bound gives
joint confidence at least \(1-\delta\). The localization width condition
ensures, through the induction in the proof skeleton
of~\Cref{thm:generalconvergence} below, that every per-neuron displacement is
at most \(R\), which closes that induction. Consequently, every parameter block remains in the fixed
neighborhood on which the constraint-wise constants are valid.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
\phantomsection
    \label{proof:skeleton}
Set \(c_\eta=1-\eta\lambda_0\). We prove jointly by strong induction that
\begin{equation}
 \theta_{(j)}\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \mathcal L(\theta_{(j)})\leq c_\eta^j\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)})
 \qquad(0\leq j\leq n).
 \label{eqn:inductionhypo}
\end{equation}
The assertion is immediate at \(n=0\).

Suppose it holds through \(n=k\). The per-neuron part of~ 
\Cref{lem:stronginduction1}, using only the Jacobians at
\(\theta_{(0)},\ldots,\theta_{(k)}\), which satisfy the displacement bound,
gives
\begin{equation*}
 \max_m\|\theta_{m,(k+1)}-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{4B_*\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2}{\sqrt{d_1}\lambda_0}
 \leq R.
\end{equation*}
Thus \(\theta_{(k+1)}\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\). Convexity places the
full update segment there as well. The local gradient-Lipschitz bound is
therefore available throughout this set.

The global-displacement part of~\Cref{lem:stronginduction1}, the estimate for the
Jacobian perturbation in~ 
\Cref{prop:NTKposdef_eachiter}, and the initialization event imply
\[
 \frac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N
 \preceq\mathbf K_{(k)}
 \preceq\Lambda\mathbf I_N.
\]
Using~\Cref{prop:NTKtaylor} for the residual $\mathbf r_{(k)}$
from~\Cref{def:pinn_loss} gives the exact error recursion
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbf r_{(k+1)}
 =(\mathbf I_N-2\eta\mathbf K_{(k)})\mathbf r_{(k)}-\mathbf R_{(k)}.
\end{equation*}
\Cref{lem:spectralonestep} now yields
\[
 \|\mathbf r_{(k+1)}\|_2
 \leq\sqrt{c_\eta}\,\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2.
\]
Squaring and applying the induction hypothesis proves the loss assertion at
\(k+1\), and the per-neuron estimate proves the displacement assertion.
These two conclusions close the argument.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prop:NTKtaylor}
    Under the condition in~\Cref{assump:general} and the gradient descent algorithm setup in~ 
    \Cref{def:gradient_descent}, suppose the segment
    \([\theta_{(n)},\theta_{(n+1)}]\) lies in a convex set on which
\(\theta\mapsto\mathbf v_P(\theta)\) is continuously differentiable; apart from
this and the squared loss, the proof uses neither the
representation~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} nor the
bounds~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}. Under~\Cref{assump:general} this
holds when \(\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}\) and the segment lies in the
prescribed per-neuron
    parameter neighborhood.
    Then the difference in prediction between consecutive iterations admits
    the decomposition
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf v_P(\theta_{(n+1)})-\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(n)})
    &=2\eta\mathbf K_{(n)}\mathbf r_{(n)}+\mathbf R_{(n)},
\end{align*}
where
\(\Delta\theta_{(n)}:=\theta_{(n+1)}-\theta_{(n)}
=-\eta\nabla\mathcal L(\theta_{(n)})\) and
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf R_{(n)}
 =\int_0^1
 \left[\mathbf J(\theta_{(n)}+s\Delta\theta_{(n)})-\mathbf J_{(n)}\right]
 \Delta\theta_{(n)}\,ds.
 \label{eqn:gradient_integral_remainder}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The fundamental theorem of calculus on the update segment gives
\begin{align*}
 \mathbf v_P(\theta_{(n+1)})-\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(n)})
 &=\int_0^1\mathbf J(\theta_{(n)}+s\Delta\theta_{(n)})
   \Delta\theta_{(n)}\,ds\\
 &=\mathbf J_{(n)}\Delta\theta_{(n)}+\mathbf R_{(n)}.
\end{align*}
By the chain rule,
\[
 \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_{(n)})
 =2\mathbf J_{(n)}^\top
   \left(\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(n)})-\mathbf v_T\right).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \mathbf J_{(n)}\Delta\theta_{(n)}
 =2\eta\mathbf J_{(n)}\mathbf J_{(n)}^\top
   \left(\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(n)})\right),
\]
which is the stated decomposition.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{prop:NTKposdef_eachiter}
    Under the condition in~\Cref{assump:general} and gradient descent in~ 
    \Cref{def:gradient_descent}, suppose
    \(\theta_{(0)},\ldots,\theta_{(k)}\) lie in the prescribed per-neuron
    parameter neighborhood and the fixed design has a positive-definiteness certificate
    as in~\Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate}, with
    \(0<\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)\) a certified
    lower bound. Let \(\Lambda\geq\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})}
    \lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K(\theta))\) be a deterministic upper bound. Fix
    \(0<\delta<1\) and set
    \(c_{\mathrm{Ch}}=\frac14+\frac34\log\frac34\). If the induction hypothesis in~ 
    \cref{eqn:inductionhypo} holds through \(k\), \(0<\eta\Lambda\leq1/2\), and
    \begin{equation*}
    d_1\geq\max\!\left\{
      \frac{R_K}{c_{\mathrm{Ch}}\lambda_0}\log\frac{N}{\delta},
      (320+128\sqrt6)
      \frac{L_*^2\Lambda\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2^2}{\lambda_0^3}
    \right\},
    \end{equation*}
    then
    \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\geq\lambda_0/2\) on the
    initialization event \(\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\geq3\lambda_0/4\}\)
of~\Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth} intersected with the event
\(\theta_{(0)}\in(\operatorname{supp}\mu)^{d_1}\), which holds almost surely
under~\Cref{assump:main}; by the first width term
and~\Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth}, this intersection has
probability at least \(1-\delta\).
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
On the initialization event,
\[
 \sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J_{(0)})
 =\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})}
 \geq\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_0}.
\]
The uniform Lipschitz bound for each neuron's gradient and the block structure of
the Jacobian columns associated with different neurons give, as
in~\cref{eqn:direct_jacobian_perturbation},
\begin{equation*}
 \|\mathbf J_{(k)}-\mathbf J_{(0)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}
       \|\theta_{(k)}-\theta_{(0)}\|_2.
\end{equation*}
Indeed, the squared operator norm of a horizontal concatenation is at most the
sum of the squared norms of its neuronal components.

For $k\geq1$, sum the global one-step estimate
of~\Cref{lem:parameterdifferencestep6} over \(j=0,\ldots,k-1\): each
\(\theta_{(j)}\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\), so
\(\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K_{(j)})\leq\Lambda\), and the induction hypothesis
gives \(\|\mathbf r_{(j)}\|_2\leq(1-\eta\lambda_0)^{j/2}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\).
On the initialization event,
\(\Lambda\geq\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\geq3\lambda_0/4\), so
\(0<\eta\lambda_0\leq\frac43\eta\Lambda\leq\frac23\), and the geometric-series
argument in the proof of~\Cref{lem:stronginduction1} gives (the case $k=0$ is
trivial),
\begin{equation*}
 \|\theta_{(k)}-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{4\sqrt\Lambda}{\lambda_0}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2.
\end{equation*}
Because
\[
 320+128\sqrt6
 =\frac{64}{(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)^2},
\]
the width condition implies
\[
 \|\mathbf J_{(k)}-\mathbf J_{(0)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{\sqrt3-\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_0}.
\]
Singular-value perturbation therefore yields
\[
 \sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J_{(k)})
 \geq\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_0}.
\]
Squaring proves
\(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\geq\lambda_0/2\).
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:parameterdifferencestep6}
Under the row-regularity condition in~\Cref{assump:general} and gradient descent in~ 
\Cref{def:gradient_descent}, let $n\geq1$ be an integer. If
$\theta_{(n-1)}$ lies in the prescribed per-neuron parameter neighborhood and
$\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K_{(n-1)})\leq\Lambda$, then
\begin{equation*}
 \|\theta_{(n)}-\theta_{(n-1)}\|_2^2
 \leq4\eta^2\Lambda\|\mathbf r_{(n-1)}\|_2^2.
\end{equation*}
Moreover, each unit satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|\theta_{m,(n)}-\theta_{m,(n-1)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{2\eta B_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}
       \|\mathbf r_{(n-1)}\|_2.
 \label{eqn:one_step_block_motion}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
The gradient update and $\mathbf K_{(n-1)}=\mathbf J_{(n-1)}
\mathbf J_{(n-1)}^\top$ give the exact identity
\begin{align*}
\|\theta_{(n)}-\theta_{(n-1)}\|_2^2
&=4\eta^2\|\mathbf J_{(n-1)}^\top\mathbf r_{(n-1)}\|_2^2\\
&=4\eta^2\mathbf r_{(n-1)}^\top\mathbf K_{(n-1)}
\mathbf r_{(n-1)},
\end{align*}
and the spectral bound proves the global estimate.
For the per-neuron claim, the block Jacobian and corresponding change are
\begin{align*}
 \mathbf J_{(n-1),m}
 &=d_1^{-1/2}\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{m,(n-1)}),\\
 \theta_{m,(n)}-\theta_{m,(n-1)}
 &=2\eta\mathbf J_{(n-1),m}^\top\mathbf r_{(n-1)}.
\end{align*}
Because \(\theta_{(n-1)}\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\), the row bounds
\(\|\nabla h_i\|_2\leq B_i\) in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} apply at
\(\theta_{m,(n-1)}\); summing them over \(i\in[N]\) and
using~\cref{eqn:abstract_aggregate_constants} together with
\(\|\cdot\|_2\leq\|\cdot\|_F\) gives
\(\|\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{m,(n-1)})\|_2\leq B_*\), which proves~ 
\cref{eqn:one_step_block_motion}.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:stronginduction1}
    Under the conditions in~\Cref{thm:generalconvergence} and gradient descent
    in~\Cref{def:gradient_descent}, suppose
    \(\theta_{(0)},\ldots,\theta_{(k)}\) lie in the prescribed per-neuron
    parameter neighborhood. If the
    induction hypothesis~\cref{eqn:inductionhypo} holds through \(k\),
    then, with \(x_\eta=\eta\lambda_0\),
    \begin{align*}
      \|\theta_{(k+1)}-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
      &\leq
      \frac{2(1+\sqrt{1-x_\eta})\sqrt\Lambda}{\lambda_0}
      \|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
      \leq\frac{4\sqrt\Lambda}{\lambda_0}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2,
      \\
      \max_m\|\theta_{m,(k+1)}-\theta_{m,(0)}\|_2
      &\leq
      \frac{2(1+\sqrt{1-x_\eta})B_*}{\sqrt{d_1}\lambda_0}
      \|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
      \leq\frac{4B_*}{\sqrt{d_1}\lambda_0}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2.
   \end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By~\cref{eqn:inductionhypo},
\(\|\mathbf r_{(n)}\|_2\leq(1-x_\eta)^{n/2}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\).
Summing the global one-step estimate in~ 
\Cref{lem:parameterdifferencestep6} gives
\[
 \|\theta_{(k+1)}-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
 \leq
 2\eta\sqrt\Lambda\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
 \sum_{n=0}^{k}(1-x_\eta)^{n/2}.
\]
Applying the same argument to~\cref{eqn:one_step_block_motion}, followed by a
maximum over \(m\), produces the analogous expression with
\(\sqrt\Lambda\) replaced by \(B_*/\sqrt{d_1}\). Finally,
\[
 \frac{\eta}{1-\sqrt{1-x_\eta}}
 =\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x_\eta}}{\lambda_0}
 \leq\frac2{\lambda_0},
\]
which proves both claims. All one-step estimates use only the iterates through
\(k\), each of which satisfies the per-neuron displacement bound.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:residualtermstep}
    Under the conditions in~\Cref{thm:generalconvergence} and the update
    in~\Cref{def:gradient_descent}, suppose the update segment
    \([\theta_{(k)},\theta_{(k+1)}]\) lies in the prescribed per-neuron
    parameter neighborhood. Then
    \begin{equation*}
        \left\| \mathbf{R}_{(k)} \right\|_2
        \leq \frac{2L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}\,\eta^2\Lambda
        \left\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\right\|_2^2.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
For any two points in this convex set, the decomposition
of the Jacobian by neurons and the gradient-Lipschitz bounds
in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} give
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathbf J(\theta')-\mathbf J(\theta)\|_2
 \leq\frac{L_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}\|\theta'-\theta\|_2.
 \label{eqn:jacobian_lipschitz_global}
\end{equation}
