Indeed, after squaring, the norm of the horizontal concatenation is at most the
sum of the squared operator norms of its blocks.
Using~\cref{eqn:gradient_integral_remainder} and~ 
\cref{eqn:jacobian_lipschitz_global},
set $\Delta\theta_{(k)}=\theta_{(k+1)}-\theta_{(k)}$ and obtain
\[
 \|\mathbf R_{(k)}\|_2
 \leq\int_0^1\frac{sL_*}{\sqrt{d_1}}
       \|\Delta\theta_{(k)}\|_2^2\,ds
 =\frac{L_*}{2\sqrt{d_1}}\|\Delta\theta_{(k)}\|_2^2.
\]
Finally, the one-step estimate in~\Cref{lem:parameterdifferencestep6} gives
\[
 \|\Delta\theta_{(k)}\|_2^2
 \leq4\eta^2\Lambda\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2^2,
\]
which proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:spectralonestep}
Suppose the induction hypothesis~\cref{eqn:inductionhypo} holds through
iteration $k$, the update segment $[\theta_{(k)},\theta_{(k+1)}]$ lies in
$\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})$,
$\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\geq\lambda_0/2$, and
$\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\leq\Lambda$. Under the width and step-size
conditions of~\Cref{thm:generalconvergence},
\begin{equation*}
 \|\mathbf r_{(k+1)}\|_2
 \leq\sqrt{1-\eta\lambda_0}\,\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Set \(x_\eta=\eta\lambda_0\) and \(y_\eta=\eta\Lambda\). Because
\[
 \frac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N
 \preceq\mathbf K_{(k)}
 \preceq\Lambda\mathbf I_N,
 \qquad y_\eta\leq\frac12,
\]
all eigenvalues of \(\mathbf I_N-2\eta\mathbf K_{(k)}\) are nonnegative and
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathbf I_N-2\eta\mathbf K_{(k)}\|_2\leq1-x_\eta.
 \label{eqn:linearized_error_contraction}
\end{equation}
The width condition controlling the Jacobian perturbation in~ 
\Cref{thm:generalconvergence} implies
\[
 d_1\geq(3+2\sqrt2)
 \frac{L_*^2\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2^2}{\lambda_0^2}.
\]
If \(\mathbf r_{(k)}=0\), the update and remainder both vanish, so the result is
immediate. Otherwise, because
\(\sqrt{3+2\sqrt2}=1+\sqrt2\), the induction hypothesis and the Taylor-remainder
bound in~\Cref{lem:residualtermstep} imply
\begin{align}
 \frac{\|\mathbf R_{(k)}\|_2}{\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2}
 &\leq\frac{2L_*\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2}{\sqrt{d_1}}\eta^2\Lambda\nonumber\\
 &\leq2(\sqrt2-1)x_\eta y_\eta
 \leq(\sqrt2-1)x_\eta.
 \label{eqn:relative_remainder_bound}
\end{align}
\Cref{prop:NTKtaylor} with \(n=k\), together with
\(\mathbf r(\theta)=\mathbf v_T-\mathbf v_P(\theta)\), gives
\[
 \mathbf r_{(k+1)}
 =(\mathbf I_N-2\eta\mathbf K_{(k)})\mathbf r_{(k)}-\mathbf R_{(k)}.
\]
For \(0<x_\eta\leq1/2\),
\[
 \sqrt{1-x_\eta}-(1-x_\eta)
 =x_\eta\frac{\sqrt{1-x_\eta}}{1+\sqrt{1-x_\eta}}
 \geq(\sqrt2-1)x_\eta.
\]
Combining this inequality with~ 
\cref{eqn:linearized_error_contraction,eqn:relative_remainder_bound} proves the
claim.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:exponent_normalization}
For \(\varrho>0\), consider the one-parameter family
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf u(\mathbf x;\theta)
 =\frac1{d_1^{\varrho}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}
  \sigma(\mathbf w_m^\top\mathbf x+\gamma b_m)\mathbf a_m,
 \label{eqn:exponent_network}
\end{equation}
with \(\theta_m\), \(d_\theta\), and the trained parameters exactly as
in~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}. The choice \(\varrho=1/2\)
is~\cref{eqn:network_main} and is the only member used elsewhere in this paper.
For a nonlinear constraint of degree \(p\geq2\) we single out the
\emph{degree-matched} exponent \(\varrho_p=(2p-1)/(2p)\), for which the overall normalization \(d_1^{-2p\varrho_p}=d_1^{-(2p-1)}\) of a degree-\((p,p)\) kernel block supplies exactly one factor \(d_1^{-1}\) for each of the \(2p-1\) neuron sums that the block formally contains: the \(2p-2\) prediction factors and the sum over neurons in the tangent Gram entry.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:composite_nonlinear_rows}
Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) and a family \(\mathcal L=[n]\) (an index set, unrelated to the
loss \(\mathcal L(\theta)\) of~\Cref{def:pinn_loss}) of scalar linear
observations of the network, each satisfying the row-regularity condition
of~\Cref{assump:general} at \(\varrho=1/2\), with per-neuron maps
\(h_\ell(\boldsymbol\xi,\mathbf a)=\mathbf a^\top\mathbf f_\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)\)
as in~\cref{eqn:predictionmap} and constants \(A_{0,\ell},B_\ell,L_\ell<\infty\)
as in~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}. Under~\cref{eqn:exponent_network},
the value of observation \(\ell\) is
\begin{equation}
 Q_\ell(\theta)=\frac1{d_1^{\varrho}}\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}h_\ell(\theta_m),
 \qquad
 \mathbf Q(\theta)=(Q_1(\theta),\ldots,Q_n(\theta))^\top .
 \label{eqn:base_family_representation}
\end{equation}
A \emph{composite row} is \(P_i(\theta)=\pi_i(\mathbf Q(\theta))\) for a fixed
\(\pi_i\in C^1(\mathbb R^n)\); the loss scale \(s_i\) of~\Cref{def:linear_pde}
is absorbed into \(\pi_i\), so \(P_i\) is the full loss-scaled row and
\(\mathbf K(\theta)\) of~\cref{eqn:loss_kernel_main} is the full tangent Gram
matrix. The row is \emph{affine} when \(\pi_i\) is affine and \emph{genuinely
nonlinear} otherwise, and it is a \emph{degree-\(p\) polynomial row} when
\(\pi_i\) is a polynomial of degree \(p\). For a multiset
\(J=(j_1,\ldots,j_q)\) with entries in \(\mathcal L\) we write
\(\mathcal M_J(\theta)=\prod_{s=1}^qQ_{j_s}(\theta)\) for the associated
monomial and call \(q=|J|\) its degree; every polynomial row is a finite linear
combination of monomials, and by bilinearity every kernel entry is the
corresponding combination of the \emph{monomial blocks}
\(K^{J,J'}=\sum_{m}\langle\nabla_{\theta_m}\mathcal M_J,
\nabla_{\theta_m}\mathcal M_{J'}\rangle\).
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:composite_kernel_identity}
Let the rows be composite as in~\Cref{def:composite_nonlinear_rows} under the
exponent \(\varrho\). Then for every \(\theta\) whose neuron blocks all lie in
\(\operatorname{supp}\mu+\overline{\mathbb B}_R(\mathbf0)\),
where~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds} provides \(\nabla h_\ell\) (almost
surely, every \(\theta\in\mathcal T_R(\theta_{(0)})\) qualifies), every
\(m\in[d_1]\), and every
\(i,j\in[N]\),
\begin{equation}
 \nabla_{\theta_m}P_i(\theta)
 =\frac1{d_1^{\varrho}}
  \boldsymbol\Psi_{\mathcal L}(\theta_m)^\top\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Q(\theta)),
 \qquad
 [\mathbf K(\theta)]_{ij}
 =d_1^{1-2\varrho}\,
  \nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Q(\theta))^\top
  \widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}(\theta)\,
  \nabla\pi_j(\mathbf Q(\theta)).
 \label{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel}
\end{equation}
In particular, for monomials \(J=(j_1,\ldots,j_q)\) and
\(J'=(l_1,\ldots,l_{q'})\) of degrees \(q\) and \(q'\),
\begin{equation}
 K^{J,J'}(\theta)
 =d_1^{1-2\varrho}
  \sum_{r=1}^{q}\sum_{t=1}^{q'}
  \Bigl(\prod_{s\neq r}Q_{j_s}(\theta)\Bigr)
  \Bigl(\prod_{s\neq t}Q_{l_s}(\theta)\Bigr)
  \bigl[\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}(\theta)\bigr]_{j_rl_t}.
 \label{eqn:polynomial_kernel_identity}
\end{equation}
Both identities hold at every width and every such parameter value; no expectation,
limit, or approximation is involved.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Only the \(m\)-th summand of~\cref{eqn:base_family_representation} depends on
\(\theta_m\), so \(\nabla_{\theta_m}Q_\ell(\theta)
=d_1^{-\varrho}\nabla h_\ell(\theta_m)\), and the chain rule gives the first
display. Since the neuron blocks exhaust every trainable parameter and
\(\mathbf K=\mathbf J\mathbf J^\top\) by~\cref{eqn:loss_kernel_main},
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K(\theta)]_{ij}
 =\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\langle\nabla_{\theta_m}P_i,\nabla_{\theta_m}P_j\rangle
 =d_1^{-2\varrho}\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Q)^\top
  \Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^{d_1}\boldsymbol\Psi_{\mathcal L}(\theta_m)
   \boldsymbol\Psi_{\mathcal L}(\theta_m)^\top\Bigr)\nabla\pi_j(\mathbf Q),
\end{equation*}
which is the second. For the monomial form, apply the second identity with \(\pi_i\) and \(\pi_j\) replaced by the monomial maps \(\pi_J(\mathbf z)=\prod_{s=1}^{q}z_{j_s}\) and \(\pi_{J'}(\mathbf z)=\prod_{s=1}^{q'}z_{l_s}\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). Then \(\mathcal M_J=\pi_J\circ\mathbf Q\) and \(\mathcal M_{J'}=\pi_{J'}\circ\mathbf Q\), and
\(\nabla\pi_J(\mathbf Q(\theta))
=\sum_{r=1}^q\bigl(\prod_{s\neq r}Q_{j_s}(\theta)\bigr)\mathbf e_{j_r}\), with the same formula for \(\pi_{J'}\). Here \(\mathbf e_\ell\) is the \(\ell\)-th standard basis vector of \(\mathbb R^n\), not of \(\mathbb R^{d_2}\).
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:base_family_limits}
Assume~\Cref{assump:main} and let the base family satisfy
\Cref{assump:general}. Put
\(\widetilde Q_\ell(\theta)=d_1^{-1/2}\sum_mh_\ell(\theta_m)\), so that
\(\mathbf Q(\theta)=d_1^{1/2-\varrho}\widetilde{\mathbf Q}(\theta)\). At
initialization, as \(d_1\to\infty\):
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \(\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}(\theta_{(0)})
 \to\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\) in probability, and almost surely under the
 nested-width convention of~\Cref{thm:linearNTK};
\item under~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))},
 \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}(\theta_{(0)})\Rightarrow
 \mathbf Z\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\), jointly
 with the convergence in item~\textup{1};
\item without~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))}, with
 \(m_\ell=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}h_\ell(z)\), one has
 \(d_1^{\varrho-1}Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})\to m_\ell\), almost surely along
 nested widths as in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} and in probability under fresh
 resampling.
\end{enumerate}
Moreover \(|m_\ell|\leq A_{0,\ell}\),
\(|[\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}]_{\ell\ell'}|\leq A_{0,\ell}A_{0,\ell'}\)
and \(|[\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty]_{\ell\ell'}|\leq B_\ell B_{\ell'}\).
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
By~\Cref{assump:main} the vectors \(\theta_{m,(0)}\) are i.i.d.\ and lie in
\(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) almost surely. The matrices
\(\boldsymbol\Psi_{\mathcal L}(\theta_{m,(0)})
\boldsymbol\Psi_{\mathcal L}(\theta_{m,(0)})^\top\) are i.i.d.\ and bounded
entrywise by \(B_\ell B_{\ell'}\) through Cauchy--Schwarz
and~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}, so item~1 is statement one
of~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} applied to the design \(\mathcal L\), with the same
convention governing the mode of convergence. For item~2 the random vectors
\((h_\ell(\theta_{m,(0)}))_{\ell}\) are i.i.d., bounded by \((A_{0,\ell})_\ell\),
hence square integrable, and centered by~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))}; the
multivariate Lindeberg--L\'evy theorem gives the stated Gaussian limit, which is
degenerate exactly when \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}\) is singular. Joint
convergence follows from Slutsky's theorem, which requires no independence
between the two components, and indeed they are strongly dependent, being built
from the same neurons; it applies because the second limit is
\emph{deterministic}. Item~3 is the strong law for the same bounded i.i.d.\@
summands along nested widths, and the weak law otherwise. The three bounds are immediate
from~\cref{eqn:abstract_one_neuron_bounds}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop:nonlinear_ntk_nondeterminism}
Assume~\Cref{assump:main}, let the base family satisfy~\Cref{assump:general}
and~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))}, let \(\varrho=1/2\), and let \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\) be
composite rows. Then, as \(d_1\to\infty\):
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item jointly in all entries,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf K_{(0)}\Longrightarrow
 \mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z)
 :=\mathbf D\boldsymbol\pi(\mathbf Z)\,\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\,
   \mathbf D\boldsymbol\pi(\mathbf Z)^\top,
 \qquad
 \mathbf Z\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}),
 \label{eqn:nonlinear_kernel_weak_limit}
\end{equation}
where the rows of \(\mathbf D\boldsymbol\pi(\mathbf q)\in\mathbb R^{N\times n}\)
are \(\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf q)^\top\);
\item if \(\pi_i\) and \(\pi_j\) are affine with
 \(\nabla\pi_i\equiv\boldsymbol\beta_i\) and
 \(\nabla\pi_j\equiv\boldsymbol\beta_j\), the corresponding limit is the
 deterministic constant
 \(\boldsymbol\beta_i^\top\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\boldsymbol\beta_j\),
 which is the entry \([\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty]_{ij}\) supplied
 by~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} for those rows;
\item if \([\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z)]_{ij}\) is not almost
 surely constant, then \([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}\) converges in probability to no
 constant whatsoever, so at \(\varrho=1/2\) no deterministic infinite-width kernel exists for that
 entry, either almost surely along nested widths or in probability;
\item if every \(\pi_i\) is a polynomial, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E\bigl[[\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}\bigr]
 \to\mathbb E\bigl[[\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z)]_{ij}\bigr],
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}\bigl([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}\bigr)
 \to\operatorname{Var}\bigl([\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z)]_{ij}\bigr).
 \label{eqn:nonlinear_kernel_variance_limit}
\end{equation}
Hence whenever the right-hand variance is positive the entrywise standard
deviation of \(\mathbf K_{(0)}\) is \(\Theta(1)\) in \(d_1\), in contrast with
the \(O(d_1^{-1/2})\) standard deviation of the affine case.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
\emph{Item 1.} At \(\varrho=1/2\) we have
\(\mathbf Q=\widetilde{\mathbf Q}\) and the prefactor
in~\cref{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel} equals one. By items~1 and~2
of~\Cref{lem:base_family_limits},
\(\bigl(\mathbf Q(\theta_{(0)}),\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}(\theta_{(0)})
\bigr)\Rightarrow(\mathbf Z,\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty)\) in
\(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). The map
\((\mathbf q,\mathbf G)\mapsto\mathbf D\boldsymbol\pi(\mathbf q)\mathbf G
\mathbf D\boldsymbol\pi(\mathbf q)^\top\) is continuous because each \(\pi_i\)
is \(C^1\); the continuous mapping theorem
and~\cref{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel} give the claim.

\emph{Item 2} is immediate, \(\nabla\pi_i\) and \(\nabla\pi_j\) being constant, together
with \(\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}\langle\nabla(\boldsymbol\beta_i^\top\mathbf h)(z),
\nabla(\boldsymbol\beta_j^\top\mathbf h)(z)\rangle
=\boldsymbol\beta_i^\top\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\boldsymbol\beta_j\), where \(\mathbf h=(h_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathcal L}\).

\emph{Item 3.} Convergence in probability to \(c\) implies convergence in
distribution to \(\delta_c\); weak limits are unique, so
\([\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z)]_{ij}=c\) almost surely,
contrary to hypothesis.

\emph{Item 4.} Fix \(r\geq1\). Rosenthal's inequality for independent
mean-zero summands together with \(|h_\ell|\leq A_{0,\ell}\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\)
gives a constant \(C_r\) with
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E|Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})|^{2r}
 \leq C_r\bigl[(\mathbb Eh_\ell^2)^r+d_1^{1-r}\mathbb E|h_\ell|^{2r}\bigr]
 \leq2C_rA_{0,\ell}^{2r},
\end{equation*}
uniformly in \(d_1\); since \(\|\mathbf Q\|_2^{2r}\leq n^{r}\sum_\ell
|Q_\ell|^{2r}\) and \(r\geq1\) is arbitrary, Lyapunov's inequality shows that
every moment of \(\|\mathbf Q(\theta_{(0)})\|_2\) is bounded
uniformly in \(d_1\). Also
\(\|\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}\|_2\leq
\operatorname{tr}\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}\leq\sum_\ell B_\ell^2\)
almost surely, the first inequality because
\(\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}\succeq\mathbf0\). If \(\pi_i\) has degree
\(p_i\) then \(\|\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf q)\|_2\leq c_i(1+\|\mathbf q\|_2)^{p_i-1}\),
so by~\cref{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel}
\(\sup_{d_1}\mathbb E|[\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}|^4<\infty\). A family bounded in
\(L^4\) is uniformly integrable, and so is the family of its squares; weak
convergence then transfers the first two moments. In the affine case
\([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}\) is an average of \(d_1\) i.i.d.\ bounded terms, whence
variance \(O(d_1^{-1})\).
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:base_family_certificates}
Assume~\textup{(\(\mathsf C_{\mathrm{iso}}\))} and let
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty\) denote the output-weight block of
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\), that is
\([\mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty]_{\ell\ell'}
=\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\langle[\mathbf f_\ell]_q,[\mathbf f_{\ell'}]_q
\rangle_{L^2(\mu_h)}\). Then
\begin{equation}
 \boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}
 =c_{\mathbf a}\mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty,
 \qquad
 \mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\succeq
 \mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty .
 \label{eqn:base_family_certificate_identity}
\end{equation}
Consequently \(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty\succ0\) implies both
\(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}\succ0\) and
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\succ0\). That hypothesis is the output-block
positive-definiteness certificate of
\Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate} applied to the \emph{base family},
not to the composite design; when the base observations are pointwise
differential rows and the clauses \(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}\),
\(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}\) of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} hold,
\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} certifies it exactly when the evaluated
coefficient vectors of the base observations are linearly independent at every
sampled location, which holds for the base family
\(\{\partial_tu,u,\partial_xu,\partial_{xx}u\}\) of the conservation-law row.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Because \(\partial h_\ell/\partial a_q=[\mathbf f_\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)]_q\), the
\(d_2\) output-weight coordinates contribute exactly
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty\)
to~\cref{eqn:base_family_matrices}, that contribution depending on \(z\) only
through \(\boldsymbol\xi\), while the remaining \(d_0+1\) coordinates contribute
a positive-semidefinite matrix; this is the second relation. For the first,
\begin{equation*}
 [\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}]_{\ell\ell'}
 =\mathbb E\bigl[\mathbf f_\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)^\top\mathbf a\mathbf a^\top
   \mathbf f_{\ell'}(\boldsymbol\xi)\bigr]
 =\mathbb E_{\mu_h}\bigl[\mathbf f_\ell^\top
   \mathbb E[\mathbf a\mathbf a^\top\mid\boldsymbol\xi]\mathbf f_{\ell'}\bigr]
 =c_{\mathbf a}\mathbb E_{\mu_h}\bigl[\mathbf f_\ell^\top
   \mathbf f_{\ell'}\bigr].\qedhere
\end{equation*}
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:nonlinear_diagonal_dichotomy}
Assume the hypotheses of~\Cref{prop:nonlinear_ntk_nondeterminism} with every
\(\pi_i\) a polynomial, and assume \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}\succ0\) and
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\succ0\); by
\Cref{lem:base_family_certificates}, under~\textup{(\(\mathsf C_{\mathrm{iso}}\))}, the single condition
\(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L,\mathrm{out}}^\infty\succ0\) suffices. Then for every
\(i\in[N]\),
\begin{equation*}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ii}\ \text{has a deterministic weak limit}
 \iff\pi_i\ \text{is affine}.
\end{equation*}
In particular, if row \(i\) is genuinely nonlinear then \(\mathbf K_{(0)}\)
converges in distribution to a genuinely random matrix,
\(\operatorname{Var}([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ii})\) converges to a strictly positive limit, and
there is no population kernel to which a matrix Chernoff argument such
as~\Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth} could transfer.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
If \(\pi_i\) is affine the limit is deterministic by item~2
of~\Cref{prop:nonlinear_ntk_nondeterminism}. Conversely, write
\(\mathbf A=(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty)^{1/2}\), which is invertible.
By~\cref{eqn:nonlinear_kernel_weak_limit},
\([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ii}\Rightarrow\|\mathbf A\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Z)\|_2^2\).
Suppose this limit equals a constant \(c^2\) almost surely. Since
\(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}\succ0\), the law of \(\mathbf Z\) has a
positive density on \(\mathbb R^n\), and
\(\mathbf z\mapsto\|\mathbf A\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf z)\|_2^2\) is continuous, so
the open set on which it differs from \(c^2\) would have positive probability
unless it is empty; hence \(\|\mathbf A\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf z)\|_2^2=c^2\) for
\emph{every} \(\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^n\). Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\) be the
components of the polynomial map \(\mathbf A\nabla\pi_i\), so
\(\sum_kp_k^2\equiv c^2\), and let \(d=\max_k\deg p_k\). If \(d\geq1\), write
\(\hat p_k\) for the degree-\(d\) homogeneous part of \(p_k\); the degree-\(2d\)
homogeneous part of \(\sum_kp_k^2\) is \(\sum_k\hat p_k^2\), which must vanish
identically because \(\sum_kp_k^2\) is constant and \(2d>0\). A finite sum of
squares of real polynomials vanishes identically only if every summand does, so
\(\hat p_k\equiv0\) for all \(k\), contradicting \(d\geq1\). Hence
\(\mathbf A\nabla\pi_i\) is constant and, \(\mathbf A\) being invertible,
\(\pi_i\) is affine. The final assertion combines this with item~4
of~\Cref{prop:nonlinear_ntk_nondeterminism}.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:product_row_nondeterminism}
Assume the hypotheses of~\Cref{prop:nonlinear_ntk_nondeterminism}. Let
\(\pi_i(\mathbf q)=\boldsymbol\beta_i^\top\mathbf q+q_aq_b\) for some
\(a,b\in\mathcal L\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and let
\(\pi_j\) be affine with \(\nabla\pi_j\equiv\boldsymbol\beta_j\). Put
\(\boldsymbol\kappa_j=\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\boldsymbol\beta_j\). Then
\begin{equation}
 [\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}\Longrightarrow
 \mathcal N\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_i^\top\boldsymbol\kappa_j,\ \varsigma_{ij}^2\bigr),
 \qquad
 \varsigma_{ij}^2=\bigl\|[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_ah_b
  +[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_bh_a\bigr\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2 .
 \label{eqn:product_row_limit_variance}
\end{equation}
The limit is nondegenerate exactly when
\([\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_ah_b+[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_bh_a\neq0\) in
\(L^2(\mu)\); the linear part \(\boldsymbol\beta_i\), which carries the
\(\partial_tu\) and \(-\nu\partial_{xx}u\) terms of a conservation-law residual,
shifts the mean and cannot remove the fluctuation. If \(a\neq b\) and
\(h_a,h_b\) are linearly independent in \(L^2(\mu)\), then \(\varsigma_{ij}^2>0\)
whenever \(([\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_a,[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_b)\neq(0,0)\).
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Here \(\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf z)=\boldsymbol\beta_i+z_b\mathbf e_a+z_a\mathbf e_b\),
so~\cref{eqn:nonlinear_kernel_weak_limit} gives
\([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ij}\Rightarrow\boldsymbol\beta_i^\top\boldsymbol\kappa_j
+[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_aZ_b+[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_bZ_a\), an affine function of
a Gaussian vector and hence Gaussian. With
\(\mathbf v=[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_b\mathbf e_a+[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_a
\mathbf e_b\), the variance is
\(\mathbf v^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}\mathbf v
=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}([\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_ah_b(z)
+[\boldsymbol\kappa_j]_bh_a(z))^2\)
by~\cref{eqn:base_family_matrices}.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- example-21: body_md -->
\label{ex:convective_row_nondegeneracy}
Take \(d_2=1\), assume clause \(\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}\)
of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, so that \(\sigma\) is real analytic and
nonpolynomial, \(\gamma>0\), and \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)
\neq\varnothing\), and assume~\textup{(\(\mathsf C_{\mathrm{iso}}\))}. Let
\(\ell_0,\ell_1\in\mathcal L\) index the value and the \(\partial_{x_1}\)
observation at one interior collocation point \(\mathbf x_i\), so that the
convective term of a quadratic-flux conservation law is
\(Q_{\ell_0}Q_{\ell_1}\), the product row of~\Cref{cor:product_row_nondeterminism}
with indices \(\ell_0,\ell_1\). Then \(h_{\ell_0}\) and \(h_{\ell_1}\) are
linearly independent in \(L^2(\mu)\). Indeed, write a neuron as
\(z=(\boldsymbol\xi,a)\) with \(\boldsymbol\xi=(\mathbf w,b)\) and scalar output
weight \(a\). A vanishing combination \(c_0h_{\ell_0}+c_1h_{\ell_1}=0\) reads
\(\mathbb E[a^2G(\boldsymbol\xi)^2]=0\) with
\(G(\mathbf w,b)=\widetilde G(\mathbf w,\gamma b)\), where
\(\widetilde G(\mathbf w,v)=c_0\sigma(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i+v)
+c_1w_1\sigma'(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i+v)\);
by~\textup{(\(\mathsf C_{\mathrm{iso}}\))} this forces \(G=0\)
\(\mu_h\)-almost surely, hence by continuity on \(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h\), which contains a
nonempty open set, and the identity theorem for real-analytic functions gives
\(G\equiv0\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\). Since \(\gamma>0\), the map
\(b\mapsto\gamma b\) is onto \(\mathbb R\), so \(\widetilde G\equiv0\) on
\(\mathbb R^{d_0+1}\). But \(\widetilde G\) is a function of the
form~\cref{eqn:jinwu_specialized_polynomial} with a single physical site and
index set contained in \(\{\mathbf0,\mathbf e_1\}\); for a single site the
conclusion of~\Cref{lem:jinwu_sigma_independence} is that the associated
function is not identically zero, which forbids \(\widetilde G\equiv0\) unless
\(c_0=c_1=0\). This settles the \(L^2\) half of the nondegeneracy condition
in~\Cref{cor:product_row_nondeterminism}; the condition on
\(\boldsymbol\kappa_j\) depends on the particular affine row \(j\) and is not
verified here, which is why the statement that holds without that condition is the diagonal one
in~\Cref{cor:nonlinear_diagonal_dichotomy}.
<!-- end example-21 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:nonlinear_mechanism}
When every row is affine, with \(\nabla\pi_i\equiv\boldsymbol\beta_i\), \(\nabla_{\theta_m}P_i=d_1^{-1/2}\boldsymbol\Psi_{\mathcal L}(\theta_m)^\top\boldsymbol\beta_i\)
depends on neuron \(m\) alone, the per-neuron Gram blocks are i.i.d.,
\(\mathbf K_{(0)}\) is an empirical mean, and both the law of large numbers in
\Cref{thm:linearNTK} and the matrix Chernoff bound
of~\Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth} apply verbatim. For a composite
row, \cref{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel} multiplies the same block by the
global factor \(\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Q(\theta))\), which all \(d_1\) neurons
share. The blocks remain exchangeable but are no longer independent, and the
shared factor is precisely the quantity governed by the central limit theorem:
it fluctuates at scale \(\Theta(1)\) and does not self-average at any width.
Conditionally on \(\mathbf Q(\theta_{(0)})\) that factor is frozen and
\(\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}(\theta_{(0)})\) is the only remaining source
of randomness; the conditioning also destroys the independence of its summands,
so a quenched analysis would have to re-establish its concentration rather than
inherit it. Such an analysis is not excluded here, and we do not carry one out.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:nonlinear_no_spectral_floor}
The eigenvalue floor that drives~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} is lost as
well, not only the population kernel. Suppose row \(i\) is quadratic with
\(\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf z)=\boldsymbol\beta_i+2\mathbf C_i\mathbf z\) and
\(\boldsymbol\beta_i\in\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf C_i)\), and let
\(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}\succ0\). The hypothesis on
\(\boldsymbol\beta_i\) holds for a pure product row
\(\pi_i(\mathbf q)=q_aq_b\); it fails for a residual row whose linear part lies
outside \(\operatorname{Range}(\mathbf C_i)\), such as
\(\pi_i(\mathbf q)=s_i(q_1+q_2q_3-\nu q_4)\), for which this remark says
nothing. Under it, \(\{\mathbf z:\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf z)=\mathbf0\}\) is a
nonempty affine set, so for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the open set
\(\{\mathbf z:\|\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf z)\|_2<\varepsilon\}\) is nonempty and is
charged by \(\mathbf Z\). Since \(\lambda_{\min}\) is continuous, the continuous
mapping theorem and~\cref{eqn:nonlinear_kernel_weak_limit} give
\(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\Rightarrow
\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z))\), and the latter
is at most \(\|\mathbf A\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Z)\|_2^2\) with
\(\mathbf A=(\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty)^{1/2}\), the smallest eigenvalue of
a symmetric matrix being at most any diagonal entry. Hence \(0\) lies in the
support of the limiting law of \(\lambda_{\min}\), and the portmanteau theorem
applied to an open set gives, \emph{for each} \(\varepsilon>0\), a constant
\(p_\varepsilon>0\) with
\begin{equation*}
 \liminf_{d_1\to\infty}
 \Pr\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})<\varepsilon\}\geq p_\varepsilon .
\end{equation*}
Here one may take \(p_\varepsilon=\Pr\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z))<\varepsilon\}\), which tends to \(\Pr\{\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^\infty_{\boldsymbol\pi}(\mathbf Z))=0\}\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\); that limit is zero for some designs and equals one for others, for instance whenever \(N>n\) or two rows have everywhere parallel gradients, in which case \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})=0\) at every width; what
matters is that it does not decrease with \(d_1\), so no deterministic
\(\lambda_0>0\) can play the role it plays in~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}.
A \(p\)-th-power boundary row \(\pi_i(\mathbf q)=s_iq_\ell^{\,p}\), \(p\geq2\), is
the extreme case: \([\mathbf K_{(0)}]_{ii}\Rightarrow
s_i^2p^2Z_\ell^{2p-2}[\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty]_{\ell\ell}\), whose law
accumulates at \(0\) whenever
\([\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}]_{\ell\ell}>0\).
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:polynomial_scaling_trichotomy}
Assume~\Cref{assump:main}, let the base family satisfy~\Cref{assump:general}
and~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))}, and fix monomials \(J,J'\) of degrees
\(q,q'\geq1\). Define the homogeneous polynomial of degree \(q+q'-2\)
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf z)
 =\sum_{r=1}^{q}\sum_{t=1}^{q'}
  \Bigl(\prod_{s\neq r}z_{j_s}\Bigr)\Bigl(\prod_{s\neq t}z_{l_s}\Bigr)
  [\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty]_{j_rl_t}.
 \label{eqn:limit_polynomial}
\end{equation}
Then, with \(\mathbf Z\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf0,
\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\),
\begin{equation}
 d_1^{-(q+q')(1/2-\varrho)}K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})
 \Longrightarrow\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z),
 \qquad
 Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})=d_1^{1/2-\varrho}\widetilde Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)}),
 \label{eqn:trichotomy_scaling}
\end{equation}
and \(\Phi_{J,J'}\) does not depend on \(\varrho\). Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item if \(\varrho>1/2\), then \(Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})\to0\) and
 \(K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})\to0\) in probability, the latter at the order
 \(d_1^{(q+q')(1/2-\varrho)}\), which is exact whenever \(\Phi_{J,J'}\) does
 not vanish identically on \(\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\);
\item if \(\varrho=1/2\), then \(Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})\Rightarrow Z_\ell\) and
 \(K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})\Rightarrow\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)\), both of order
 one, and the kernel limit is deterministic if and only if \(\Phi_{J,J'}\) is
 constant on \(\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\). For \(q=q'=1\) both
 products in~\cref{eqn:limit_polynomial} are empty, so
 \(\Phi_{J,J'}\equiv[\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty]_{j_1l_1}\) and the limit is
 always deterministic; for \(q+q'\geq3\) a constant \(\Phi_{J,J'}\) must vanish
 on \(\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\), so the limit is random unless
 it is the constant \(0\);
\item if \(\varrho<1/2\), then \(|Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})|\to\infty\) in
 probability whenever \([\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}]_{\ell\ell}>0\), and
 \(|K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})|\to\infty\) in probability unless \(\Phi_{J,J'}\)
 vanishes identically on \(\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Substituting \(Q_\ell=d_1^{1/2-\varrho}\widetilde Q_\ell\)
in~\cref{eqn:polynomial_kernel_identity} produces \((q-1)+(q'-1)\) factors
\(d_1^{1/2-\varrho}\), so the total prefactor is
\(d_1^{1-2\varrho+(q+q'-2)(1/2-\varrho)}=d_1^{(q+q')(1/2-\varrho)}\), and the
remaining expression is
\(\sum_{r,t}(\prod_{s\neq r}\widetilde Q_{j_s})
(\prod_{s\neq t}\widetilde Q_{l_s})[\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}]_{j_rl_t}\).
By~\Cref{lem:base_family_limits} and the continuous mapping theorem applied to
the polynomial map \((\mathbf z,\mathbf G)\mapsto\sum_{r,t}(\prod_{s\neq
r}z_{j_s})(\prod_{s\neq t}z_{l_s})G_{j_rl_t}\), this
converges weakly to \(\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)\),
giving~\cref{eqn:trichotomy_scaling}. Item~1 follows by Slutsky's theorem.
For item~3, write \(Y_n=d_1^{-(q+q')(1/2-\varrho)}K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})\),
so that \(Y_n\Rightarrow\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)\). A polynomial that does not
vanish identically on \(V=\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\) has a
Lebesgue-null zero set in \(V\), and the law of \(\mathbf Z\) has a density
on \(V\), so \(\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)\neq0\) almost surely. Fix \(T\) and
\(\varepsilon>0\) and set \(\varepsilon_n=Td_1^{-(q+q')(1/2-\varrho)}\to0\).
Once \(\varepsilon_n<\varepsilon\), the portmanteau theorem for the open set
\(\{|\cdot|>\varepsilon\}\) gives
\(\liminf_n\Pr\{|K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})|>T\}
=\liminf_n\Pr\{|Y_n|>\varepsilon_n\}
\geq\Pr\{|\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)|>\varepsilon\}\),
and letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) shows that
\(|K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})|\to\infty\) in probability. The divergence of
\(Q_\ell\) is the same argument with \(Z_\ell\) in place of
\(\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)\).

For item~2 the prefactor is \(1\). Write
\(V=\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\), so the law of \(\mathbf Z\) is
supported on \(V\) and equivalent to Lebesgue measure there. If
\(\Phi_{J,J'}\equiv c\) on \(V\) then \(\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)=c\) almost
surely; conversely, if \(\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)=c\) almost surely then the
continuous function \(\Phi_{J,J'}-c\) vanishes Lebesgue-almost everywhere on
\(V\) and hence identically on \(V\). When \(q+q'\geq3\), \(\Phi_{J,J'}\) is
homogeneous of degree \(D=q+q'-2\geq1\) and \(V\) is a linear subspace, so
\(t\mathbf z\in V\) and \(c=\Phi_{J,J'}(t\mathbf z)=t^Dc\) for all
\(\mathbf z\in V\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\); taking \(t=0\) forces \(c=0\). When
\(q=q'=1\) the polynomial is the stated constant.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:no_deterministic_polynomial_ntk}
Under the hypotheses of~\Cref{thm:polynomial_scaling_trichotomy}, let
\(q+q'\geq3\) and let \(\varrho\geq1/2\) be fixed. If
\(K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})\) converges in probability to a deterministic limit,
that limit is \(0\). At the degree-matched exponent \(\varrho_p=(2p-1)/(2p)\)
with \(q=q'=p\geq2\) one has, at every width,
\begin{equation}
 K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})=d_1^{-(p-1)}\,\Phi^{(d_1)}_{J,J'},
 \qquad
 Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})=d_1^{-(p-1)/(2p)}\widetilde Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)}),
 \label{eqn:degree_matched_rates}
\end{equation}
where \(\Phi^{(d_1)}_{J,J'}\Rightarrow\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)\); so both the
kernel block and the prediction converge to zero, the displayed orders being
attained whenever \(\Phi_{J,J'}\) does not vanish identically on
\(\operatorname{Range}(\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L})\) and
\([\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}]_{\ell\ell}>0\). The remaining exponents,
\(\varrho<1/2\), already make the prediction \(Q_\ell\) itself diverge whenever \([\boldsymbol\Sigma_{\mathcal L}]_{\ell\ell}>0\) (item~3 of~\Cref{thm:polynomial_scaling_trichotomy}).
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
For \(\varrho>1/2\) the prefactor in~\cref{eqn:trichotomy_scaling} tends to
\(0\) while the residual factor is bounded in probability, so the limit is
\(0\). For \(\varrho=1/2\), convergence in probability to \(c\) implies
convergence in distribution to \(\delta_c\), so
\(\Phi_{J,J'}(\mathbf Z)=c\) almost surely, and the dichotomy established in
item~2 of~\Cref{thm:polynomial_scaling_trichotomy} forces \(c=0\). The
displayed rates are \(2p(1/2-\varrho_p)=-(p-1)\) and
\(1/2-\varrho_p=-(p-1)/(2p)\).
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:normalized_kernel_linearization}
For \(\varrho>1/2\) every block tends to zero, the affine ones included,
because~\cref{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel} carries the factor
\(d_1^{1-2\varrho}\); a step size scaled up by \(d_1^{2\varrho-1}\), as in the
learning-rate scaling of~\citet{Jiang2026}, sees the rescaled matrix
\(d_1^{2\varrho-1}\mathbf K(\theta_{(0)})\) instead. Under the hypotheses
of~\Cref{thm:polynomial_scaling_trichotomy},
\(\mathbf Q(\theta_{(0)})=d_1^{1/2-\varrho}\widetilde{\mathbf Q}(\theta_{(0)})
\to\mathbf0\) in probability, because \(\widetilde{\mathbf Q}(\theta_{(0)})\)
converges in distribution, and
\(\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}(\theta_{(0)})\to\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\)
in probability by~\Cref{lem:base_family_limits}. Since every
\(\nabla\pi_i\) is continuous, \cref{eqn:composite_row_exact_kernel} and the
continuous mapping theorem give
\begin{equation*}
 d_1^{2\varrho-1}[\mathbf K(\theta_{(0)})]_{ij}
 \to\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf0)^\top\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\nabla\pi_j(\mathbf0)
 \qquad\text{in probability}.
\end{equation*}
This limit is deterministic, but it is the Gram matrix of the rows linearized
at the zero prediction, \(\mathbf Q\mapsto\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf0)^\top\mathbf Q\):
every monomial block of total degree at least three drops out, in agreement
with~\Cref{cor:no_deterministic_polynomial_ntk}, and a row without a linear
part, such as the product \(Q_1Q_2\), contributes a zero row and column. A
larger exponent therefore restores determinism at initialization only by
removing the nonlinearity from the kernel there. Along training, fitting
nonzero targets moves the predictions away from zero, the factors
\(\nabla\pi_i(\mathbf Q(\theta_{(k)}))\) move with them, and nothing in this
section controls the kernel there. This is the regime
of~\citet{Sirignano2026}, whose limit dynamics start from zero output and are
driven by a deterministic kernel that depends on the evolving solution.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{prop:uncentered_branch}
Drop~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))} and let
\(m_\ell=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}h_\ell(z)\). Then, almost surely along nested
widths as in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK} and in probability under fresh resampling,
\begin{equation}
 d_1^{\,1-(q+q')(1-\varrho)}K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})
 \longrightarrow
 \sum_{r=1}^{q}\sum_{t=1}^{q'}
 \Bigl(\prod_{s\neq r}m_{j_s}\Bigr)\Bigl(\prod_{s\neq t}m_{l_s}\Bigr)
 [\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty]_{j_rl_t},
 \qquad
 d_1^{\varrho-1}Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})\to m_\ell .
 \label{eqn:uncentered_limit}
\end{equation}
At \(\varrho=\varrho_p\) and \(q=q'=p\) the kernel prefactor is exactly \(1\)
and the limit is deterministic and generically nonzero, while for a block of
total degree \(q+q'<2p\) the prefactor is \(d_1^{(q+q')/(2p)-1}\to0\). This
branch is nevertheless inadmissible on two counts: the prediction grows as
\(d_1^{1-\varrho_p}=d_1^{1/(2p)}\); and forcing an order-one prediction by
and forcing an order-one prediction by taking \(\varrho=1\) makes every block, the affine ones included, of order \(d_1^{-1}\). That uniform factor is not the obstruction by itself: a step size scaled up by \(d_1\), as in~\Cref{rem:normalized_kernel_linearization}, removes it, and by~\cref{eqn:uncentered_limit} at \(\varrho=1\) every rescaled block \(d_1K^{J,J'}(\theta_{(0)})\) then has a deterministic limit, which is generically nonzero for every \((q,q')\). Under that step size, however, each neuron's parameters move by an amount of order \(\eta\) per step instead of \(O(\eta d_1^{-1/2})\), so the per-neuron localization behind~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence} is unavailable.
\(d_1^{-1}\). It also contradicts the centering hypothesis used
by~\Cref{lem:initial_residual_bound} and~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Write \(Q_\ell=d_1^{1-\varrho}\bar Q_\ell\) with
\(\bar Q_\ell=d_1^{-1}\sum_mh_\ell(\theta_m)\to m_\ell\), almost surely along
nested widths and in probability under fresh resampling, by item~3
of~\Cref{lem:base_family_limits}. Substituting
in~\cref{eqn:polynomial_kernel_identity} gives the prefactor
\(d_1^{1-2\varrho+(q+q'-2)(1-\varrho)}=d_1^{(q+q')(1-\varrho)-1}\), and the
stated limit follows in the same two modes from the continuous mapping
theorem, since \(\widehat{\mathbf K}_{\mathcal L}\to
\mathbf K_{\mathcal L}^\infty\) in the same mode by item~1
of~\Cref{lem:base_family_limits}. At \(\varrho=\varrho_p\) the
exponent is \((q+q')/(2p)-1\), which is \(0\) for \(q=q'=p\).
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:degree_matching}
\Cref{prop:uncentered_branch} isolates the one regime in which the
degree-matched exponent behaves as intended. Without the \(p\)-th-power
boundary transform, a residual--boundary block of a degree-\(p\) constraint has
total degree \(q+q'=p+1\), hence order \(d_1^{(1-p)/(2p)}\to0\) against an
order-one interior block; raising the boundary row to the \(p\)-th power
restores \(q+q'=2p\) for every block between top-degree monomials and equalizes their orders; a block involving a lower-degree monomial has \(q+q'<2p\) and, by~\Cref{prop:uncentered_branch}, tends to \(0\). That accounting
is correct \emph{only} without centering. Under~\textup{(\(\mathsf C\))} the
ordering reverses, because the block order
\(d_1^{(q+q')(1/2-\varrho)}\) \emph{decreases} in total degree when
\(\varrho>1/2\); the transform still equalizes the orders, but at the common
value \(d_1^{-(p-1)}\), that is, it equalizes them at zero. At \(\varrho=1/2\)
with centering there is no hierarchy at all, since the prefactor is \(1\) for
every \((q,q')\), so the transform is not needed for its stated purpose; what
fails there is determinism, not order. Finally, if one allows a
width-dependent mean \(m_\ell\asymp d_1^{-\delta}\) with
\(\delta\in[0,1/2]\), outside~\Cref{assump:main}, then an order-one prediction
forces \(\varrho=1-\delta\) and the block order collapses to
\(d_1^{2\delta-1}\) independently of \(q\) and \(q'\); a nonvanishing kernel
then forces \(\delta=1/2\) and hence \(\varrho=1/2\). This is not exact
centering: the mean enters at the scale of the fluctuations, so, whenever
\(c_\ell=\lim_{d_1\to\infty}d_1^{1/2}m_\ell\) exists and a triangular-array
central limit theorem applies, \(Q_\ell(\theta_{(0)})\Rightarrow
c_\ell+Z_\ell\), a shifted version of the Gaussian-fluctuation regime
of~\Cref{sec:nonlinear_nondeterminism}, which treats only \(c_\ell=0\). The
obstruction is centering together with degree, not the exponent. We record this
last observation as a scaling heuristic only; it is used nowhere else.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:uncentered_reachability}
\Cref{prop:uncentered_branch} requires \(m_\ell=\mathbb E_{z\sim\mu}h_\ell(z)
\neq0\). In general
\(m_\ell=\mathbb E\bigl[\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]^\top
\mathbf f_\ell(\boldsymbol\xi)\bigr]\), and
\(m_\ell=\mathbb E[\mathbf a]^\top\mathbb E[\mathbf f_\ell]\) when the output
weight is drawn independently of \(\boldsymbol\xi\). Giving the output weight
a nonzero mean is therefore not sufficient. If the activation is odd and the
hidden law \(\mu_h\) is symmetric about the origin, then \(\mathbf f_\ell\) is
odd in \(\boldsymbol\xi\), so \(\mathbb E[\mathbf f_\ell]=\mathbf0\) and
\(m_\ell=0\) for every output-weight law drawn independently of
\(\boldsymbol\xi\); the prediction is then pure fluctuation and, at the
degree-matched exponent, decays as \(d_1^{1/2-\varrho_p}=d_1^{-(p-1)/(2p)}\),
the rate in~\cref{eqn:degree_matched_rates}, rather than growing. With output
weights drawn independently of \(\boldsymbol\xi\), reaching the branch
therefore requires an asymmetric hidden law or a nonodd activation;
\Cref{assump:main} does not impose that independence, and a conditional mean
\(\mathbb E[\mathbf a\mid\boldsymbol\xi]\) that is not even in
\(\boldsymbol\xi\) can reach the branch as well.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:nonlinear_numerics}
The predictions
of~\Cref{cor:nonlinear_diagonal_dichotomy,cor:no_deterministic_polynomial_ntk, 
prop:uncentered_branch,rem:uncentered_reachability} were checked directly for
\(\sigma=\tanh\), \(\gamma=1\), \(d_0=d_2=1\), collocation points
\(x_1=0.3\) and \(x_2=-0.7\), per-neuron parameters
\(\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]^3\) in the centered runs, widths
\(d_1\in\{64,256,1{,}024,4{,}096,16{,}384\}\), and \(100\)
independent initializations per width. The base observations are the values
\(Q_1=u(x_1)\) and \(Q_2=u(x_2)\) with loss scale \(1\); the linear row is
\(Q_1\), the product row is \(Q_1Q_2\), and each Gram entry below is the
diagonal entry of the tangent Gram matrix at initialization for that row.
Over that \(256\)-fold range of widths, \(d_1\operatorname{Var}\) of the
linear-row entry stays between \(4.55\times10^{-2}\) and
\(6.26\times10^{-2}\), while the variance of the product-row entry stays
between \(1.83\times10^{-2}\) and \(3.95\times10^{-2}\), with no trend
comparable to the \(256\)-fold decay of a concentrating quantity; at
\(d_1=16{,}384\) the product-row variance is about \(5.0\times10^{3}\) times
the variance of the linear-row entry, consistent with the dichotomy
of~\Cref{cor:nonlinear_diagonal_dichotomy}, under which this ratio diverges as
\(d_1\to\infty\). At \(p=2\) and \(\varrho_2=3/4\) with centered output
weights, the seed mean of \(d_1\) times the degree-\((2,2)\) block
\(K^{J,J}\), \(J=(1,2)\), stays between \(0.124\) and \(0.153\). Since
\cref{eqn:degree_matched_rates} is exact at every width, this quantity is the
seed mean of \(\Phi^{(d_1)}_{J,J}\), which on the same initializations equals
the \(\varrho=1/2\) product-row entry; the factor \(d_1^{-1}\) is therefore
not measured independently, and what the run checks is that
\(\Phi^{(d_1)}_{J,J}\) stays of order one. The uncentered runs draw the output
weights from \(\operatorname{Unif}[0,2]\) (mean \(1\)). With the hidden bias law also
shifted to \(\operatorname{Unif}[0,2]\), which makes the hidden law asymmetric
as~\Cref{rem:uncentered_reachability} requires for \(m_\ell\neq0\), the seed
mean of \(|u(x_1;\theta_{(0)})|\) at \(\varrho_2=3/4\) divided by
\(d_1^{1/4}=d_1^{1-\varrho_2}\) stays between \(0.651\) and \(0.658\),
consistent with the growth rate of~\Cref{prop:uncentered_branch}; with the symmetric hidden bias law
\(\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]\) it instead decays, from \(1.7\times10^{-1}\) at \(d_1=64\) to
\(4.7\times10^{-2}\) at \(d_1=16{,}384\), as that remark predicts. The run is
the nonlinear kernel-variance experiment of the accompanying code, under its
tracked configuration.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:nonlinear_scope}
\Cref{prop:nonlinear_ntk_nondeterminism,cor:nonlinear_diagonal_dichotomy, 
thm:polynomial_scaling_trichotomy,cor:no_deterministic_polynomial_ntk} concern
the tangent Gram matrix at initialization. They say nothing about
\(\mathbf K(\theta_{(k)})\) for \(k\geq1\), where \(\mathbf Q(\theta)\) has
drifted and is no longer a sum of i.i.d.\ terms, and they do not assert that
gradient descent fails on nonlinear PINNs; in particular they do not contradict
the global convergence analysis for nonlinear PDEs of~\citet{Sirignano2026},
which works at an exponent \(\varrho>1/2\) with zero initial output, where
by their own limit theorem, not by~\Cref{rem:normalized_kernel_linearization} (whose hypotheses their full-support initialization and population residual do not meet), the rescaled kernel at
initialization is deterministic and along training depends on the evolving
solution, nor the stability-based error analyses
of~\citet{Mishra2023,DeRyck2024}, which do not route through a tangent
kernel. What they rule out is the specific proof architecture used
here, which follows the two-layer analysis of~\citet{Du2019} and the
limiting-kernel picture of~\citet{Jacot2018,Lee2019} as specialized to PINNs
by~\citet{Wang2022}: a deterministic population kernel, a width threshold
obtained by transferring a population eigenvalue through a matrix concentration
inequality, and a spectral floor propagated along the trajectory. At
\(\varrho=1/2\), under a single genuinely nonlinear polynomial row and the hypotheses of~\Cref{cor:nonlinear_diagonal_dichotomy}, none of the
three exists in the required form; at \(\varrho>1/2\) the first exists only
for the rows linearized at zero. What remains open, and is not excluded by anything above, is
whether, for a design with no row to which~\Cref{rem:nonlinear_no_spectral_floor} applies (that remark puts \(0\) in the support of the limiting law of \(\lambda_{\min}\) as soon as one row is a pure product or a \(p\)-th power), a random but uniformly positive definite limiting kernel would still
yield convergence, and whether layerwise or coordinatewise scalings outside the
one-parameter family of~\Cref{def:exponent_normalization} behave differently.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:depth_h_network}
Fix a depth $H\geq1$ and hidden widths $d^{[1]},\ldots,d^{[H]}$, and set
$d^{[0]}=d_0$ and $d^{[H+1]}=d_2$, the input and output dimensions
of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}; the bracketed superscript is a layer
index, so no $d^{[l]}$ with $l\in[H]$ is to be read as one of the two-layer
symbols $d_0,d_1,d_2$, and $d^{[1]}=d_1$ when $H=1$. For $l\in[H]$ let
$\mathbf W^{[l]}\in\mathbb R^{d^{[l]}\times d^{[l-1]}}$ and
$\mathbf b^{[l]}\in\mathbb R^{d^{[l]}}$, and let
$\mathbf W^{[H+1]}\in\mathbb R^{d^{[H+1]}\times d^{[H]}}$. With the activation
$\sigma$ and the fixed bias scale $\gamma\geq0$
of~\Cref{def:ntk_parameterization}, define
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbf t^{[1]}(\mathbf x)
 &=\mathbf W^{[1]}\mathbf x+\gamma\mathbf b^{[1]},\\
 \mathbf t^{[l]}(\mathbf x)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt{d^{[l-1]}}}\mathbf W^{[l]}\mathbf y^{[l-1]}(\mathbf x)
   +\gamma\mathbf b^{[l]},
 \qquad l=2,\ldots,H,\\
 \mathbf y^{[l]}(\mathbf x)
 &=\sigma\bigl(\mathbf t^{[l]}(\mathbf x)\bigr),
 \qquad l\in[H],\\
 \mathbf u(\mathbf x;\theta)
 &=\frac1{\sqrt{d^{[H]}}}\mathbf W^{[H+1]}\mathbf y^{[H]}(\mathbf x),
\end{aligned}
\label{eqn:depth_network}
\end{equation}
with $\sigma$ applied entrywise,
$\theta^{[l]}=(\mathbf W^{[l]},\mathbf b^{[l]})$ for $l\in[H]$,
$\theta^{[H+1]}=\mathbf W^{[H+1]}$, and
$\theta=(\theta^{[1]},\ldots,\theta^{[H+1]})\in\mathbb R^{D_\theta}$ with
$D_\theta=\sum_{l\in[H]}d^{[l]}(d^{[l-1]}+1)+d^{[H+1]}d^{[H]}$. Every listed
parameter is trained. The rows of~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, the loss, the
residual, and the definitions
$[\mathbf J(\theta)]_{i,:}=\nabla_\theta P_i(\theta)^\top$ and
$\mathbf K(\theta)=\mathbf J(\theta)\mathbf J(\theta)^\top$
of~\Cref{def:pinn_loss} apply to~\cref{eqn:depth_network} unchanged, with
$\mathbf J(\theta)\in\mathbb R^{N\times D_\theta}$ in place of the two-layer shape
$\mathbb R^{N\times d_1d_\theta}$ recorded there, which is the only clause of
that definition that refers to the architecture. Write
$d_{\min}=\min_{l\in[H]}d^{[l]}$, let $\mathbf J^{[l]}(\theta)$ denote the
column block of $\mathbf J(\theta)$ indexed by the coordinates of
$\theta^{[l]}$, and set
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf K^{[l]}(\theta)
 =\mathbf J^{[l]}(\theta)\mathbf J^{[l]}(\theta)^\top
 \in\mathbb R^{N\times N},
 \qquad l\in[H+1].
 \label{eqn:layer_jacobian_blocks}
\end{equation}
At initialization the coordinates of $\theta_{(0)}$ are drawn independently
across layers, those within layer $l$ being i.i.d.\ from a width-independent,
compactly supported scalar law $\mu^{[l]}$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:layerwise_decomposition}
Let $\mathbf J(\theta)\in\mathbb R^{N\times D_\theta}$ be any prediction Jacobian and
partition its columns into blocks
$\mathbf J^{[1]},\ldots,\mathbf J^{[H+1]}$, for instance
the layer blocks of~\Cref{def:depth_h_network}, and set $\mathbf K^{[l]}=\mathbf J^{[l]}\mathbf J^{[l]\top}$ as in~\cref{eqn:layer_jacobian_blocks}. Then, for every $\theta$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf K(\theta)=\sum_{l=1}^{H+1}\mathbf K^{[l]}(\theta),
 \qquad
 \mathbf K^{[l]}(\theta)\succeq0,
 \label{eqn:layerwise_sum}
\end{equation}
and consequently
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K(\theta)=\bigcap_{l=1}^{H+1}\ker\mathbf K^{[l]}(\theta),
 \qquad
 \lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K(\theta))
 \geq\sum_{l=1}^{H+1}\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^{[l]}(\theta))
 \geq\max_{l\in[H+1]}\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^{[l]}(\theta)).
 \label{eqn:layerwise_kernel_and_gap}
\end{equation}
In particular $\mathbf K(\theta)\succ0$ as soon as
$\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}(\theta)\succ0$ for a single $l_\star$: certifying one
layer certifies the whole kernel. The same statements hold for the limiting
objects whenever the blockwise limits exist.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
Splitting the product $\mathbf J\mathbf J^\top$ along the column partition
gives~\cref{eqn:layerwise_sum}, and each
$\mathbf K^{[l]}=\mathbf J^{[l]}\mathbf J^{[l]\top}$ is a Gram matrix, hence
positive semidefinite. For $\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N$,
\[
 \mathbf c^\top\mathbf K(\theta)\mathbf c
 =\sum_{l=1}^{H+1}\|\mathbf J^{[l]}(\theta)^\top\mathbf c\|_2^2 ,
\]
a sum of nonnegative terms, so it vanishes if and only if every term vanishes;
and for a positive semidefinite $\mathbf M$ one has $\mathbf M\mathbf c=0$ if
and only if
$\mathbf c^\top\mathbf M\mathbf c=\|\mathbf M^{1/2}\mathbf c\|_2^2=0$, which
turns that equivalence into the kernel identity
in~\cref{eqn:layerwise_kernel_and_gap}. The eigenvalue bound is
superadditivity of $\lambda_{\min}$ over a sum of symmetric matrices, a case
of Weyl's inequality; the second inequality holds because every omitted
summand is nonnegative, each $\mathbf K^{[l]}$ being positive semidefinite. For the limiting objects, suppose each $\mathbf K^{[l]}$ converges, almost surely or in probability, to $\mathbf K^{[l],\infty}$. Then $\mathbf K$ converges in the same sense to $\sum_{l=1}^{H+1}\mathbf K^{[l],\infty}$, each $\mathbf K^{[l],\infty}$ is positive semidefinite because the positive semidefinite cone is closed, and the two arguments above used only $\mathbf c^\top\mathbf K\mathbf c=\sum_l\mathbf c^\top\mathbf K^{[l]}\mathbf c$ with positive semidefinite summands, so they apply to the limits unchanged.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:depth_row_regularity}
Consider~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} with a fixed finite family of loss-scaled
rows, and fix $\tau>0$ and $0<\delta<1$. Define the trust region as the
closed Euclidean ball
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)})
 =\bigl\{\theta:\ \|\theta-\theta_{(0)}\|_2\leq\tau\bigr\},
 \label{eqn:depth_trust_region}
\end{equation}
whose radius does not grow with the widths. A region that let every layer
block move by $\tau\sqrt{d_{\min}}$ in Frobenius norm would be too large: a
single unit could then absorb a whole layer's displacement budget, and already
at $H=1$ clause~(ii) below would force $L_1$ to grow like $\sqrt{d_1}$
whenever $\sigma''\not\equiv0$, and clause~(i) would force $\Lambda_1$ to grow
like $d_1$ for rows of order $r_{\max}\geq1$. We say that the rows satisfy
$(\mathsf G^H_\tau)$ if there are an initialization event $\mathcal E_{(0)}$
with $\Pr(\mathcal E_{(0)})\geq1-\delta/2$, constants
$\Lambda_H\geq\lambda_0>0$, $L_H<\infty$ and $\overline r^H_\delta<\infty$
independent of $d^{[1]},\ldots,d^{[H]}$, a layer index $l_\star\in[H+1]$, a
deterministic matrix $\mathbf K^{[l_\star],\infty}$, posited to be the limit in probability of $\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}_{(0)}$ as all hidden widths tend to infinity, and a width threshold
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}
=\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}(\lambda_0,N,H,r_{\max},\delta)$, which may also depend on the fixed rows, $\sigma$, $\gamma$ and the laws $\mu^{[l]}$ but not on the widths, such that
clauses (i), (ii), and (iv) hold on $\mathcal E_{(0)}$, clause (iii) is a
deterministic statement about the posited limit, and clause (v) is a
separate event whose intersection with $\mathcal E_{(0)}$ has probability at
least $1-\delta$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textup{(Uniform Jacobian envelope.)}
 $\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)})}
 \|\mathbf J(\theta)\|_2^2\leq\Lambda_H$; in particular
 $\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K(\theta))\leq\Lambda_H$ throughout the trust region.
 This generalizes the aggregate gradient bound $B_*^2$
 of~\cref{eqn:abstract_aggregate_constants}, equivalently the choice
 $\Lambda=B_*^2$ of~\Cref{thm:generalconvergence}, which at $H=1$ follows from
 the per-unit bounds $B_i$ by blockwise concatenation \emph{on the per-unit
 tube}.
\item \textup{(Jacobian Lipschitz modulus with an explicit width factor.)}
 For all $\theta,\theta'\in\mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)})$,
 \begin{equation}
  \|\mathbf J(\theta)-\mathbf J(\theta')\|_2
  \leq\frac{L_H}{\sqrt{d_{\min}}}\|\theta-\theta'\|_2 .
  \label{eqn:depth_jacobian_lipschitz}
 \end{equation}
 This generalizes~\cref{eqn:jacobian_lipschitz_global}, whose modulus
 $L_*d_1^{-1/2}$ is \emph{derived} from the per-unit constants $L_i$ by
 blockwise separability of the Jacobian columns. At depth the columns
 belonging to different units are not separable in this way: the $H=1$ grouping $\theta_m=(\boldsymbol\xi_m,\mathbf a_m)$ has no depth analogue, since for $H\geq2$ the columns of a unit of layer $l$ depend on parameters of other units, through $\mathbf y^{[l-1]}$ when $l\geq2$ and through $\partial\mathbf u/\partial\mathbf t^{[l]}$, which involves every unit of layer $l$ and the layers above, when $l<H$; so the factor
 $d_{\min}^{-1/2}$ is part of the hypothesis.
\item \textup{(Certified limiting gap at one layer.)}
 $\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^{[l_\star],\infty})\geq\lambda_0>0$. This is the
 depth analogue of~\Cref{def:positive_definiteness_certificate} together with
 the certified bound $0<\lambda_0\leq\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)}^\infty)$
 of~\Cref{thm:linearPDEsconvergence}; by~\Cref{lem:layerwise_decomposition} it
 certifies the full limiting kernel provided the remaining blockwise limits
 exist, only $\mathbf K^{[l_\star],\infty}$ being posited here. The clause
 \emph{posits} the limiting matrix: at depth it is not produced by a strong
 law over units, as it is in~\Cref{thm:linearNTK}.
 \Cref{prop:depth_h_substitution} does not consume this clause; it only ties
 $\lambda_0$ to a limiting object.
\item \textup{(Initialization concentration at the certified layer.)} If
 $d_{\min}\geq\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}$ then, on $\mathcal E_{(0)}$,
 \begin{equation}
  \lambda_{\min}\bigl(\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}_{(0)}\bigr)
  \geq\frac{3\lambda_0}{4}.
  \label{eqn:depth_init_concentration}
 \end{equation}
 The norm bound
 $\bigl\|\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}_{(0)}-\mathbf K^{[l_\star],\infty}\bigr\|_2
 \leq\lambda_0/4$ is one sufficient condition, and is the form that a
 layerwise propagation argument of the kind used by~\citet{Du2019b} would
 deliver; we state the eigenvalue bound because that is what the proof
 consumes, and because the two-layer tool being replaced,
 \Cref{prop:positive_definitenessfinitewidth}, produces
 the full-kernel counterpart $\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(0)})\geq3\lambda_0/4$ of~\cref{eqn:depth_init_concentration} directly by a matrix Chernoff bound on
 the independent positive-semidefinite per-unit matrices $\mathbf G_m$ and
 never passes through the norm bound. At depth that independence fails, as the
 discussion after~\cref{eqn:depth_schur_product} records, so the required
 input is a layerwise propagation of the initialization error, conditional at
 each layer, rather than one concentration inequality; and by the same
 discussion only $l_\star\in\{H,H+1\}$ presents a conditionally independent
 average to propagate into.
\item \textup{(Initial residual envelope.)}
 $\Pr\{\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\leq\overline r^H_\delta\}\geq1-\delta/2$, with
 $\overline r^H_\delta$ independent of the widths. This replaces
 \Cref{lem:initial_residual_bound}, whose McDiarmid step uses the decomposition
 of $\mathbf v_P(\theta_{(0)})$ into $d_1$ independent blocks, each changing
 the norm by at most $2A_{0,*}/\sqrt{d_1}$. At depth such a decomposition
 holds only conditionally on the layers below the output, and for rows of
 order $r_{\max}\geq1$ it has no width-independent bounded-difference
 constant. For centered output weights the clause follows from clause~(i)
 instead (\Cref{sec:depth_conjectural}).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop:depth_h_substitution}
Consider~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} and gradient descent as
in~\Cref{def:gradient_descent}, and suppose the rows satisfy
$(\mathsf G^H_\tau)$ of~\Cref{def:depth_row_regularity}, with constants
$\Lambda_H\geq\lambda_0>0$, $L_H$, $\overline r^H_\delta$, layer $l_\star$ and
threshold $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}$, and that
$\theta\mapsto\mathbf v_P(\theta)$ is continuously differentiable on a convex
neighborhood of $\mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)})$ (for rows of type (i) this
follows from clause $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}).
If
\begin{equation}
 d_{\min}\geq\max\left\{
 \mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}},\
 (320+128\sqrt6)
   \frac{L_H^2\Lambda_H(\overline r^H_\delta)^2}{\lambda_0^3}
 \right\},
 \quad
 4\sqrt{\Lambda_H}\,\overline r^H_\delta\leq\tau\lambda_0,
 \quad 0<\eta\Lambda_H\leq\frac12,
 \label{eqn:depth_width_conditions}
\end{equation}
then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, simultaneously for every
$k\in\mathbb N_0$,
\begin{equation}
 \theta_{(k)}\in\mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)}),
 \qquad
 \mathbf K_{(k)}\succeq\frac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N,
 \qquad
 \mathcal L(\theta_{(k)})
 \leq(1-\eta\lambda_0)^k\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)}).
 \label{eqn:depth_conclusion}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Intersecting the two events in~\Cref{def:depth_row_regularity}(iv) and (v)
leaves probability at least $1-\delta$; work on that intersection and set
$c_\eta=1-\eta\lambda_0$ and $x_\eta=\eta\lambda_0$. Exactly as
in~\cref{eqn:inductionhypo}, we prove by strong induction that
$\theta_{(j)}\in\mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)})$ and
$\mathcal L(\theta_{(j)})\leq c_\eta^j\mathcal L(\theta_{(0)})$ for
$0\leq j\leq n$; the case $n=0$ is immediate. Each step below names the
two-layer ingredient and the object that replaces it.

\emph{\textup{(S1)} Taylor decomposition.} \Cref{prop:NTKtaylor} is
architecture-free: the fundamental theorem of calculus along the update segment
and the chain rule give
$\mathbf r_{(k+1)}=(\mathbf I_N-2\eta\mathbf K_{(k)})\mathbf r_{(k)}
-\mathbf R_{(k)}$ with the gradient-integral
remainder~\cref{eqn:gradient_integral_remainder}. Its only structural input is
that the segment $[\theta_{(k)},\theta_{(k+1)}]$ lie in a convex set on which
$\theta\mapsto\mathbf v_P(\theta)$ is continuously differentiable. This is
the differentiability hypothesis of the proposition; for rows of type (i) it
holds at every depth under clause $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$
of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}, since finitely many compositions of
$C^{r_{\max}+1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ maps are again $C^{r_{\max}+1,1}$ on compact
sets, so $\mathbf J$ exists and is continuous; clause (ii) then makes it
Lipschitz on the trust region. The per-unit product
tube~\cref{eqn:abstract_product_tube} is replaced
by~\cref{eqn:depth_trust_region}, a Euclidean ball and hence convex.
Nothing else changes.

\emph{\textup{(S2)} Parameter displacement.} The global one-step estimate
of~\Cref{lem:parameterdifferencestep6} uses only
$\|\Delta\theta_{(n)}\|_2=2\eta\|\mathbf J_{(n)}^\top\mathbf r_{(n)}\|_2
\leq2\eta\sqrt{\Lambda_H}\|\mathbf r_{(n)}\|_2$, that is, clause (i) alone;
summing the geometric series as in~\Cref{lem:stronginduction1} gives
$\|\theta_{(k+1)}-\theta_{(0)}\|_2
\leq4\sqrt{\Lambda_H}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2/\lambda_0$. The \emph{per-neuron}
one-step estimate~\cref{eqn:one_step_block_motion}, which uses
$\|\boldsymbol\Psi(\theta_{m,(n)})\|_2\leq B_*$ and has no depth analogue, is
not needed: by clause (v) and the radius condition
in~\cref{eqn:depth_width_conditions},
$4\sqrt{\Lambda_H}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2/\lambda_0\leq\tau$, so
$\theta_{(k+1)}\in\mathcal T^H_\tau(\theta_{(0)})$, and convexity places the
whole update segment there. This is the step at which the shape of the
localization changes: a per-unit displacement bound is traded for the
width-independent Euclidean bound
$4\sqrt{\Lambda_H}\,\overline r^H_\delta/\lambda_0$ on the whole parameter
vector, and the per-unit conclusion is lost.

\emph{\textup{(S3)} Remainder bound.} \Cref{lem:residualtermstep} is reproved
verbatim with~\cref{eqn:depth_jacobian_lipschitz} in place
of~\cref{eqn:jacobian_lipschitz_global}:
\[
 \|\mathbf R_{(k)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{L_H}{2\sqrt{d_{\min}}}\|\Delta\theta_{(k)}\|_2^2
 \leq\frac{2L_H}{\sqrt{d_{\min}}}\eta^2\Lambda_H\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2^2 .
\]
This is the substitution that is not a free lunch: at $H=1$ the factor
$d_1^{-1/2}$ is derived from blockwise separability, whereas here it is
clause (ii).

\emph{\textup{(S4)} Spectral lower bound along training.} Here
\Cref{lem:layerwise_decomposition} earns its place. Write
$\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf A)$ for the $N$th largest singular value of
$\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{N\times D'}$, so that
$\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf A\mathbf A^\top)=\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf A)^2$; clause
(iv) forces $D'\geq N$ for the block $l_\star$, since otherwise
$\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J^{[l_\star]})=0$. By clause (iv),
$\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J^{[l_\star]}_{(0)})
=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}_{(0)})^{1/2}
\geq\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_0}$. Since
$\mathbf J^{[l_\star]}(\theta)-\mathbf J^{[l_\star]}(\theta')$ is a column
block of $\mathbf J(\theta)-\mathbf J(\theta')$, and since for any matrix
$\mathbf M$ with column blocks $\mathbf M^{[l]}$ and any
$\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N$ one has
$\|\mathbf M^{[l]\top}\mathbf c\|_2\leq\|\mathbf M^\top\mathbf c\|_2$, its
spectral norm is no larger, so~\cref{eqn:depth_jacobian_lipschitz} and (S2)
give
\[
 \bigl\|\mathbf J^{[l_\star]}_{(k)}-\mathbf J^{[l_\star]}_{(0)}\bigr\|_2
 \leq\frac{L_H}{\sqrt{d_{\min}}}\cdot
 \frac{4\sqrt{\Lambda_H}}{\lambda_0}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{\sqrt3-\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_0},
\]
the last inequality being the second width condition
in~\cref{eqn:depth_width_conditions} together with clause (v), because
$64/(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)^2=320+128\sqrt6$. Singular-value perturbation yields
$\sigma_{\min}(\mathbf J^{[l_\star]}_{(k)})
\geq\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_0}$, hence
$\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}_{(k)})\geq\lambda_0/2$, and
\cref{eqn:layerwise_kernel_and_gap} promotes this to
$\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\geq\lambda_0/2$. The upper bound
$\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf K_{(k)})\leq\Lambda_H$ comes from clause (i), a
statement about all layers; the layerwise lemma does not supply it. This step
is the exact analogue of~\Cref{prop:NTKposdef_eachiter}, with a one-layer
certificate in place of the full-kernel one.

\emph{\textup{(S5)} Spectral one-step descent.} With
$\tfrac{\lambda_0}{2}\mathbf I_N\preceq\mathbf K_{(k)}
\preceq\Lambda_H\mathbf I_N$ and $\eta\Lambda_H\leq\tfrac12$, every eigenvalue
of $\mathbf I_N-2\eta\mathbf K_{(k)}$ is nonnegative and its norm is at most
$1-x_\eta$. For the remainder, the induction hypothesis gives
$\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2\leq c_\eta^{k/2}\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2
\leq\|\mathbf r_{(0)}\|_2\leq\overline r^H_\delta$, so (S3) together with
$\eta\Lambda_H\leq\tfrac12$ gives
\[
 \|\mathbf R_{(k)}\|_2
 \leq\frac{\eta L_H}{\sqrt{d_{\min}}}\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2^2
 \leq\frac{\eta L_H\overline r^H_\delta}{\sqrt{d_{\min}}}
     \|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2 .
\]
Because $320+128\sqrt6>3+2\sqrt2$ and $\Lambda_H\geq\lambda_0$, the second
width condition implies
$d_{\min}\geq(3+2\sqrt2)L_H^2(\overline r^H_\delta)^2/\lambda_0^2$, and
$\sqrt{3+2\sqrt2}=1+\sqrt2=(\sqrt2-1)^{-1}$, so
$L_H\overline r^H_\delta/\sqrt{d_{\min}}\leq(\sqrt2-1)\lambda_0$ and therefore
$\|\mathbf R_{(k)}\|_2\leq(\sqrt2-1)x_\eta\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2$. The
concluding inequality in the proof of~\Cref{lem:spectralonestep}, whose only
inputs are the recursion of (S1), the spectral bracket, this remainder bound and $x_\eta\leq\eta\Lambda_H\leq\tfrac12$ (by $\Lambda_H\geq\lambda_0$), then gives
$\|\mathbf r_{(k+1)}\|_2\leq\sqrt{c_\eta}\,\|\mathbf r_{(k)}\|_2$.

\emph{\textup{(S6)} Closing the induction.} Squaring (S5) proves the loss
assertion at $k+1$ and (S2) proves the localization assertion, which closes the
strong induction and gives~\cref{eqn:depth_conclusion}. Every arithmetic
constant is the two-layer one, with $(B_*^2,L_*,d_1,\overline r_\delta)$
replaced throughout by $(\Lambda_H,L_H,d_{\min},\overline r^H_\delta)$, the
matrix-Chernoff threshold by $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}$, and the per-unit
localization condition by the radius condition.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:depth_jacobian_constants}
Consider~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} with the pointwise rows
of~\Cref{def:linear_pde} of largest order $r_{\max}$, under clause
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} and with compactly
supported $\mu^{[1]},\ldots,\mu^{[H+1]}$, with $\int z\,d\mu^{[l]}(z)=0$ for
$l=2,\ldots,H+1$. For every $\tau>0$ and
$0<\delta<1$ there are an event $\mathcal E_{(0)}$ with
$\Pr(\mathcal E_{(0)})\geq1-\delta/2$ and a constant $C_0<\infty$ depending
only on $\sigma$, $\gamma$, $r_{\max}$, $\tau$, a common bound
$M\geq\sup\{|z|:z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu^{[l]},\ l\in[H+1]\}$,
$\overline\Omega$ and the row data, but not on $H$ or on the widths, such that
clauses (i) and (ii) of~\Cref{def:depth_row_regularity} hold, whenever
$d_{\min}\geq C_0\log(2(H+1)/\delta)$, on
$\mathcal E_{(0)}$ with
\begin{equation}
 \max\bigl\{\Lambda_H,\;L_H^2\bigr\}\leq C_0^{(1+r_{\max})H},
 \label{eqn:depth_constant_rate}
\end{equation}
and, given a $\lambda_0$ as in clause (iii), the threshold
$\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}$ of clause (iv) obeys the same
exponential rate in $(1+r_{\max})H$, times a factor polynomial in $N$,
$\lambda_0^{-1}$ and $\log(1/\delta)$.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:depth_faa_di_bruno}
The differential order is what
separates~\Cref{conj:depth_jacobian_constants} from the corresponding
statement at order zero. A strong-form row has Jacobian row
$s_i\sum_{q=1}^{d_2}\sum_{\alpha\in I_{iq}}a_{iq\alpha}(\mathbf x_i)\,
\nabla_\theta\partial^\alpha_{\mathbf x}u_q(\mathbf x_i;\theta)^\top$, a fixed
linear combination, with coefficients from the row data, of terms with
$|\alpha|\leq r_{\max}$; it therefore suffices to consider one term
$\nabla_\theta\partial^\alpha_{\mathbf x}u_q(\mathbf x_i;\theta)$, and
in~\cref{eqn:depth_network} the spatial derivative obeys
\begin{equation}
 \partial_{x_j}\mathbf y^{[l]}
 =\operatorname{diag}\bigl(\sigma'(\mathbf t^{[l]})\bigr)
 \frac1{\sqrt{d^{[l-1]}}}\mathbf W^{[l]}\,\partial_{x_j}\mathbf y^{[l-1]},
 \qquad l=2,\ldots,H,
 \label{eqn:depth_x_derivative_chain}
\end{equation}
with $\partial_{x_j}\mathbf y^{[1]}
=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(\mathbf t^{[1]}))\mathbf W^{[1]}\mathbf e_j$. Each
of the $|\alpha|$ spatial derivatives therefore inserts one further scaled
weight factor into every layer of the chain, and Fa\`a di Bruno expands
$\partial^\alpha$ into a sum over the ways of distributing those derivatives
among the $H$ compositions, with $\sigma^{(p)}$, $p\leq r_{\max}$, at each
node; the parameter gradient then appends the usual backward chain. Bounding
the result term by term multiplies $H$ layer factors, each of which now carries
up to $r_{\max}$ weight insertions, which is the route to the rate
in~\cref{eqn:depth_constant_rate}. Three things are unproved. The bound itself:
a layerwise induction of the kind used by~\citet{Du2019b} at order zero is the
natural route, but the jet enlargement described
below~\cref{eqn:depth_schur_product} has no counterpart there.
Width-independence: unlike the two-layer case it cannot be read off from
compactness of a fixed tube, because the ball~\cref{eqn:depth_trust_region}
lies in a space whose dimension grows with the widths and, for $H\geq2$, its
units are coupled. And sharpness: we do not know that
an exponential rate in $(1+r_{\max})H$ is necessary, nor even that an
exponential rate in $H$ is necessary at $r_{\max}=0$ for laws normalized to
the activation, as the factor $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{z\sim N(0,1)}\sigma(z)^2)^{-1}$
of~\citet{Du2019b} normalizes them; without such a normalization,
which~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} does not impose, the envelope can grow
exponentially in $H$ already at $\theta_{(0)}$. On that last point the
comparison with~\citet{Du2019b} must be drawn carefully. Their $2^{O(H)}$ arises in both phases of the fully connected analysis. At
initialization it is the constant in the propagation of the initialization
error through the layers, for the Gram matrix
$\varepsilon_H\lesssim2^{O(H)}\varepsilon_1$, and this is the analogue of the
threshold $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{init}}$ in clause (iv). During training it is
the layerwise amplification of the weight displacement into the change of the
layer outputs and of the Gram matrix, and of the weight norms into the size of
the gradient. This produces the $n^4\lambda_{\min}^{-4}$ term of their width
and the factor $2^{-O(H)}$ in their step size, and it is the analogue of the
modulus $L_H$ and the envelope $\Lambda_H$, the quantities
that~\cref{eqn:depth_x_derivative_chain} governs. Because these are upper
bounds, they are not evidence that any of the three must grow exponentially;
Du et al.\ add that fully connected networks need not depend exponentially on
$H$, and the factor is replaced by $\mathrm{poly}(H)$ under residual
scaling. The qualitative
smoothness requirement is, by contrast, unchanged with depth: finitely many
compositions of $C^{r_{\max}+1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ maps are again
$C^{r_{\max}+1,1}$ on compact sets, so clause $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$
of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes} remains the right regularity to impose. What
degrades with depth is quantitative, not qualitative.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- conjecture-2: body_md -->
\label{conj:depth_positivity_criterion}
Consider~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} with the pointwise rows
of~\Cref{def:linear_pde}, under the depth-$H$ analogue of clause
$\mathsf P_{\mathrm{pd}}$ of~\Cref{assump:pde_classes}: $\sigma$ real analytic
and nonpolynomial, $\gamma>0$, $\int z\,d\mu^{[l]}(z)=0$ for $l=2,\ldots,H$,
and hidden-parameter laws $\mu^{[l]}$ whose
supports have nonempty interior. For every $H\geq1$ there is a layer
$l_\star\in\{H,H+1\}$ for which $\mathbf K^{[l_\star]}_{(0)}$ converges in
probability, as $d_{\min}\to\infty$ uniformly over the width profile
$(d^{[1]},\ldots,d^{[H]})$, to a deterministic matrix
$\mathbf K^{[l_\star],\infty}$, and
\begin{equation}
 \ker\mathbf K^{[l_\star],\infty}
 =\Bigl\{\mathbf c\in\mathbb R^N:
 \sum_{i\in I_{\mathbf x}}c_i\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x)=\mathbf0
 \ \text{ at every sampled site }\mathbf x\Bigr\},
 \label{eqn:depth_positivity_kernel}
\end{equation}
the sitewise coefficient nullspace of~\cref{eqn:exact_dntk_rank}. Consequently
clause (iii) of~\Cref{def:depth_row_regularity} holds with some $\lambda_0>0$
exactly when every local family
$\{\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x):i\in I_{\mathbf x}\}$ is linearly independent, at
every depth.
<!-- end conjecture-2 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:depth_positivity_criterion}
\Citet{Du2019b} certify positivity of their limiting Gram matrix for value
rows, for an analytic nonpolynomial activation, under the hypothesis that no
two training inputs are parallel. That is the wrong criterion for PINN rows.
\Cref{prop:limiting_ntk_rank} makes positivity a \emph{sitewise coefficient
rank} condition, as in~\cref{eqn:exact_dntk_rank}: site geometry is neither
necessary nor sufficient for degeneracy. It is not necessary: a row with
$\mathbf b_i(\mathbf x_i)=\mathbf0$ has $P_i(\theta)=0$ for every $\theta$,
hence gives $\mathbf K(\theta)$ a zero row, however well separated the sites
are (\Cref{sec:prior_work_comparison}). It is not sufficient, and two worked
examples place the obstruction in the coefficients instead:
\Cref{ex:shared_point_rank_obstruction} exhibits two rows at one shared site
that are singular for one choice of operator coefficients and positive definite
for another, and~\Cref{ex:vector_coupling_rank_obstruction} exhibits three
coupled vector rows at a single site with
$\nabla_\theta P_3=\nabla_\theta P_1+\nabla_\theta P_2$. The second example
transfers to depth unconditionally, and it is worth isolating what it proves:
an exact linear dependence among the loss-scaled rows \emph{as functionals of}
$\mathbf u$ is an identity in $\theta$, so the associated null direction lies
in $\ker\mathbf K(\theta)$ at every width, every depth, every architecture and
every iterate, and no input-separation hypothesis can repair it.
\Cref{conj:depth_positivity_criterion} asserts that the positive direction
transfers as well. Its restriction of $l_\star$ to $\{H,H+1\}$ is not a
convenience: by the discussion after~\cref{eqn:depth_schur_product} these are
the only blocks that are, conditionally on the layers below, averages over the
units of one layer of i.i.d.\ terms, hence the only blocks for which the conditional-independence route to the finite-width concentration of clause~(iv) is available. The restriction concerns that concentration, not the existence of a limit: for value rows and Gaussian initialization, the layerwise induction by which~\citet{Jacot2018} identify the deep NTK yields the sequential infinite-width limit of every block, but it supplies no finite-width rate. Of the two, $l_\star=H+1$ is the more
convenient, for the reason the two-layer certificates use
$\mathbf K^\infty_{\mathrm{out}}$: the output block's Jacobian involves only
the order-$r_{\max}$ jet of the layer-$H$ features, so the criterion is again a
statement about the span of a feature family evaluated against the rows. The
gap is precise. The two-layer proof separates features by analyticity in the
parameters of a \emph{single} neuron together with
$\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{supp}\mu_h)\neq\varnothing$; at depth the layer-$H$ feature
is a composition whose law is determined by the layers below, and that
propagated law is controlled in the depth literature only through moments.
For Gaussian initialization, positivity at pairwise-distinct sites is
nevertheless known at every depth: \citet{Carvalho2025} prove the
value-observation NTK strictly positive definite at distinct inputs with bias,
and at nonzero, pairwise nonproportional inputs without it, for continuous,
almost everywhere differentiable, nonpolynomial activations;
\citet[Theorem~2]{Jin2026} prove the infinite-width covariance and DNTK
positive definite for $\gamma>0$, smooth nonpolynomial or RePU $\sigma$, and
one linear differential row per site whose coefficients do not all vanish
there; and~\citet{Du2019b} certify their last-hidden-layer block for analytic
nonpolynomial activations under non-parallel inputs in the bias-free scaling.
None of these treats the compactly supported laws
of~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} or co-located and coupled rows, and we therefore
regard~\Cref{conj:depth_positivity_criterion} as open for $H\geq2$, even at
$r_{\max}=0$; at $H=1$ it holds with $l_\star=2$,
by~\cref{eqn:exact_output_dntk_nullspace}.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:depth_literature}
For an ordinary supervised loss at differential order zero an analogue of the depth-$H$
program has been carried out, but only under Gaussian initialization, in bias-free parameterizations and under input-separation hypotheses; for~\Cref{def:depth_h_network} its positivity step remains open even at $r_{\max}=0$, as~\Cref{rem:depth_positivity_criterion} records. \Citet{Du2019b} prove global linear convergence of
gradient descent for deep fully connected networks, ResNets and convolutional
ResNets on the squared loss over value observations, in a bias-free
parameterization with a uniform hidden width $m$, standard Gaussian
initialization, normalized inputs $\|\mathbf x_i\|_2=1$, targets $|y_i|=O(1)$,
and an activation that is Lipschitz with a Lipschitz derivative, their guiding
example being softplus and their positivity proposition additionally requiring
analyticity and nonpolynomiality. They use exactly the layerwise decomposition
of~\Cref{lem:layerwise_decomposition}, work with the block of the last hidden
layer, localize by the averaged Frobenius norm
$m^{-1/2}\|\mathbf W^{[l]}_{(k)}-\mathbf W^{[l]}_{(0)}\|_F$ rather than by a
per-neuron tube, and require for the fully connected architecture a width
$m=\Omega\bigl(2^{O(H)}\max\{n^4\lambda_{\min}^{-4},\,n\delta^{-1},\,
n^2\lambda_{\min}^{-2}\log(Hn/\delta)\}\bigr)$ and a step size
$\eta=O\bigl(\lambda_{\min}2^{-O(H)}n^{-2}\bigr)$, where, in their notation, $n$ is the sample size (our $N$) and
$\lambda_{\min}$ is the least eigenvalue of their limiting Gram matrix of the
weights of the last hidden layer, the analogue of $\mathbf K^{[H],\infty}$ and
not of the output block $\mathbf K^{[H+1],\infty}$; they attribute the exponential factor to the instability of the fully
connected architecture, which in their analysis amplifies perturbations
through the layers both at initialization and during training, and reduce it
to $\mathrm{poly}(H)$ by the residual scaling.
\Citet{AllenZhu2019} and~\citet{Zou2020} prove convergence for deep ReLU
networks under separation conditions on the training inputs, each training a proper subset of the layers (the output layer is held fixed) from a He-type Gaussian initialization, with width and iteration count polynomial in the depth already for fully connected networks. For ReLU at that initialization the fully connected architecture therefore does not by itself force the $2^{O(H)}$ of~\citet{Du2019b}, as their own discussion anticipates; the two settings are not directly comparable (ReLU and input separation versus a smooth analytic activation and $\lambda_{\min}$), and since ReLU violates clause $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{reg}}$ these rates do not decide the sharpness question of~\Cref{rem:depth_faa_di_bruno}. Both results are again for an
ordinary empirical loss. \Citet{Jacot2018} and~\citet{Lee2019} identify and
freeze the deep NTK in the infinite-width limit, once more for value
observations. None of these results covers a row of positive differential
order, and none supplies the jet structure described
below~\cref{eqn:depth_schur_product}. On the PINN side, \citet{Wang2022}
write the finite-width joint residual--boundary NTK for an arbitrary
architecture but prove its infinite-width limit and its constancy along
gradient flow only for a one-hidden-layer network on a one-dimensional
Poisson problem (the constancy only on a finite horizon $[0,T]$ and under assumed width-uniform bounds on the parameters and on the time-integrated residuals along the flow), and note that multiple hidden layers are not covered by
their theory. At depth, \citet[Theorem~2]{Jin2026} prove, for standard-Gaussian parameters, a positive bias scale and sequentially infinite widths, that the limiting output covariance and DNTK are positive definite at pairwise-distinct sites carrying one nonzero linear differential row each. This is the Gaussian analogue of clause~(iii) of~\Cref{def:depth_row_regularity} at the output layer, in their parameterization with an output bias; it does not reach the compactly supported laws or the repeated sites of~\Cref{conj:depth_positivity_criterion}, and it is not a training statement. The depth-$H$ training statement we are aware of assumes
what~\Cref{def:depth_row_regularity} makes explicit rather than proving it:
\citet{Gan2025} prove uniform convergence in
probability of the operator-transformed kernel for a deep bias-free network
with a single fixed linear differential operator and state a training theorem
that assumes limiting-Gram positivity and uniform gradient continuity. The
kernel-convergence question for general, possibly nonlinear operators is
studied by~\citet{Zhou2024}, but for two-layer pointwise PINNs under a width
scaling $d_1^{-\varrho}$, so that result is not a depth-$H$ statement either. We are
aware of no finite-width discrete-gradient-descent guarantee for depth-$H$
PINNs with joint residual and boundary rows of arbitrary fixed order; that is
what proofs
of~\Cref{conj:depth_jacobian_constants,conj:depth_positivity_criterion},
together with~\Cref{prop:depth_h_substitution}, would deliver for centered
output weights, clause (v) then following from clause (i)
(\Cref{sec:depth_conjectural}).
<!-- end remark-17 -->
